title: Broncos vs. Chiefs: 3 Players to Watch in Week 8
summary: The Denver Broncos host the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday. It’s a shot for Denver to earn their fourth straight victory. Even better, the Broncos can be the top team in the AFC West by beating the Chiefs. In order to make that happen, these three players will have to perform at a high level. […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 11: Alex Singleton #49 of the Denver Broncos reacts after a fumble recovery during the fourth quarter of the game against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos host the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday. It’s a shot for Denver to earn their fourth straight victory. Even better, the Broncos can be the top team in the AFC West by beating the Chiefs. In order to make that happen, these three players will have to perform at a high level. Bo Nix — Quarterback One good performance can be a catalyst and confidence boost for players hoping to get things going in the right direction. It wasn’t perfect by any means, but quarterback Bo Nix’s outing versus the Arizona Cardinals had quite a few bright spots. It also answered a few lingering questions Broncos Country and many analysts. The concerns on Nix’s ability to run should be put to bed after his transcendent 62-yard touchdown gallop. What I liked even more was his aggressiveness and willingness to throw the ball down the field. Nix was able to make some tight down the field throws against Cover 2 shells and delivered a handful of impressive throws on middle of the field concepts. Those splash plays were hard to come by in prior games. Steve Spagnuolo’s defense has been one of the best in the NFL to start the season. Even though their top two corners from last season are playing elsewhere, their passing defense has still been stellar. They’ve done a good job limiting explosive plays and keeping most top targets from doing much damage through the air. Nix and the Broncos’ aerial attack had just 115 passing yards in Week 1. That won’t be good enough to earn a victory on Sunday, so improvement will be necessary. Keep in mind, the Chiefs have forced ten turnovers in six games, with two in four contests—including two against the Broncos on Monday Night Football . Nix will need to find a way to be effective and not turn the ball over. Alex Singleton — Linebacker Alex Singleton’s Week 1 outing against the Chiefs was a big disappointment. Though it’s safe to say Singleton has really turned things around since then. In fact, this last three game stretch might be the best Broncos Country has seen from Singleton donning orange and blue. Against the Cardinals, Singleton was a heat-seeking missile. He notched an incredible 19 tackles and came away with several quarterback pressures and a key sack. That earned him AFC Defensive Player of the Week honors. Running back Kenneth Walker has been an explosive playmaker for the Chiefs. He is the engine that makes their offense go and certainly one of the NFL’s premier offensive weapons. Everyone knows limiting his impact is a big key to the game. Walker was absolutely dominant in Kansas City’s Week 1 pummeling of the Broncos. However, the Seattle Seahawks found a way to shut last year’s Super Bowl MVP in their Week 7 win over the Chiefs. He can be stopped. This time around, I’m optimistic Singleton and the Broncos’ defense will execute far better this time around and slow down Kansas City’s rushing attack. Jonah Coleman — Running Back As the Broncos gear up for the second half stretch of the season, establishing a formidable rushing attack will be critical. Last week against the Cardinals, the Broncos put together their best run game performance of the season. Rookie running back Jonah Coleman was a big part of that and was productive with his touches. After the game, Head Coach Sean Payton vowed to get Coleman more touches moving forward. That seems like a good bet with RJ Harvey’s status versus the Chiefs in doubt . I expect this to be a tough and gritty matchup with both teams trying to dictate the pace of the game on the ground. Denver’s offense has struggled to convert third downs all season long. There is no simple fix to that issue. However, I believe getting quality yards on early downs would certainly help. They have been in far too many third-and-long situations. Head Coach Sean Payton has been insistent trying to rectify the Broncos’ first down passing woes since he took over playcalling duties. This Sunday, I’d like to see a little more emphasis running consistently on first down—especially early on in games. Coleman has performed well that regard in limited playing time. He is averaging 4.7 yards per carry on first downs. He’s also more effective than J.K. Dobbins on second down rushes. I’d like to see Denver showcase the rookie running back against the Chiefs. It’s a big opportunity for him to show he should be leading the Broncos’ rushing group moving forward.

title: Future Broncos: A 2027 NFL Mock Draft for Denver
summary: Happy Halloween, Broncos Country. The end of October is here, and the halfway point of college football season is upon us. That makes it the right time to do my annual Mocktober installment for my Future Broncos series. The Broncos are projected to have nine picks in the 2027 NFL Draft. It’s expected they will […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - OCTOBER 29: Denver Broncos mascot Miles performs in an inflatable halloween costume during a game between the Kansas City Chiefs and the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on October 29, 2023 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Happy Halloween, Broncos Country. The end of October is here, and the halfway point of college football season is upon us. That makes it the right time to do my annual Mocktober installment for my Future Broncos series. The Broncos are projected to have nine picks in the 2027 NFL Draft. It’s expected they will earn a fourth-round compensatory pick for John Franklin-Myers. Additionally, they’ll receive a seventh-round pick from the Saints to finalize the Devaughn Vele trade. Based on their current record and strength of schedule, the Broncos are slated to pick 27th next April. This is sort of no man’s land for picking in the first round. I used Pro Football Network’s mock draft simulator to help with the exercise, used their consensus board for player rankings, and adhered to their trade calculator. And yes—I did make two big trades to get playmakers for Denver. 27th Overall, First Round — Carter Smith, OT — Indiana I’ve discussed several first-round options for the Broncos in earlier segments such as Ole Miss defensive tackle Will Echoles, Oregon tight end Jamari Johnson, Minnesota offensive lineman Greg Johnson, and Georgia linebacker Chris Cole. None of them were available when I was on the clock. That being said, I still view offensive line as a premier need for Denver. Garett Bolles and Mike McGlinchey won’t be around forever. Plus, the Broncos could use more talent across the board. This pick might probably will come off as a mild reach to a lot of folks, but Indiana offensive tackle Carter Smith would be a good selection for the Broncos. I think he is a prospect who will gain a lot of steam leading up to April. Smith (6’5”, 310 pounds) has manned down the Hoosiers left tackle position since 2023. Playing over 3,000 snaps, he boasts a lot of experience and will finish his decorated collegiate career with over 50 starts at the position. His coaches laud him for his leadership and toughness. Moreover, the tape shows a player who is disciplined and is great at pass protection and run blocking. The big question surrounding Smith, as well as some other top offensive linemen in this year’s class, is if they have the requisite length to stick at tackle instead of moving to the outside. That doesn’t concern me too much, because his technique is outstanding. Head Coach Sean Payton has continuously stated he values experience and positional versatility when scouting offensive lineman. Smith checks all those boxes and gives the Broncos a potential high-end starter at multiple positions. What’s not to like? 47th Overall, Second Round — Luke Reynolds, Tight End — Virginia Tech It wouldn’t be a fun Halloween mock draft without projecting the trade. In this scenario, I have Denver sending their second-round selection (#59), their fourth-round compensatory pick for Franklin-Myers (#135), and a future fourth-round pick in 2028 to the Dallas Cowboys. It seems like a logical move, since the Cowboys could use a little bit more draft capital. Finding an impact tight end is a big desire for Broncos Country. A player I discussed early on in the process was Virginia Tech tight end Luke Reynolds. I predicted back in September he would gain steam and wind up being a Top 50 selection. I still think that happens. The junior standout has continued to play at a high level. He now has 50 catches, 493 receiving yards, and 6 touchdowns in eight games for the Hokies. Overall, Reynolds is well-rounded player that can make a difference inline a run blocker and be versatile and legitimate threat in Denver’s passing game. Last year, over half a dozen went off on the board during Day 2. If Denver wants to upgrade the position via the draft, they’ll have to make a move early on to get one of the best prospects. I think sending off a few extra Day 3 picks to snag a prospect of Reynolds’ caliber would be well worth it. 60th Overall, Second Round — Reed Harris, WR — Arizona State Now, the fun is just getting started. Perhaps you think it’s not realistic to see Denver be big time draft day movers up the board twice on Day 2. After all, Denver has maneuvered down the board recently. They basically had to since they’ve been without first round picks for three of five seasons and needed to recoup ammo. That’s all fine and dandy, but let’s face it—finding a potential replacement for Courtland Sutton has to be on their radar. He hasn’t made much of a difference this year at all. Moreover, he carries a substantial cap hit next season. Though that’s not the only reason they should make an early investment at the position. Jaylen Waddle hasn’t made a big impact in his first season with the team. Unfortunately, Pat Bryant has been injured, Marvin Mims Jr. is a free agent, and next year is the last of Troy Franklin’s rookie contract. I have no doubt the Broncos’ brass will be looking to add more weapons to improve their offensive production. They need a needle mover at the position. For this trade, I sent #92 in the third round, #162 in the fifth round, a 2028 third-round pick to snag #60 from the Cleveland Browns. That’s a big price to pay, but to target a player who is a favorite fit of mine for Denver, I felt it was worth it. Earlier this month, I highlighted Arizona State wide receiver Reed Harris. He has continued to impress since then and now has 47 catches for a conference leading 800 receiving yards and 8 touchdowns. Harris is coming off a 6 catch, 147-yard performance against Kansas State last Saturday. There’s no doubt #3 is easily one of the best contested catch and deep ball receivers in this year’s draft. He lines up with Payton’s size desires (6’5”, 220 pounds) and would give Denver a dynamic threat who could help them out immediately as a rookie. Quite honestly, he likely won’t be on the board late in the second round. But for the purposes of this exercise, I had to pounce when I saw he was still available. Three picks in, three long-term issues addressed on offense which has been Denver’s biggest issue in 2026. Day 3 Selections 128th Overall, Fourth Round: Jyaire Hill, CB — Michigan Hill has been a mainstay in the Wolverines secondary the past three seasons and a productive player. In over thirty games as a starter, the senior standout has 112 tackles, 11 tackles for loss, 2 sacks, and 3 interceptions. I was surprised he was ranked so lowly on their board. He’s got good size (6’2″, 190 pounds) and covers well from both man and zone. I think he’s a good fit for Vance Joseph’s defense with true boundary potential. Adding to the secondary makes sense with a lot of starting players with their contracts running out in the next two seasons. 208th Overall, Sixth Round: Drayk Bowen, LB — Notre Dame Bowen has been a productive starting linebacker for the Fighting Irish. He has played in 47 games and notched 197 tackles, 10 tackles for loss, and 4.5 sacks to date. He won’t be a premier playmaker in coverage, but his high football IQ, toughness in run support, and special team’s ability would make him a valuable addition to Denver’s linebacking corps. He reminds me quite a bit of Josey Jewell. 229th Overall, Seventh Round (via New Orleans): Sheridan Wilson, C — Texas Tech Wilson is a fifth-year senior who has started at the pivot for the Red Raiders since 2024. He will finish his collegiate career with nearly 3,000 snaps. As noted earlier, Payton values experience and Wilson has a lot of it. He is also regarded as one of the best pass blocking centers in this year’s class. With Alex Forsyth in the last year of his contract and Luke Wattenberg’s up-and-down play, finding a developmental prospect at center would be wise for the Broncos. 245th Overall, Seventh Round:…

title: Broncos vs Chiefs 5 questions: How does the Seattle loss impact KC?
summary: Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs were riding high. Just about everyone was twitterpated that the Chiefs were undefeated and “back.” Then Mahomes and Kansas City got curbstomped by the Seattle Seahawks. Now what? How is Chiefs Kingdom feeling after the first six games of the season? And how does the Seattle game weigh […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 25: Derick Hall #58 of the Seattle Seahawks forces Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs to fumble during the third quarter at Lumen Field on October 25, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs were riding high. Just about everyone was twitterpated that the Chiefs were undefeated and “back.” Then Mahomes and Kansas City got curbstomped by the Seattle Seahawks. Now what? How is Chiefs Kingdom feeling after the first six games of the season? And how does the Seattle game weigh into that? Kansas City looks to get back on track this Sunday against the Denver Broncos, who get a shot at revenge from Week 1. To get some answers, we go “behind enemy lines” with Maurice Elston from Arrowhead Pride . MHR: How is Chiefs Kingdom feeling after the first six games of the season? How does the game in Seattle weigh into that? Maurice : Chiefs Kingdom gets very antsy after losses like the one we saw in Seattle. The fan base can turn quickly. Kansas City went from 5-0 and looking Super Bowl-bound to the sky falling overnight. Suddenly, every offseason decision Brett Veach made is being questioned, the coaches have failed to develop the receivers, and every weakness on the roster is supposedly fatal. If I had to put a number on it, I would say 80% of Chiefs Kingdom panicked after that loss. The other 20% understands that it is still the NFL, where any team can lose if it comes out flat against a quality opponent. Seattle punched Kansas City in the mouth, and the Chiefs never really responded. Sometimes a team needs a game like that to wake it up and expose the holes that might have been hidden by winning. It gives the coaches an opportunity to identify the problems and make the necessary adjustments. Even if the Chiefs do not win Sunday, a competitive performance that shows Seattle was an outlier would reassure the fan base. However, another flat performance would turn some of the normal frustration into legitimate concern. MHR: What is the consensus on Patrick Mahomes coming back from his knee injury? What is he doing well? Where is he struggling? Maurice : I think Mahomes has shown that the knee is healed enough for him to play his game. He does not look afraid to move around the pocket, escape pressure, or take off when an opportunity presents itself. Through six games, he has completed 64.9% of his passes for 1,474 yards, nine touchdowns, and four interceptions. He has also played well from under center and within the play-action passing game Kansas City has built around Kenneth Walker III. When the protection holds up, and Mahomes trusts what is around him, he still looks capable of taking over a game. However, I do not believe he is completely back to 100% yet. From the eye test, his full speed and explosiveness have not entirely returned. There are plays where the old Mahomes might have escaped, but he cannot quite get away now. The knee also appears to remain in the back of his mind, which is understandable after such a serious injury. He has done a good job avoiding unnecessary hits, which is exactly what you want from your franchise quarterback. At the same time, playing behind two backup offensive tackles against Seattle made him look uncomfortable and antsy in the pocket. His recovery has progressed well, but the combination of lingering physical limitations and inconsistent protection has prevented him from completely returning to his old form. MHR: How does Kansas City get the win on Sunday? What must the Chiefs do offensively and defensively? Maurice : Offensively, the Chiefs need to return to what worked in Week 1: lean on Kenneth Walker III. Denver has an excellent defense overall, but it has been vulnerable against the run. The Broncos are allowing 133.3 rushing yards per game and 4.57 yards per carry. Walker ran for 173 yards against them in the season opener. Kansas City must remain patient with the running game, even if Walker does not find immediate success. The Chiefs abandoned the run too quickly in Seattle after falling behind. They need to put Mahomes under center, make Denver respect Walker, and use play action to slow down the Broncos’ pass rush. Defensively, the Chiefs need to stop Denver’s running game and force Bo Nix to carry the offense. I do not consider Nix an elite quarterback, but he has a knack for making significant plays at important moments. His 62-yard touchdown run against Arizona is a perfect example. Kansas City must rush with discipline, keep Nix inside the pocket, and consider using a spy in situations where he is likely to scramble. Steve Spagnuolo should also give him disguised coverages that force him to process after the snap. In Week 1, Kansas City pressured Nix on more than half of his dropbacks. He completed only four of 13 passes for 11 yards and an interception when pressured. If the Chiefs can contain his mobility and make him consistently beat them from the pocket, I like their chances. MHR: What do you make of the current spread? What is your best bet for Sunday’s game? Maurice : The Chiefs are currently 1.5-point road favorites, with the moneyline sitting around -118. I think that is a fair spread for a divisional game between two teams separated by only half a game in the AFC West. The fact that Kansas City remains favored on the road after its performance in Seattle—and with Denver riding a three-game winning streak—shows how much confidence the market still has in Mahomes and Andy Reid responding after a loss. My best bet is Chiefs -1.5. If you want the safer option and do not care about laying a little extra juice, I also like Kansas City on the moneyline at -118. My predicted score has the Chiefs winning by seven, so both plays fit how I expect the game to unfold. The total is 40.5, and my score prediction lands at 41 points, so I would stay away from that number. MHR: How does this game unfold on Sunday? What is your prediction? Maurice : This game will be much closer than the 31-10 result we saw in Week 1. I do not expect a blowout in either direction. I think it becomes a physical divisional fight that remains close entering the fourth quarter. Walker should have another productive game, although the Chiefs may have to remain patient if Denver slows him down early. Andy Reid cannot abandon the run at the first sign of trouble. Sticking with Walker will create play-action opportunities and make life easier for Mahomes. You rarely see Mahomes play as poorly as he did in Seattle, and you almost never see him produce two performances like that in consecutive weeks. I expect him to rebound, while Reid simplifies the offense and gets him into a better rhythm. Jaylon Moore’s potential return at right tackle would also be significant because it would provide more stability in pass protection. If the game is close late, I trust Mahomes to make the decisive plays. With Kansas City at 5-1 and Denver at 5-2, this is an important early battle for control of the AFC West. I expect the Chiefs to respond to the Seattle loss and leave Denver with a hard-earned victory. Chiefs 24, Broncos 17.
author: Ian St. Clair

title: RJ Harvey’s knee injury is not believed to be serious
summary: The Denver Broncos ruled running back RJ Harvey out for their game against the Kansas City Chiefs, but with no word or comment on the severity of the knee injury he seemingly suffered in practice this week. A source told The Denver post that the injury does not appear to be serious: It really stinks […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 15: RJ Harvey #12 of the Denver Broncos celebrates with Quinn Meinerz #77 after scoring a touchdown against the Seattle Seahawks during the second quarter of the game at Empower Field At Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Andrew Wevers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos ruled running back RJ Harvey out for their game against the Kansas City Chiefs, but with no word or comment on the severity of the knee injury he seemingly suffered in practice this week. A source told The Denver post that the injury does not appear to be serious: RJ Harvey’s injury is not believed to be severe or hold him out long term, a source told @denverpost Harvey was ruled out by the #broncos for Sunday’s game vs. Chiefs, but encouraging news for the 2nd-year RB. pic.twitter.com/L50Cj7Z5TS — Sam Jane (@sam_jane230) October 30, 2026 It really stinks that Denver won’t have him in the biggest regular season game of the season so far, but at least the injury doesn’t appear to be serious. They are two games away from the Bye Week, so maybe putting him into rehab mode for a return after the bye would make the most sense. The Broncos need some juice in the run game now, though, so maybe its time to find out if Jonah Coleman is the dude. Broncos daily recap Vance Joseph emphasizes the importance of limiting Kenneth Walker’s impact Slowing down running back Kenneth Walker will be mission critical for the Denver Broncos to defeat the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday. “This one is important to us:” Broncos ready for another shot at KC The Broncos know what’s at stake when they face Kansas City again, and Bo Nix made it clear this is one Denver wants. Potent quotables Sean Payton Opening statement “Final day here. Any questions?” On managing RB J.K. Dobbins’ workload throughout the season “I think one of the challenges sometimes with three back is it’s much easier with two to get the balance. He’s doing well. It’s a deep room. I like the way they’re playing in general. So with him, his numbers have peaked. There are certain times when you look at this analytical data we have now that you can see burst and speed. So we like the depth there.” On RB RJ Harvey’s status “No status right now.” On if he talks with players about sharing opportunities “Yes, a lot. Each one’s different, but you’re always when you’re installing plays, there’s certain—you’re wanting to make sure there are these targets that they see in the plan. It’s important. Then even after the game, there are times where maybe that a certain player didn’t get some of the looks that we were hoping, but you’re always paying attention to that.” On if a player having a ‘hot hand’ influences opportunities during the flow of a game “There’s a little bit of that. It’s easier to have that at running back than some of your receiver sets. Yes, there’s a little bit of that.” On adjusting the game plan in real time “I think it’s within the framework of a game plan, there are certain things that are more specific to receivers and tight ends that maybe are a little bit more flexible at running back.” On the qualities that make him comfortable with K Wil Lutz “There’s a consistency. He’s made a lot of big kicks. Earlier in the week, [G] Ben Powers was celebrating a 30th birthday. I asked our guys, ‘Give me the playoff experience.’ Starting with Ben, six years, and [DT] D.J. [Jones], six playoff years. Then I think it went to ‘Huf’ (S Talanoa Hufanga), seven, and [T Mike] McGlinchey. Then it kept climbing up, and Lutz was at 10. So some of those big moments and having been in that position, that matters.” On originally bringing K Wil Lutz to New Orleans “It was that old message, ‘Pay attention.’. In training camp, often times guys lock in on the depth chart. What they don’t understand is they’re competing against everyone in the league at that position. So we had a kicking battle. Every day in the media, it was who made what, both of those guys back and forth. Then we brought Wil in after the final cut and had a workout. We signed him, and then released both the other two kickers. There would be just an example of that. So I think as a player, it can be very easy to just narrow in on the depth chart when you can’t possibly understand the depth chart around the league.” On the keys to sustained success in red-zone defense “I think the first thing is you have to be able to stop the run. Most teams that are playing well offensively in the red zone have a little bit more efficiency in the run game. I think what’s really important is that four-point play. When you get to a third down in the red zone, understanding you can get off the field, that’s a big deal.” On what he likes about the jumbo formation “I think it is game dependent. It’s a great question. I think that it depends on some weeks, like last week if you’re putting a game plan together and let’s say there’s a play you like against their base defense, well you want to make sure you get their base defense. One way to do that is to put the jumbo in. Another way is to put your true full[back]. So sometimes if you’re putting something in that is designed for the base defensive structure, you want to make sure that… Today we’re getting all these defenses now can play like a sub-Buffalo. So last week was one of those games where there were certain things we wanted to do against the base, and we wanted to ensure that we were getting that.” On using an offensive formation to dictate the defensive personnel on the field “If we’re going to put a game plan together, and let’s say we’re going to discuss six runs that we want against their base defense. I’ll always say, ‘Well, how do we make sure.’ If we put ‘Traut’ (TE Adam Trautman) and [TE] Evan [Engram] in the game, we may very well get a sub defense to that. So if we’re going to design something for base, we want to make sure that we’re getting it. That’s one example.” On the message to the team that this is a big game, but they will play in bigger ones “I think that’s right. I think everyone understands it’s a divisional game. Here it is on the schedule. We’ve done a good job just compartmentalizing. Way back when, you put the season into quarters. We don’t do that. I know who we play this week, next week. Then there’s a bye. Then after that… It’s a divisional game, and those are important. That’s what it is.” On why he stopped dividing the season into quarters “I don’t know that I ever really, maybe a year or two. I can’t think of the exact. I just know that I didn’t like the idea of saying, ‘We’re going to finish 3-1 in each quarter.’ What if we want to win 14 in a row? You know what I mean. So that’s probably one of the reasons.” On the importance of stopping the run against the Chiefs “The big point [Defensive Coordinator] Vance [Joseph] made all week was our pursuit to the ball, hats to the ball. The pursuit to the football, you never know when you’re that important guy. Seattle did a good job of populating the football against a really good runner and a really good run offense. So I think the first thing you start with is, ‘All of us are playing with clean eyes and pursuing to the ball, effort to the ball.’ It’s something that I know he feels like we can do a better job of compared to Week 1.” On if he doesn’t have to overemphasize messages to the team this week since they experienced Week 1 “Yes, no question. In other words, these guys are grown men. They recognize the things we didn’t do well, offensively, defensively.” On if he thought Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes’ career would play out like this “You go through all these drafts. You can never project… If I felt like this was going to be the end product, we would’ve gotten to [No.] 1 [overall pick]—whatever it took. (Laughs) That’s the tricky thing about the draft.” On if he thinks he got the pre-draft evaluation right on Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes “You’re really looking at these pods of players. title: Vance Joseph emphasizes the importance of limiting Kenneth Walker’s impact
summary: The Denver Broncos and Kansas City Chiefs square off in one of the most anticipated Week 8 matchups on Sunday. Nearing the halfway point of the regular season, this rivalry battle will have significant implications in a tough AFC playoff race. It’s certainly a winnable game for the Broncos who are riding the highs of […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - SEPTEMBER 29: Defensive coordinator Vance Joseph of the Denver Broncos walks on the field before a game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Empower Field at Mile High on September 29, 2025 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos and Kansas City Chiefs square off in one of the most anticipated Week 8 matchups on Sunday. Nearing the halfway point of the regular season, this rivalry battle will have significant implications in a tough AFC playoff race . It’s certainly a winnable game for the Broncos who are riding the highs of a three-game winning streak. However, they’ll need to play much better this time around in one particular area to have a shot at notching their sixth victory of the season—stopping the run. In the Broncos’ Week 1 loss to the Chiefs on Monday Night Football , their defensive performance was disastrous. They failed to contain running back Kenneth Walker who had one of the best games of his career in his debut for Kansas City. Last year’s Super Bowl MVP scampered for 173 rushing yards with 1 touchdown. He added three receptions for 18 receiving yards and a score through the air. As Denver finalizes their preparations for their biggest game of the season, they know that limiting Walker’s impact is going to be an absolute must to achieve victory. Yesterday after practice, Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph “Absolutely, he’s going to make guys miss. No different than a scrambling quarterback, you can contain a guy for 20-30 plays, but it’s going to be two players where he gets out. So we need hats to the ball,” stated Joseph. “That’s where the effort part comes in. He’s going to make guys miss. It’s going to be some misses, but the effort to the ball to limit the big plays is key playing this back.” Walker has proven to be one of the most explosive playmakers in the NFL this season. He boasts four multi-touchdown performances and four games with at least 135 all-purpose yards. In six matchups, he touts 817 yards from scrimmage and is on pace to shatter career best marks in virtually every category. In 2024 and 2025, the Broncos’ defense ranked Top 5 in most metrics against the run. This season, they have taken drastic step back. They’ve allowed more explosive plays than usual, the fifth-most yards, and nearly 4.6 yards per carry to the opposition . Missed tackles have been a common issue throughout the season and a primary culprit in their regression. That was quite evident in Denver’s Week 1 loss to Kansas City. The Broncos’ defense posted an alarming 30-percent missed tackle rate in primetime. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, that outing allowed the most yards on missed tackles in NFL history , as well as the third-most missed tackles ever recorded in a game with 28. Whether it’s poor technique or bad angles, those woes can’t rear their heads on Sunday if Denver wants to beat their long-time rival. Denver’s defense has played well in their current three-game winning streak. On Sunday, every player needs to execute at a high level from the trenches all the way back to the secondary. There is no doubt Walker has been on a tear to start the season. At times, he has looked superhuman on the gridiron. Nevertheless, the Seattle Seahawks were able to stop him in his tracks last weekend. Can the Broncos do the same? We’re fixing to find out.

full_text: WELCOME TO MOVEMBER! It’s time for our sixth annual Movember Charity Drive, where we raise money for charity for the entire month of November. In addition to raising money, we’ll also be giving away prizes, running an auction, and doing a bunch of silly and humiliating stuff over on our YouTube and Twitch live streams. Here’s everything you need to know about our 2026 Pride of Detroit Movember Charity Drive. Charities (two this year!) For the third straight year, we are again raising funds for the University of Michigan Health Rogel Cancer Center , specifically for their Men’s Cancer Research Fund. Voted the highest rated center for cancer care in Michigan by the U.S. News & World Report’s Best Hospital rankings, the Rogel Center is at the cutting edge of both cancer treatment and research. Donations collected through our fundraiser will go directly toward supporting groundbreaking research, raising awareness, and providing critical resources to patients in need. We are also representing a second charity, with fundraising happening exclusively through our auction. That charity is the House of Providence , Michigan-based intervention program that aides in helping kids in foster care with educational programs and other support systems until they can find a forever home. How to donate through our campaign If you want to donate to our campaign for the Rogel Cancer Center: Simple! Just head to our donation page here. To support our charity drive for the House of Providence, check out our auction section here (more information below). Direct donations to the House of Providence are always very appreciated, but those will not go towards our final total, as we have no way to track them. Donation rewards After Movember is over, I will email donors who have reached this level of donation (it can be through multiple donations, as long as they’re made under the same name/email ), and if you qualify, you can cash in for the following rewards: $100 — Subscription to POD Direct into preseason 2027 (If you’re already a subscriber, you can gift it!) $250 — Cameo-type personalized video of your choosing $500 (new this year!) — Private group Q&A with Erik and Jeremy $750 (new this year!) — POD 2028 calendar (more info below) $1,000 — Be a guest on the PODcast Donation incentives There are also individual rewards you can earn with a single donation. To redeem a donation incentive, please make sure to list your choice in your donation message. Here are the individual rewards you can earn automatically by donating (can only choose one with each donation): $25— Write word/short phrase on podcaster’s face $50— Mute podcast host of your choice for 1 minute $100— Change Jeremy’s green screen background $300 — Egg smashed on someone’s head $500 — Host will do a celebrity impression for at least 30 seconds (must be appropriate) Auction items Our auction is going to be a little different than in previous years, but way bigger and way better. Our friends at Encore Legacy Auctions are handling the auction this year, and they have HUNDREDS of items for several different sports teams available. Five percent of the winning bids will go to the House of Providence. In addition , we’ll have several Pride of Detroit exclusive items where 100% of the proceeds will go to House of Providence . That includes some experience-based auction items, including: Grab a drink with Jeremy and Erik Play a round of disc golf with Jeremy Have a virtual NFL Draft prospect film watching session with Erik We’ll also have some Detroit Lions swag that will be added to the auction later this month. Donation goals Last year, we raised over $32,000. This year, we’ve got loftier goals and even better incentives along the way. Here’s what will happen if we collectively hit some milestones: $5,000 — Activates PODcast host punishment by Lions (see below) $10,000 — POD team runs a 5k $15,000 — POD staff has to reveal high school photos $20,000 — JCPenney-style photoshoot, resulting in a POD calendar (available for $750 donation) $25,000 — POD team does public karaoke of Toto’s “Africa” $30,000 — Jeremy learns and records a TikTok dance $35,000 — Jeremy reveals a comedy sketch from his past $40,000 — Jeremy gets frosted tips, a la Skyler Gill-Howard $45,000 — Ryan reveals college poetry $50,000 — Erik watches a 15-minute Aaron Rodgers highlight reel with “I <3 Aaron” shirt $60,000 — Jeremy dresses up like Marilyn Monroe $75,000 — Jeremy will grow out his hair for an entire year Once we hit $5,000, it will activate a new challenge that we will try to accomplish at the end of the month, based on how the Detroit Lions perform in the entire month of November (five games). Here’s how it works: For Jeremy: For every 15+ yard pass interference penalty in a Lions game, Jeremy will do 10 pushups For Ryan: For every Jared Goff TD, Ryan will review a track from Kid Rock’s new album and post it For Meko: For every Sione Vaki gain of 10+ yards, Meko will run a mile Wheel of pain For every $1,000 that we raise, we’ll spin what we endearingly call the Wheel of Pain. Here’s what last year’s wheel looked like. We’ll have some new stuff this year: Wheel of EXTREME PAIN For every $10,000 we raise, we’ll spin a wheel of MORE EXTREME versions of our Wheel of Pain. Current options: Smelling salts Fart spray in face Sour pickle balls Spicy gummy bears While not necessary, I would highly recommend donating and redeeming the above rewards while we’re live on Twitch or YouTube . Here’s when we’re live: Monday nights after the game (ETA 6-8 p.m. ET) — sometimes Sunday nights Tuesday afternoons or nights for the mailbag podcast Saturday mornings for our Madden Sims (10-11:30 a.m. ET) Marathon stream! Our Movember campaign will end with a 16-hour marathon stream from 8 a.m. ET to midnight with special guests throughout the day. Previous guests have included: ESPN’s Mina Kimes ESPN’s Ben Solak Detroit Football Network’s Justin Rogers Detroit Free Press’ Dave Birkett The Athletic’s Colton Pouncy MLive’s Ben Raven Detroit News’ Nolan Bianchi Former Lions offensive tackle Lomas Brown (part of the Lions Ring of Honor) Former Lions safety Glover Quin Former Lions wide receiver Herman Moore Lions play-by-play radio announcer Dan Miller The date for the final marathon stream is Saturday, November 28. Donations will be accepted through the end of the month. If you have any questions about our campaign, feel free to comment below or reach out to me via Twitter. NOW GET DONATING!

title: Minnesota Vikings vs. Detroit Lions preview: 5 small weaknesses in Vikings defense
summary: Riding a two-game winning streak, the Detroit Lions have a massive home-field opportunity to knock the NFL’s last remaining undefeated team off its warship throne, move within striking distance of first place in the NFC North, and exact revenge for last year’s two defeats to the Vikings, both highly uncharacteristic of the team’s identity under […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 02: Detroit Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (14) leaps high for a catch during the Detroit Lions versus the Minnesota Vikings game on Sunday November 2, 2025 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Riding a two-game winning streak, the Detroit Lions have a massive home-field opportunity to knock the NFL’s last remaining undefeated team off its warship throne, move within striking distance of first place in the NFC North, and exact revenge for last year’s two defeats to the Vikings, both highly uncharacteristic of the team’s identity under Dan Campbell. Prior to last season, Campbell had won five straight games against Kevin O’Connell, including four in a row with Brian Flores as defensive coordinator. The Lions’ quest to regain the throne of the North will ride on the shoulders of their All-Pro-caliber backfield duo of Jared Goff and Jahmyr Gibbs, and an offense facing a Vikings defense under Flores that is off to a historically lethal start, pillaging opponents on its way to a 6-0 record (11 wins straight dating back to last season). With the stakes incredibly high for Halloween weekend, this week’s preview dives into the cranium of Detroit’s Megamind, Drew Petzing, as he squares off against not just Flores but his former quarterback, Kyler Murray. We’ll examine how the Lions’ offense can keep the monsters from underneath their bed. Note: Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics are sourced from NFL Pro, FTN Fantasy, Pro Football Reference, SumerSports, or Pro Football Focus. The Trojan Norse The Minnesota Vikings’ pass defense, with its 70.0%+ blitz rate, has been nightmare fuel for opposing quarterbacks. They lead the league in EPA/dropback allowed (-0.323), success rate allowed (38.2%), sack rate (10.1%), and pressure rate (38.6%). The Vikings’ unpredictable, overwhelming, exotic blitzes have tricked offenses so thoroughly that teams are frightened to run play-action passes, worried that quarterbacks momentarily turning their backs to the defense to sell the run fake could hinder their processing and lead to immediate negative plays. Teams are averaging only a 19.3% play-action pass rate against Minnesota (31st), totaling just 40 such dropbacks. The Packers had 10 play-action dropbacks in Week 1 against the Vikings, and no offense has exceeded that total in a game since. The Saints and Colts combined for only six play-action dropbacks over the last two weeks. Meanwhile, the Lions’ offense ranks fourth this season with a 33.3% play-action pass rate and has recorded at least 11 such dropbacks in every game. Against play-action passes this season, the Vikings’ defense is allowing 7.9 yards per attempt (19th), +0.003 EPA/dropback (12th), a 48.3% success rate (11th), and a staggering 13.8% explosive pass rate (27th). The inherent risk of turning your back to Minnesota’s defense and becoming the Headless Hurler is still real, as the Vikings have recorded a 16.2% sack rate (1st) and 48.6% pressure rate (1st) against play-action dropbacks. The Vikings haven’t quite been tested against play action this season, with their matchup against the Bears coming in a monsoon, hardly a fair test of their passing attack. They’ll also face the Bills next week, an offense with the league’s second-highest play-action rate. While Minnesota remains formidable against play action, particularly with its ability to generate pressure and sacks, its defense ranks outside the top 10 in several metrics. It hasn’t been nearly as historically dominant against play action as it has against the run and on traditional dropbacks. As Petzing illuminated last week, and as Lions fans have witnessed for years, Jared Goff is a different breed of beast as a precision processor when it comes to play-action passing . Detroit’s offensive line is also above average in pass protection, with room to improve as its younger players develop and the heady Cade Mays continues acclimating at the pivot. Now it’s a matter of proving they aren’t afraid of the dark when facing Minnesota’s pressure packages and are willing to challenge the Vikings with the play-action passing game that has been a staple of Detroit’s offense. The Devil’s in the Dropback Continuing on the topic of counterpunches to the Vikings flooding pass-rush lanes with second-level defenders such as Eric Wilson, Blake Cashman, the immortal Harrison Smith, and Josh Metellus. There’s another potential wrinkle for Detroit’s offense. It’s not often the Vikings are forced to defend straight dropbacks from under center. No team really is in this era of the NFL, but the Lions could be equipped to do it. The Lions are averaging only 1.8 such dropbacks per game this season, but Jared Goff has completed 6-of-9 passes (66.7% completion percentage, 6th) for 84 yards (9.3 yards per attempt, 3rd) and two touchdowns (t-2nd). Detroit also ranks in the top 10 in success rate and explosive pass rate on under-center straight dropbacks, while its 4.7 yards after catch per attempt ranks fourth. They do need to be careful, however, as they’ve allowed a 40.0% quarterback pressure rate (7th) and one sack on these plays. Luckily, straight dropbacks from under center have helped disarm the Vikings a bit. Flores’ furious, fully fanged forces have faced 15 under-center, non-play-action dropbacks this season (10th), allowing opponents to complete 9-of-14 passes (64.3% completion percentage, 6th) for 132 yards (9.4 yards per attempt)—nearly a first down per pass attempt, albeit on a small sample size! Minnesota also ranks in the bottom 10 in success rate and explosive pass rate allowed on these plays. Perhaps most surprisingly, they’ve generated pressure on just 13.3% of those dropbacks (t-27th). The real treat is that the Vikings’ defense is allowing a league-worst 6.4 yards after catch per attempt on such passes. Perhaps all those aggressive, mugged-up looks at the line of scrimmage are proving hazardous, with defenders scrambling to get into coverage position after the snap and missing tackles. This preview is about finding the small levers the Lions’ offense can pull against the most dangerous defense in the league. The Vikings’ pass defense feels inevitable. Stay on the field long enough, and they’ll get you. They’ll force you into mistakes. Just like with play-action passes, straight dropbacks from under center offer a small avenue to exploit Minnesota’s aggression, get its defenders on their heels, and produce chunk plays. It’s an opportunity to move downfield quickly, catch Flores’ defense with its pants down, and get the ball into the hands of Detroit’s best playmakers with room to operate. Ragnarök Meets Rah Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown can be a ghoul to opposing defenses. It’s part of why he’s a three-time consecutive All-Pro, and his hands, toughness, and consistency have helped him slay the Vikings in the past. Over his last six games against the Vikings, St. Brown has averaged 10.8 targets, 8.3 receptions, 100.7 receiving yards, 0.5 touchdowns, and 5.1 first downs per game. That production is more menacingly consistent than Michael Myers terrorizing Haddonfield, Illinois. And as much as everyone loves Dr. Loomis, Flores might as well be playing his role, desperately trying and repeatedly failing to contain the Michael Myers of Detroit’s offense. Against the blitz this season, St. Brown has recorded 25 targets, 16 receptions, 204 receiving yards, three touchdowns, and 70 yards after catch. All five rank in the top 10 among wide receivers against the blitz. He’s been a ball magnet for Jared Goff when defenses bring extra rushers. Last season, St. Brown was targeted 61 times against the blitz, hauling in 39 receptions (2nd) for 593 receiving yards (2nd), four touchdowns, and 329 yards after catch (1st). The Sun God has been Detroit’s secret weapon against the blitzkrieg. As a secondary sidekick, while Sam LaPorta hasn’t experienced…

title: Lions, Vikings Week 8 injury designations: Kerby Joseph OUT, starting CB questionable
summary: The Detroit Lions (4-2) and Minnesota Vikings (6-0) have declared their injury designations ahead of their Week 8 matchup at Ford Field, and as most expected, Lions All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph has been ruled out because he isn’t quite ready for game action. Additionally, Lions’ starting corner Roger McCreary was added to the injury report […]
full_text: Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph (31) practices during OTAs at Detroit Lions headquarters and training facility in Allen Park on Thursday, May 30, 2024. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (4-2) and Minnesota Vikings (6-0) have declared their injury designations ahead of their Week 8 matchup at Ford Field, and as most expected, Lions All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph has been ruled out because he isn’t quite ready for game action. Additionally, Lions’ starting corner Roger McCreary was added to the injury report on Friday and is listed as questionable. Let’s take a look at Friday’s injury report and get you up to date with what we know. Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded . Ruled OUT S Kerby Joseph (Knee, PUP) — Days remaining in injury evaluation clock: 18 Joseph returned to practice on Wednesday and has slowly been acclimating back to football activities, sticking to individual and group drills over the first few practices. “He’s done a good job,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said at his Friday press conference. “It’s good so far. Now there again, we haven’t taken any team reps. It’s all been individual and group. But he’s handled that well. That was kind of the point. We just progress him slowly here, work him in. We get him a little bit more today of that type of work. Plus, we surplus after the fact. We still do some rehabilitation, get him some of those miles that he’s not getting right now that he normally gets; the running, the volume. And then next week we’ll have him in real practice. So he’ll do the (individual drills) and all that. That’ll be the plan.” While Joseph was not present during the portion of Friday’s practice made available to the media, Detroit News’ Nolan Bianchi later clarified that Joseph was initially working in another area and joined his teammates later in practice . It’s also worth noting that Joseph was spotted wearing a compression sleeve on his knee, but Campbell noted those are often used to prevent or minimize swelling and reminded folks that Joseph is still in the “infant stages” of this acclimation process. Questionable CB Roger McCreary (foot) — added to the injury report on Friday McCreary was added to the injury report on Friday, and it’s unclear when his injury occurred. With so little information, we will have to wait for the team to announce any further updates between this report and game time. If McCreary can’t play, look for Ennis Rakestraw to get the start at outside corner. Not listed with an injury designation RB Jahmyr Gibbs (shoulder) RB Jacob Saylors (neck) WR Amon-Ra St. Brown (ankle) OT Penei Sewell (rest) DT Alim McNeill (rest) DT Tyleik Williams (illness) EDGE Aidan Hutchinson (rest) EDGE DJ Wonnum (rest) CB Ennis Rakestraw (ankle) All players in this section were limited or did not practice earlier in the week but returned to full practices Thursday and Friday—save Rakestraw—and do not require an injury designation for Sunday’s game. They’re good to go. Rakestraw was limited most of the week, but it looks like he will play this weekend. He’s become an integral part of the Lions defensive back rotation, operating as CB3 and taking on starting outside corner responsibilities the majority of the time the Lions are in subpackage sets. full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 22: Kerby Joseph #31 of the Detroit Lions reacts during an NFL football game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on September 22, 2025 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph has had an extremely long road to get back on the field after suffering a knee injury that caused him to miss most of the 2025 season. Over a year after his last game appearance, Joseph made his first practice appearance this week. And on Friday, after two days of work on the field, Joseph spoke with the media for a brief three minutes. “Nostalgic, man. Nostalgic, brah. Just being back out feels nostalgic, man,” Joseph said about his first practices of the season. Joseph was absent from the media availability portion of Friday’s practice, and while he didn’t provide any insight into why he took the day off, he insisted he was still putting in plenty of work behind the scenes, and that sometimes he works “in silence.” Detroit News reporter Nolan Bianchi later confirmed that Joseph did indeed attend practice, joining the team after the media viewing window closed . It’s obviously been a tough journey for Joseph. While he wasn’t ready to detail all the treatments and steps it took for him to get back on the field— he directed reporters to his YouTube page , where he’ll “tell y’all everything you need to know”—he did talk about some of the emotional journey. “I know how to keep my head in focus, man. I just have to get on my knees and pray. You know what I’m saying?” Joseph said. “There’s going to be ups and downs in this league. I’m known that from rookie year. (It’s been) a roller coaster, especially with this knee. Man, I’m praying more for the ups than downs. If I go down, I know the only way is up.” Joseph didn’t provide a timeline for his return, just noting that he is “ Zuper eager” to get back on the field and he’ll take the field when God wants him to be on the field. But he did offer a warning. “I haven’t practiced in a long time, so this week felt pretty good being out there. I’m still him. I hope y’all ain’t forget. I’m still him.” Coach Dan Campbell provided a bit of a clearer map for recovery. “We just kind of progress him slowly here, work him in. We get him a little bit more today of that type of work. Plus, we surplus after the fact,” Campbell said. “We still do some rehabilitation, get him some of those miles that he’s not getting right now that he normally gets, the running, the volume. And then next week we’ll have him in real practice. So, he’ll sort of do the indi(viduals) and all that. That’ll be the plan.” With Joseph’s 21-day window open, the Lions can activate him to the 53-man roster at any point. That won’t happen this week against the Vikings, but Detroit will have to make a determination on Joseph’s status by November 18, prior to their Week 11 game against the Buccaneers.

title: Dan Campbell gives injury update on Isiah Pacheco, Kerby Joseph
summary: This offseason, the Detroit Lions signed Isiah Pacheco to contend for the team’s RB2 spot after trading David Montgomery to the Houston Texans. Unfortunately, Pacheco dealt with a MCL injury in training camp and while rehabbing, he suffered a more serious back injury that required surgery. The latest we heard was that it was a […]
full_text: ALLEN PARK, MICHIGAN - JULY 29: Isiah Pacheco #10 of the Detroit Lions runs during Detroit Lions Training Camp at Detroit Lions Meijer Performance Center on July 29, 2026 in Allen Park, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images This offseason, the Detroit Lions signed Isiah Pacheco to contend for the team’s RB2 spot after trading David Montgomery to the Houston Texans. Unfortunately, Pacheco dealt with a MCL injury in training camp and while rehabbing, he suffered a more serious back injury that required surgery. The latest we heard was that it was a 12-week injury and Pacheco could return by December . On Friday, coach Dan Campbell offered an update. “He’s progressing well,” Campbell said. “Yeah, I do think there’s a chance we could get him back in late December, mid-December maybe. There’s a chance here.” Campbell praised the work Pacheco has been putting in for rehab. “He’s put a tremendous amount of work in, and he’s doing pretty good,” Campbell said. “…Pacheco is—you go back there, and he’s ready to go, man. It’s just a matter of letting it continue to heal, but he’s doing a good job.” Campbell also provided an update on Kerby Joseph, who returned to practice this week. Campbell noted that Joseph has responded well to the work in practice, but that they haven’t started to work him into team drills yet. “He’s done a good job,” Campbell said. “It’s good so far. Now there again, we haven’t taken any team reps. It’s all been individual and group. But he’s handled that well.” The plan is to progress him slowly, get him some after-practice cardio that he’s not getting in practice, and work him into more team drills next week. Campbell didn’t outright say it, but the heavy implication is that Joseph will be out for this week against the Vikings. Joseph was wearing a compression sleeve on Thursday after not wearing one on Wednesday, but Campbell noted not to read into that. “Any way you can reduce any swelling that could be or minimize it, you’re always going to do that with anything: elbow, shoulder, people coming of an injury,” Campbell said. “So that’s not—Like i said, we’re in the infant stage of this. It’s been positive to this date. So that’s the best way to say that.” UPDATE: Joseph was not at practice on Friday, but here’s the full quote from Campbell before practice on the plan for him: “He’s done a good job. It’s good so far. Now there again, we haven’t taken any team reps. It’s all been individual and group. But he’s handled that well. That was kind of the point. We just progress him slowly here, work him in. We get him a little bit more today of that type of work. Plus, we surplus after the fact. We still do some rehabilitation, get him some of those miles that he’s not getting right now that he normally gets; the running, the volume. And then next week we’ll have him in real practice. So he’ll do the (individual drills) and all that. That’ll be the plan.” UPDATE 2: Apparently, Joseph did practice, after the media was no longer present: Received clarification on this: Joseph was only absent during the portion of practice that was accessible to the media. He came out later in the session — Nolan Bianchi (@nolanbianchi) October 30, 2026 Short updates on LB Devin White, S Thomas Harper In the middle of his update on Pacheco, Campbell gave an unprompted update on linebacker Devin White, who suffered a broken forearm three weeks ago that is believed to have needed surgery. White was in the locker room this week without anything protective on his arm, and Campbell noted he’s progressing well. “Devin White’s doing pretty good, too,” Campbell said. White must miss three more games before he’s eligible to return to practice, meaning the earliest he could play is Week 11 vs. the Buccaneers. Campbell was also asked about reserve safety Thomas Harper, who landed on injured reserve after suffering an ankle injury against the Buffalo Bills in Week 2. Harper is now eligible to return to practice, and Campbell indicated he’s close to healthy enough to play. “He’s doing pretty good,” Campbell said. “If we need him or (he was) on call, I think he’s close to being ready to go.” Unfortunately for Harper, it sounds like the Lions may put his return on hold a bit. Campbell seemed to indicate that they are happy with the current status of the safety room—with Brian Branch’s return to the lineup last week and Kerby Joseph’s return to practice this week, along with Chuck Clark and Keith Abney filling out the room. If the Lions chose to return him to practice, they’d only have three weeks to either place him on the 53-man roster or place him on injured reserve. Campbell indicated they don’t want to start that clock yet, because they could hit the end of that 21-day period and still not need him on the roster. “It’s just a matter of you got who you’ve got, and (if) you start that (evaluation) clock and then you keep going here a little bit and you don’t need him, then you’ve got to IR him or you’ve got to—so we’re just kind of playing it safe. But he’s physically doing well,” Campbell said.

title: NFL predictions: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Vikings in Week 8
summary: The Detroit Lions (4-2) and Minnesota Vikings (6-0) will meet in Week 8 in an NFC North divisional clash. The Vikings are the last remaining undefeated team in the NFL, and while their defense is playing at an elite level, they’ve yet to face an offense like the Lions, making this a fantastic strength-on-strength showdown. […]
full_text: Jan 5, 2025; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs (26) runs with the ball in front of Minnesota Vikings safety Camryn Bynum (24) and scores a touchdown during the second half at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: David Reginek-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Detroit Lions (4-2) and Minnesota Vikings (6-0) will meet in Week 8 in an NFC North divisional clash. The Vikings are the last remaining undefeated team in the NFL, and while their defense is playing at an elite level, they’ve yet to face an offense like the Lions, making this a fantastic strength-on-strength showdown. “Minnesota is playing outstanding football,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said earlier in the week. “(Head coach) Kevin (O’Connell)‘s doing a hell of a job. (Defensive coordinator) Brian (Flores) is doing a hell of a job. This thing, they play very complementary football. […] I’ve got a lot of respect for this team, the way they play, but we’re looking forward to this; this will be good.” Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Vikings in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint. This week’s prediction preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook , who currently have the Lions listed at +1800 to win this year’s Super Bowl and are currently 3.5-point favorites in Week 8 . Viking s base scheme For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 8 preview: Breaking down the Vikings’ offensive and defensive schemes . Prediction 1: Counter creativity with creativity The Vikings enter this game undefeated, but outside of their NFC North games against the Packers and Bears, their opponents have been bottom-of-the-league teams, totaling seven wins and 20 losses combined. Now, they’re headed into the toughest part of their schedule, beginning with the Lions’ elite offense—the first top-10 DVOA offense they’ve faced this season. The Vikings’ success is built almost entirely on their defense, which ranks in the top 10 in virtually every meaningful defensive statistic and is top one or two in most of them. Over six games, they’ve suffocated teams with their aggressiveness (their 69% blitz rate is over 20% higher than the next-closest team), and with a veteran unit that returns most of its starters, they rarely make mistakes. I go into more detail in my breakdown of the Vikings defense in the article link above, but at their core, the Vikings are so problematic because of their creative blitzing and quarters zone coverage. On most traditional downs, the Vikings will deploy a base 3-4 defense and line up seven or eight defenders in the box and then “double mug” blitz them, meaning bring an overloaded pressure on a single side of the offensive line or straight up the middle (double A-gap). The goal is to disguise where the blitz will come from and gain an extra blitzer in one area, while unexpectedly dropping players into coverage in the opposite area. The Vikings are so efficient at disguising their intentions and getting to the quarterback quickly that they lead the NFL in pressures on 49% of pass-rushing attempts, 21 sacks, and a 10% sack rate. While the Vikings are operating at a scary level, it’s not a defense that is unfamiliar to the Lions and quarterback Jared Goff. In previous seasons, Goff has done well to manage the blitz, especially when he has a healthy offensive line. In games where Goff has succeeded, he’s found creative ways to offset the Vikings’ creativity, and his ability to stay calm under duress— he’s currently the best quarterback in the NFL vs. the blitz, with an EPA of 0.32 —has led to success in the six games this season. Here’s an excerpt from NextGenStats’ game insights: “Jared Goff has been sacked once and completed 15 of 19 passes for 162 yards and three touchdowns across 20 max blitzes faced this season (i.e., 6 or more pass rushers), resulting in a career-high 78.9% completion percentage. [….] Goff has faced a max blitz on at least six dropbacks in each of his past six meetings with the Vikings during the Brian Flores era dating back to 2023, a threshold he has reached in just three of 51 other games played over that span.” In recent weeks, purposefully or not, we’ve already seen the Lions testing some concepts to beat an overloaded blitz. Concepts like spreading out five wide, or shifting a tight end into the backfield in a fullback role, will help the Lions offense create quick outlets or adjust their protection. The Lions have also sprinkled in some 21 personnel (two running backs and one tight end), where Sione Vaki stays in to protect, allowing Jahmyr Gibbs to be an outlet for Goff’s passing game. While the Lions will need to be creative with their running backs and tight ends, their receivers will likely help Goff produce downfield. Last week, we saw the Lions deploy Amon-Ra St. Brown more on the outside, and he caught seven of his nine targets for 109 yards against the Packers. Expect more of that in this game, as the Lions will want to get St. Brown isolated vs. the Vikings’ zone, giving him more space to operate. Also, it wouldn’t be surprising to see them give St. Brown some choice routes, where he can adjust the depth based on who the Vikings blitz. As NextGenStats also pointed out, the Lions have also found a separation advantage by lining up St.Brown and Jameson Williams on the same side of the formation: “The Lions’ passing offense has been more explosive when they align to the same side through seven weeks, as they have averaged 8.0 yards per play with a 18.3% explosive-play rate on those snaps.” By pairing them, Williams can stretch the zone deep and force the defensive backs to adjust to his speed, opening things underneath for St. Brown. If the defense takes the underneath route, then they’ll have to try and stick with Williams one-on-one deep. With the Vikings’ philosophy of limiting explosive plays, look for the Lions to stress their zone and take what they have underneath. The Lions offense vs. the Vikings defense may be the NFL’s premier matchup this week. Prediction 2: Pin-and-pull The Lions won’t be able to rely only on their passing attack in this game; they’ll also need to get their rushing attack going. Detroit tends to lean on its outside zone blocking scheme, but it’ll also need to be creative and unpredictable by incorporating other concepts it’s had success with. The chart below (adapted from NFL writer Ray Carpenter ’s design) shows the EPA from the Lions rushing offense when running in specific directions vs. the Vikings’ EPA in defending those running plays. No surprise, the Lions are finding most of their rushing success behind left tackle Penei Sewell, and it lines up with where the Vikings have been weakest. But the Lions won’t simply want to run behind their All-Pro all game; they’ll need to get creative too. With the Vikings lining up so many defenders on the line of scrimmage, the Lions will want to attack those edges, and the pin-and-pull concept can cool off some of Minnesota’s aggressiveness. Let’s look at the final offensive play from the Packers game to see an ideal example of the Lions deploying a pin-and-pull concept to get outside leverage and open a massive rushing lane for Jahmyr Gibbs. On this third-and-6 play, the Lions run a toss-left to Gibbs with the tight end (Sam LaPorta) and wide receiver (Isaac TeSlaa) cracking down (“pin”) on the Packers’ two outside edge players. In concert with the “pin,” the Lions “pull” Sewell and left guard Christian Mahogany under and outside left to get out in front of Gibbs. Additionally, the Lions put St. Brown in motion, and he seals the opposite edge of the hole by blocking the corner. Here’s the pre-snap look with the blocking assignments in red: And now the results after the snap with the “pin” circled and the pull in solid red arrows: Prediction 3: Put Vikings offense behind the sticks While the Vikings defense has played lights out,…

title: Which NFL Week 8 game are you most looking forward to?
summary: I think this every year, but the 2026 NFL season feels like it is flying by. Despite October almost being over, it feels like everything just got underway a few weeks ago. With that said, I doubt many of the players feel that way. After all, the regular season is a grind that players and […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - DECEMBER 26: Jarran Reed #90 of the Seattle Seahawks sacks Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears during the third quarter at Soldier Field on December 26, 2024 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images I think this every year, but the 2026 NFL season feels like it is flying by. Despite October almost being over, it feels like everything just got underway a few weeks ago. With that said, I doubt many of the players feel that way. After all, the regular season is a grind that players and coaches often refer to as a marathon, as opposed to an all-out sprint. Filled with peaks and valleys, veteran teams learn not to ride the waves. Just try your best to keep stacking wins as you head into the holiday months. That is where we find the Detroit Lions in their Week 8 matchup against the Minnesota Vikings. After securing their first divisional win against the Green Bay Packers in Week 7, they will be looking to improve to 2-0 in the division, and 5-2 overall on the year. If you are looking for a fresh take on that game, be sure to check out Anthony Balaj’s three key matchups article. I know a lot of fans enjoy the Lions being in primetime windows, or even the 4 p.m. ET slot like they were against Green Bay. Still, there is something nice about the Lions’ game against Minnesota being at 1 p.m. ET. If you are at home, you can simply flip the channel to the next game. For me, I have about a 15-minute drive before I can be on my couch for the afternoon slate of games. That brings us to our question of the day—which game other than the Lions vs. Vikings are you most looking forward to in Week 8? My answer: I am going with the “Monday Night Football” game between the Chicago Bears and the defending Super Bowl Champion Seattle Seahawks. The Bears are riding high right now, currently firmly in the mix for what is looking like it will be an ultra-competitive NFC North race. Seattle got out of the gates a bit slow, but with that defense, it’s tough to ever count them out. What about you? Which game other than the Lions are you most looking forward to in Week 8? Let us know in the comments below.

title: Detroit Lions vs. Minnesota Vikings preview, prediction: On Paper
summary: The Detroit Lions have a chance to take down the undefeated Minnesota Vikings and make a statement in a very competitive NFC North. But the Vikings and their historic defense won’t make it easy for Detroit. Let’s take a closer look at the matchup with our Lions vs. Vikings preview and prediction. It’s On Paper […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 02: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions directs his team in the second quarter against the Minnesota Vikings in the game at Ford Field on November 02, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions have a chance to take down the undefeated Minnesota Vikings and make a statement in a very competitive NFC North. But the Vikings and their historic defense won’t make it easy for Detroit. Let’s take a closer look at the matchup with our Lions vs. Vikings preview and prediction. It’s On Paper time. Lions pass offense (9th) vs. Vikings pass defense (1st) The Lions’ pass offense is coming off perhaps its most impressive performance. The Packers pass defense was the best they’ve played against so far, and they posted an impressive 119.7 passer rating and a really good 57.1% dropback success rate (sixth best of the week). For the season, they continue to establish themselves as a top-five unit in the NFL. They rank: First in passer rating (112.5) Fifth in yards per attempt (8.0) Second in dropback EPA (0.309) Fourth in dropback success rate (51.8%) The only reason they may be dragging behind in DVOA is strength (or lack of strength) of opponent. The Saints, Bills, Jets, and Cardinals all rank 20th or worse in pass defense DVOA. But last week’s performance against the Packers certainly helps Detroit’s case. In terms of pass protection, it’s been great news for Detroit. They rank second in PFF pass blocking grade (82.1), seventh in ESPN’s pass block win rate (55%), fifth in pressure percentage allowed (30.8%), and 11th in sack rate (5.1%). Obviously, this week, the key is how they manage the blitz. And they’ve been phenomenal thus far. Against the blitz, the Lions rank: Fifth in pressure percentage (35.1%) First in EPA/pass (+0.25) Eighth in sack percentage (5.4%) This will be a challenge for Minnesota. But, of course, the Vikings defense is their best unit on the team, particularly against the pass. Not a single quarterback has averaged a passer rating over 90 against the Vikings, and only Jordan Love managed over 200 net passing yards. Now, it’s worth clocking how bad the passing offenses the Vikings have faced off against. By DVOA, the best passing offense they’ve faced is Chicago (12th), but that game was played in a monsoon. Here’s where the rest of the teams rank: Packers (18), Bucs (25), Dolphins (26), Saints (24), Colts (31). Still, the Vikings aren’t just beating up bad teams, they’re destroying them. For the season, the Vikings rank: First in passer rating allowed (61.7) Fourth in yards per attempt (6.1) First in dropback EPA (-0.226) First in dropback success rate (35.5%) Obviously, their pass rush is what really kills teams. Their ridiculous 68.4% blitz rate is 26.1% higher than any other team, and it has resulted in the top pressure rate (48.8%) and sack rate (10%) in the NFL. Player to watch: LB Blake Cashman. I believe Cashman should be in the running for Defensive Player of the Year. Cashman does everything for the Vikings defense, including blitzing (4.5 sacks), coverage (five passes defended), and being a menace in the run game (six tackles for loss). He has PFF’s second-highest grade among linebackers (86.2) with ridiculous grades in pass rush (86.2, 3rd), coverage (75.1, 9th) and run defense (70.9, 25th). Advantage: Draw. This is a top-five unit vs. the top unit in the NFL. But the Vikings have yet to be tested like Detroit will test them, and the Lions are coming off a strong performance against what was the No. 2 pass defense in the NFL last week. This one can truly go either way. Lions run offense (14th) vs. Vikings run defense (9th) The Lions run game has been a statistical enigma this year. The inconsistencies are both hard to watch and tough to comprehend. On a play-by-play basis, the Lions remain a pretty damn good running game. They rank: 15th in yards per carry (4.2) 19th in rush EPA (-0.108) Third in success rate (46.9%) The high success rate and mediocre EPA/YPC usually suggests a lack of explosive plays, and that is true to some degree. The Lions are 10th in amount of 10-yard rushes (21), but they have just two rushes of 20+ yards (only two teams have fewer). But the bigger concern is the high percentage of negative plays. Detroit’s “stuffed” rate (0 or negative yardage runs) is 20.9%, the third highest in the league. To be producing the third-highest success rate but also the third-highest stuffed rate is literal insanity. It speaks to how good the run game is outside of these negative plays, but the lapses in blocking are frustrating and really throws the Lions’ offense off-balance. One answer to the problem could be rushing in lighter formations, as Detroit gets less and less efficient with the more tight ends they put out there: You're definitely onto something. Lions' EPA/rush by formation: 11 personnel: 0.06 (10th) 12 personnel: -0.07 (17th) 13 personnel: -0.48 (28th) (via @SumerSports ) https://t.co/rUOeIW00VF — Jeremy Reisman (@DetroitOnLion) October 29, 2026 Despite the inconsistencies, the Lions run blocking does seem to be very good. They rank fifth in PFF run blocking grade (73.2), fourth in adjusted line yards, and 20th in ESPN run block win rate. Minnesota has given up a few big days on the ground this year, but they’ve also faced some of the best rushing attacks in football (and two of the worst). Overall, they’re still among the best in the league: 21st in yards per carry allowed (4.2) Second in rush EPA (-0.212) First in rushing success rate (31.2%) Unfortunately for Detroit, they are also very good at creating negative plays in the run game. Their 19.1% stuffed rate ranks eighth in the NFL. They’re also stellar in another facet of the run game Detroit struggles at: short-yardage situation. The Lions are converting short-yardage situations just 60% of the time (21st), while the Vikings are allowing a power success rate of only 58% (ninth). Player to watch: Jalen Redmond. The Vikings’ 291-pound defensive tackle is currently PFF’s No. 1 graded interior defender against the run (90.5). He will give the Lions’ guards a handful on Sunday. Advantage: Vikings +1. There’s enough opportunity for the Lions to find some success here, but the inconsistencies are a huge concern right now, and if Detroit continues to allow negative plays in the run game, it will set up nightmare down-and-distances for Jared Goff. Vikings pass offense (27th) vs. Lions pass defense (24th) The Kyler Murray project is off to a slow start. It hasn’t been a disaster—as the Vikings are generally avoiding negative plays (18 sacks, 22nd; two interceptions, t-third)—but the efficiency is quite poor. 15th in passer rating (90.7) 22nd in yards per attempt (6.6) 25th in dropback EPA (-0.029) 30th in success rate (38.6%) It’s hard to pin down exactly where things are going wrong. Obviously, the Vikings have a strong set of receivers in Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison and T.J. Hockenson—Murray’s current favorite target. And while the offensive line isn’t great, the pass blocking statistics are fine: 11th in pressure rate allowed (32.7%), 10th in PFF pass blocking grade, but 30th in sack rate (9.9%). That suggests Murray has been holding onto the ball longer than normal and his 2.91 average seconds to throw (12th) does support that. And while he is certainly capable and willing to evade pressure with his feet, he hasn’t been consistent at it. Ultimately, I think this is just a relatively poor passing attack that doesn’t throw the ball deep often (Murray is 23rd in average depth of target and 15th in deep shot percentage), and hasn’t found its groove. Detroit is slowly climbing out of the basement with their pass defense. For the season they rank: 25th in passer rating (102.2) 17th in yards per attempt (7.3) 28th in dropback EPA (0.242) 28th in dropback success rate (50.0%) But over the last two games, the Lions rank: 15th in passer rating (87.8) 20th in dropback EPA (0.140)…
