title: More women have accused Josh Jacobs of abuse
summary: According to NBC 26, a second woman has accused Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs of abuse, per new records. The woman reported the incident to police in June after Jacobs’ first investigation — which ended with him pleading no contest to abuse and criminal damage to property charges — made news, but stated […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to NBC 26 , a second woman has accused Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs of abuse, per new records. The woman reported the incident to police in June after Jacobs’ first investigation — which ended with him pleading no contest to abuse and criminal damage to property charges — made news, but stated that the incident occurred in January of 2022. Here is what the records state, per NBC 26: According to the records, the woman alleged Jacobs slapped her across the face and later took the her cellphone as she attempted to leave his residence. The woman told investigators that Jacobs grabbed her by the hair, threw her onto a bed, pinned her down and later threw her onto the floor. The woman also alleged Jacobs spit on her and grabbed her by the throat. Jacobs and the victim in his initial abuse case are currently suing the Hobart-Lawrence Police Department , in an attempt to keep some evidence — namely a video of the incident — permanently sealed, based on requested privacy. The NFL has allowed Jacobs to return to the field for the Packers after serving six games on the commissioner exempt list. Still, the league has not ruled on a potential Jacobs suspension — and an active investigation is underway, with the league still interested in the video . Because of his time on the commissioner exempt list, Jacobs’ six weeks there will be considered “time served” whenever a suspension is announced. The league learned the hard way after Ray Rice’s appeal, though, that they only get to make one ruling for one infraction of the personal conduct policy, no matter the public reaction. In this case, the NFL chose to save their one press of the suspension button until more dust has settled. The league has not made a statement on whether they are aware of this second accusation or when they were made aware of the accusation. Currently, Jacobs is on the Packers’ active roster, has not lost any money — as his time on the commissioner exempt list is not equal to a suspension — and he played north of 70 percent of Green Bay’s running back snaps on Thursday Night Football in Week 8 . Update: It appears that there is a third woman who has accused Jacobs of abuse, per NBC 26. Another woman contacted police later that month, telling them that during an argument in April of 2021 Jacobs grabbed her by the arms and bicep area, pushed her against a wall near a window and threw her belongings outside the home. She said she suffered bruising to her arms and pain and swelling in her rib area. The woman told the Hobart/Lawrence police that she called the police at the time. She said she later contacted the unnamed police department and said she was told it was not being investigated as a domestic incident because she and Jacobs were not in a relationship at the time. The records released to NBC 26 say detectives with the Hobart/Lawrence Police Department received records from that call. Those records indicated responding officers observed no visible signs of injury, bruising, or damage consistent with a physical altercation. Update #2: Another incident has been alleged, and NBC 26 has published the video of Jacobs’ arrest: The report later described a phone call with a third woman in July who told Hobart/Lawrence Police that in May 2022 Jacobs placed his hands on her head and neck, dragged her, scratched her chest, and took possession of her cell phone after it fell to the floor. She said she suffered bruising to her arm and scratches to her chest which she said remained visible for about a month, according to the records. The woman told Hobart/Lawrence Police she did not report the incident to police or seek medical treatment at the time. She said Jacobs told her she could be deported, and because of that she did not believe she could report the incident to law enforcement. The report said police were given that woman’s information by the initial victim in the May 2026 case that led to Jacobs’ arrest and conviction.

title: Packers By The Numbers: Stats from the Week 8 win over the Panthers
summary: As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers’ most recent game, courtesy of SumerSports. Today we’re looking at the 27-19 win over the Carolina Panthers in Week 8. First things first: it’s the first time in history the Packers have won a game directly following […]
full_text: Tork Mason/Green Bay Press-Gazette | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers’ most recent game, courtesy of SumerSports . Today we’re looking at the 27-19 win over the Carolina Panthers in Week 8. First things first: it’s the first time in history the Packers have won a game directly following a Brewers World Series victory, so that’s certainly worth celebrating on its own merits (enjoy the parade, everybody). Offense SumerSports does not have this listed, but it is (I believe) the first time in history that a game-clinching catch was made by a receiver who was taken to the hospital mid-game . When you hear things like “that won’t show up in the box score,” I believe this is what they’re talking about. This was a game where I found myself saying, “it certainly looks like Jordan Love has time to throw,” only to check the numbers later and find out that it was not true. On the game, Love averaged 2.32 seconds to throw, 0.39 seconds below the NFL average. When he held onto the ball, it wasn’t necessarily for a long time: his average time to pressure was 2.5 seconds. In part due to the quick time to throw, Love was able to stay relatively pressure-free in this game. Despite the Panthers blitzing on 43.9% of his dropbacks (13.6% above the NFL average), Love was only pressured on 31.7% of his dropbacks (7.3% below the NFL average). That’s a walk in the park compared to what he’s been seeing this year. In this game, Love was actually better against the blitz (+0.38 EPA per Play) than when he wasn’t blitzed (-0.17 EPA per Play). In an inversion from what we’ve been seeing, Love was better on early downs (+0.14 EPA per Play) than he was on late downs (-0.06 EPA per Play). I’m curious if these numbers would look any different if Josh Whyle had stayed in the game, but the personnel mix from the Packers looks similar to how it looked last week. The main difference is that they essentially replaced the 13 personnel usage (1 RB, 3 TE, 1 WR) with 12 (that absolutely feels like it would be different if Whyle had played the full game). The pass rate was high last week (70.8% in Week 7), and I expected that to continue this week. Despite a lackluster run game (again), they were at 61.2% pass rate this week. That holds fairly consistent from quarter-to-quarter. If you strip out the red zone it’s still in that range: they had a 64.3% pass rate outside the red zone this week. Coming into the game, the Panthers’ run defense was much worse than the pass defense, so this feels like a response to that. It didn’t work. The run game was – once again – really bad. They gained 66 yards on 26 attempts (with 40 of those 66 yards coming after contact), for an EPA per Play of -0.12 and a Success Rate of 30.8%. They had a positive EPA when running Man (most likely just Duo), but nothing else touching positive EPA. Basically, good when running Man concepts, fine when running Inside Zone, terrible when trying anything else. Christian Watson had a monster day: 8 catches (on 10 targets) for 113 yards (+0.20 EPA per Reception). His target % in the red zone was 0%, which feels like a problem. If you look at the best red zone scoring offenses, they typically have at least 1 of these 3 things: A quick-twitch running QB A good running game A freak WR Love can move once he starts rolling, but he’s not a quick-twitch running QB. We know they don’t have a run game. Watson fits the bill as a freak WR, and he has had success in this area in the past. I’d like to see some more targets for Watson in this area going forward. Coming into this game, the Packers were scoring TDs on 51.7% of their trips to the red zone, 22nd in the league. It can be tough to score in the red zone, but targeting your tall WR could be a nice place to start. Matthew Golden’s drop monster reared its ugly head again, but he also turned in a very nice day. He’s already a problem for opposing defenses. If he can stop dropping passes every game, he’s going to be an absolute demon. (He didn’t really have drop issues in college so it’s baffling that this keeps happening. I keep waiting for the drops to clean up and they just haven’t yet.) Defense Despite the Panthers only being in 11 personnel on 60% of their offensive snaps, the Packers played Nickel on 72.9% of their defensive snaps. Typically when they play base, they take Javon Bullard off the field and I am not a fan of defensive alignments that don’t have Bullard. I’m curious how much of this is because of Zaire Franklin’s absence. And, if it is, will this approach change when Zaire is back? They’re a better defense with Bullard on the field, so I like seeing numbers like this. I mentioned Love’s time to throw earlier: Bryce Young did not have a much better day. The Packers blitzed on 31.9% of his dropbacks (1.6% above the NFL average) and pressured Young on 51.1% of his dropbacks (12.1% above the NFL average). Young averaged 2.57 seconds to throw and had an ADOT (Average Depth of Target) of 4.6 yards. In other words, he was pressured a lot and was looking to check it down when pressured. When kept clean, Young had an EPA per Play of +0.17. However, when pressured, he dropped to -0.54 EPA per Play. Contributing to that pressure was Dani Dennis-Sutton, whom I love dearly. He posted a team-best pressure rate of 26.3%, with an average time to pressure of 2.11 seconds. After a couple of lackluster weeks, Lukas Van Ness showed up in this game as well. Albums listened to: Sennen – New Quiet ; Fenne Lily – Win Win

title: Packers Winners and Losers: Week 8 vs. the Panthers
summary: On a short week after a disappointing loss, the Green Bay Packers bounced back, defeating the Carolina Panthers on Thursday Night Football, 27-19. Heading into this week, the Packers are sitting in last place in the NFC North, but are still very much in the thick of the Wild Card battle as a member of […]
full_text: (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images On a short week after a disappointing loss, the Green Bay Packers bounced back, defeating the Carolina Panthers on Thursday Night Football , 27-19. Heading into this week, the Packers are sitting in last place in the NFC North, but are still very much in the thick of the Wild Card battle as a member of the toughest division in the league. The Milwaukee Brewers brought some of their championship magic to Lambeau Field on Thursday , and it looks like it rubbed off. Let’s take a look at the best and worst, as the Packers jump to 5-3 on the season. Winner: Tucker Kraft The Packers TE has had an up and down season so far since returning from a torn ACL he sustained in 2025. There have been drops, missed plays, and just an overall sense of hesitation from Kraft, as can be expected from someone returning from such a brutal injury. That being said: he looked pretty great on Thursday. He had the Packers’ first score of the game, an absolute missile from QB Jordan Love. He also caught every single pass which came his way—6 total, for 53 yards. YUP 📺: Prime Video pic.twitter.com/Q5IOsYnPq3 — Green Bay Packers (@packers) October 30, 2026 Winner: Christian Watson Speaking of players returning from brutal injuries. WR Christian Watson went down hard while making a 53-yard catch in the 2nd quarter, was coughing up blood on the sidelines, went to the hospital and…came back into the game, ending the night leading all receivers in receptions and yards. I can’t say I’ve seen anything like this. Watson finished the night catching 8 of 10 targets for 113 yards. 1. Christian Watson picks up a chest injury after completing a 53-yard catch 2. Watson steps into an ambulance and heads to a nearby hospital to get it checked 3. Watson returns from the hospital and is eager to step back onto the pitch. 4. Watson makes a dramatic "WWE-style"… pic.twitter.com/8v8sAOJrWq — EssentiallySports (@ES_sportsnews) October 30, 2026 Winner: Jordan Love Another day at the Do-It-All Factory for QB Jordan Love, another great game with one boneheaded throw . With one receiver in the hospital, another dropping his ~86th touchdown this year, and zero run game, Love still found a way to lead the offense to their 5th win of the season. With the pocket collapsing, it was no problem for him: just throw while you’re on the run. He had some really gorgeous plays on Thursday, once again showing he can fit the ball only where the receiver is able to get it, and overall made some magic out of nothing. Love finished the night 30 for 41 (73%), with 3 TDs, 1 INT, and a 106.6 rating. It’s not outrageous to suggest that the Packers are 0-8 without him at QB, and for that reason, he’s made his way into the MVP conversation (at the bottom of the list, but he’s there!) All 30 completions from Jordan Love? All 30 completions from Jordan Love! pic.twitter.com/YdbD3ohuYC — NFL (@NFL) October 30, 2026 Winner: Ty’Ron Hopper Um, hello???? With Edgerrin Cooper out for the season, and Zaire Franklin inactive, we saw a ton of LB Ty’Ron Hopper on Thursday. He. Looked. GREAT. He had some great stops at the point of catch, preventing plays from extending. He came out of NOWHERE to force a quick Bryce Young throw, and the Panthers were forced to punt. There were some great PBUs. There was an interception. I mean, this guy did everything last night. He finished the night with 8 tackles, 1 sack, 1 INT, 3 PDs, and 2 QB hits. I can’t confirm, but I think it’s probably pretty good when you’re the first Packer since Charles Woodson to record 3 PDs, a sack, and a pick in the same game. Ty'Ron Hopper is having himself a game. He tips and picks the ball. A one man show. pic.twitter.com/MknPkfIwq9 — Lily Zhao (@LilySZhao) October 30, 2026 Loser: Trey Smack The rookie K had another game we’d all like to forget, missing an XP after the Packers scored their first TD of the game. He can no longer be trusted, and as a result, the Packers opted to punt while on the Panthers 37 yard line, instead of attempting a FG. When he finally made his first XP of the night, the crowd pop sounded like the Brewers had won the World Series again. I wouldn’t count on the Packers cutting a guy they traded up to draft this year, but we shouldn’t be surprised if they finally start working out some kickers. Trey Smack DOINKS the extra point off the upright 👀 It remains 6-3, Packers over the Panthers. That was one loud DOINK 😂 (via @NFL ) pic.twitter.com/iS6FNMRCiS https://t.co/ey1cXsBv64 — ClutchPoints (@ClutchPoints) October 30, 2026 Loser: Josh Jacobs The RB finished the day with 1 rushing TD and just 39 yards on 21 carries, a paltry 1.9 average. He caught all 6 targets for 13 receiving yards, and 1 more receiving TD. He also pled no contest to battery in September after a May 2026 incident involving his former girlfriend. ✌️ TDs for Josh Jacobs pic.twitter.com/OsiVzbTbsH — FantasyPros (@FantasyPros) October 30, 2026 The 5-3 Packers have a much needed mini-bye week, and won’t play again until November 8th, when they head to New England to face off against the 4-3 Patriots during the day’s later slate of games. Let’s hope there’s some semblance of a run game, and our kicker’s leg doesn’t fall off.

title: Packers’ running game can’t close out Panthers in win
summary: The Packers had two chances to end the game against the Carolina Panthers and couldn’t close out either opportunity. The first came after the Panthers scored a touchdown (but missed the two-point conversion) to narrow the Packers’ lead to eight points. They kicked the ball back to the Packers with just over 5:30 to go […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 29: Josh Jacobs #8 of the Green Bay Packers runs the ball against Tre'von Moehrig #7 of the Carolina Panthers during the second quarter at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Packers had two chances to end the game against the Carolina Panthers and couldn’t close out either opportunity. The first came after the Panthers scored a touchdown (but missed the two-point conversion) to narrow the Packers’ lead to eight points. They kicked the ball back to the Packers with just over 5:30 to go in the game, and the offense promptly went nowhere. A screen pass to Tucker Kraft on first down was called back. Jordan Love threw incomplete to Matthew Golden on the re-do of first down, and although there was a lot of contact, no flag flew for defensive pass interference. On second down, Josh Jacobs caught a short checkdown pass but went out of bounds, stopping the clock. Then, after a bad snap on third down, Jordan Love was called for an intentional grounding penalty (a completely legit one, too, in a welcome change). Less than a minute had elapsed from the game clock and the Packers hadn’t attempted a run. The Panthers couldn’t generate a game-tying drive, turning the ball over on downs with 2:41 to go. Josh Jacobs scraped out eight yards on two carries, then Christian Watson, broken rib and all, caught a third down pass to convert, forcing the Panthers to burn their final timeout. With 2:28, the Packers just needed one first down to end any chance of the Panthers pulling off something miraculous. Instead, the Packers went the wrong way. Jacobs lost three yards, then gained one total yard back on his next two attempts, forcing the Packers to punt the ball away with about 30 seconds remaining. Carolina had a long way to go and no timeouts to help them, but they were technically in business until a Dani Dennis-Sutton sack put them in an even deeper hole. Their final lateral-heavy play went nowhere, and the game mercifully ended. The questions, however, were just starting. Why couldn’t the Packers close out the game, especially on their second chance? Matt LaFleur didn’t have an answer. “It was disappointing. I would say it’s disappointing,” he said. “Obviously got the one first down, and then we tried to lean on the run game and we went backwards. So that’s an area of emphasis that we have to improve upon because it puts a lot of pressure on your pass game to continue to just find ways to move the ball down the field.” LaFleur is right to focus on the run game. If there’s ever a time when you have to be able to move the ball on the ground, it’s in those crucial close-out drives. Keeping the clock moving while grinding out yards is perhaps the purest form of football; as every coach since the dawn of time has pointed out, as long as you can eke out three yards on every play (cloud of dust optional), your offense is technically unstoppable. You will never run out of downs and you can drain the clock at will. The Packers cannot do that, and Matt LaFleur is obviously frustrated. “We have got to find something that we can hang our hat on in the run game and unfortunately we have not done that yet,” he said. At least his assessment is accurate. As long as the Packers struggle to run the ball, the passing game will have to shoulder more and more of the load. That’s not necessarily a bad thing; Jordan Love has shown he’s more than capable of carrying the load (he’s on pace for career highs in just about every passing stat that matters), but the more you lean on him, the more things can break down. Take Love’s ill-advised interception early in the fourth quarter. Are the Packers taking end zone shots on 3rd and 8 if they thought there was a chance they could set themselves up for a short fourth down run instead? We’ll never know, but it makes you wonder, and the more passing plays you feel like you have to call, the more opportunities arise for one poor decision to result in a turnover. LaFleur doesn’t seem optimistic that things are going to turn around, either. Asked if he was seeing anything that makes him optimistic better rushing days ahead, he was blunt. “I mean, if I’m being honest, not a lot right now. And that’s our job as coaches. We got to figure it out because it’s not good enough.” It certainly isn’t, but at this point any improvement would be a surprise.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: Matt LaFleur explains Packers’ offensive line decisions
summary: Another week, another new offensive line configuration in Green Bay. This time, the Packers had three different starters than in their last game, featuring new or different faces at all three interior line spots. Aaron Banks made his long-awaited (or, perhaps, long-feared, depending on your opinion of Banks) return to his left guard spot, finding […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 29: Head coach Matt LaFleur of the Green Bay Packers runs onto the field prior to an NFL football game against the Carolina Panthers at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Another week, another new offensive line configuration in Green Bay. This time, the Packers had three different starters than in their last game, featuring new or different faces at all three interior line spots. Aaron Banks made his long-awaited (or, perhaps, long-feared, depending on your opinion of Banks) return to his left guard spot, finding his way into the lineup for the first time since he played 22 snaps in Week 2. Laken Tomlinson flipped from left guard to right guard, making his first start on the right side since the Obama administration. And John Williams made his first ever NFL start at the position he played where he played game snaps for the first time ever last week. But, you know, other than that it was basically a normal week up front. Why this configuration, though? John Williams at center makes logical sense; he played there last week and is the only remaining player the Packers seem to like at the spot with Jacob Monk on injured reserve, although Jager Burton may end up there eventually. But at the guard spots, Matt LaFleur offered little explanation for the moves he made. “Well I just think when you look at it, you know, the way Laken’s been playing, you can’t take him out of the lineup. And I thought Aaron Banks coming back…so we went with that route,” he said postgame. “That’s not to take anything away from [Kevin] Zeitler. Certainly we feel good about him as well. But we thought that was the move.” There’s plenty to unpack there, assuming LaFleur is being completely forthright (and that’s a big assumption, given he has no incentive to shoot straight with us). First, LaFleur asserts Tomlinson has been playing well. “Playing well” might be a bridge too far for me, but he’s at least better than Donovan Jennings, Jager Burton, and Jacob Monk, so I’ll concede the point. He’s at least been okay in pass protection (and LaFleur praised the Packers’ pass protection later in his postgame remarks). Second, LaFleur seems to take it as a matter of course that Banks deserves to be in the lineup. But Banks was active last week and didn’t play. Travis Glover started at right guard and Tomlinson was at his familiar left guard spot. The lineup math there would seem to indicate LaFleur thinks Banks is worse than Glover and better than Zeitler (who was inactive against the Lions). And what of Zeitler? The Packers signed him to a one-year, $4.05 million deal on September 30, but he hasn’t been on the field for a single snap on offense so far, though he’s played 15 snaps on special teams. His contract includes heavy playing time incentives and he stands to reap some not-inconsiderable financial rewards if he hits certain playing time thresholds, but it’s hard to believe the Packers would really be pinching pennies that hard. So what gives? Is he not in game shape? Is he really not better than Tomlinson or Banks (or Glover, for that matter)? It’s a mystery, and LaFleur didn’t give us any significant explanations after the Packers’ Thursday night win. In fact,he muddied the waters even further, pointing out when asked that Tomlinson was not getting regular reps at right guard before the Packers installed him there this week. “It’s definitely a challenge and he answered the bell,” LaFleur offered of Tomlinson’s sudden appearance on the right. That may be so, but it appears to be a challenge of the Packers’ own making. But that describes a lot of their offensive line issues this year, for what it’s worth. Until the Packers can get out of their own way, it seems doubtful the offensive line will improve much more.

title: Green Bay Packers News: Run game remains abysmal despite win
summary: The Green Bay Packers had a perfect opportunity to get their running game back on track on Thursday. They were facing the Carolina Panthers, who had just allowed 258 rushing yards to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers four days earlier, and they got them on a short week. Josh Jacobs was back — and although mileage […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 29: Josh Jacobs #8 of the Green Bay Packers scores a touchdown during the second quarter against the Carolina Panthers at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers had a perfect opportunity to get their running game back on track on Thursday. They were facing the Carolina Panthers, who had just allowed 258 rushing yards to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers four days earlier, and they got them on a short week. Josh Jacobs was back — and although mileage will surely vary on whether or not an individual Packers fan thinks that’s a good thing in general, he is clearly the most talented running back on the team’s roster. So what did the Packers actually do on the ground? They picked up 66 net yards on 26 carries. One of those runs was an end-around to Savion Williams for 18 yards, so the running backs combined for 48 yards on 25 carries, less than two yards per carry on average. It does not feel like hyperbole to say that this is the worst rushing attack in Packers history, and it may well be the worst in NFL history. The fact that the Packers threw the ball on 3rd and 2 late in the game to try to run out the clock should come as no surprise, because this offense has no choice but to run through Jordan Love. And Love played well once again on Thursday night, generally getting the ball out quickly and accurately. Love had just one mistake — a terrible decision on an interception towards the end zone early in the fourth quarter — but otherwise he put up a great performance. 30 of 41 for 288 yards and three touchdowns will get the job done most days, and it certainly did against the Panthers on Sunday. The Packers still made their share of mistakes. Two fumbles, including one on the opening kickoff, could have been a death sentence against a better team. There were still drops, though Matthew Golden made up for one in the end zone with a touchdown on the very next play. But the penalty issues were better, and maybe there’s something to build on here. It just isn’t the running game. Game recap: 5 takeaways from Packers’ victory over Panthers | Packers.com While the offense still has major issues to iron out, the defense stifled Carolina for much of the game, getting some big 4th down stops and posting six sacks, one each from six different players. Christian Watson’s return from hospital leaves Packers teammates stunned | Packers Wire Watson left the game in the first half and got checked out at a local hospital, but he returned in an ambulance after halftime and made a clutch catch on 3rd-and-2 to all but seal the game. Packers Report Card: Big Win Over Panthers Comes With Two F’s | SI.com The run game, as expected, gets a failure, but so does the special teams, thanks to another missed PAT by Trey Smack and the fumble by Coleman Owen on the opening kick. Packers’ Josh Jacobs: TD celebration was ode to gospel song, not mocking arrest | ESPN I’m sorry, when you have more than 20 carries and fewer than 40 yards, it’s tough to celebrate too much at all. But the lack of awareness by Jacobs for how his “handcuffs” celebration would be perceived is just another example of poor judgment on his part. Here’s a good recap on just how badly the Packers missed their chance to get the run game going again: Patrick Stewart, legendary actor of ‘Star Trek’ and ‘X-Men’ fame, dies at 86 | AP.com No funny link tonight, just a sad one: one of the iconic actors of the last several decades, and a genuinely excellent human being, passed away this week. Shaka, when the walls fell. Go Pack Go—wherever you go! title: The Colts have gotten off the merry-go-round and onto the roller coaster.
summary: There is a great 1989 film called Parenthood. Steve Martin wants normalcy in his life, but there is a lot going on that makes this difficult for him. His grandmother offers a story about how some of her friends liked the merry-go-round, but she didn’t because it just went round and round. She preferred the […]
full_text: The Hoosier Hurricane roller coaster at Indiana Beach. 070516 News Indbeach | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co There is a great 1989 film called Parenthood. Steve Martin wants normalcy in his life, but there is a lot going on that makes this difficult for him. His grandmother offers a story about how some of her friends liked the merry-go-round, but she didn’t because it just went round and round. She preferred the ups and downs of the roller coaster. Martin didn’t really get the story as a metaphor until a little later when he was able to embrace it. Colts fans need to be ready to embrace the ride. With the Ballard era over, we can no longer expect the consistency of playing around .500 football. It had it’s minor ups and downs, but is better categorized as a boring mediocre ride. The biggest spike could have been seeing the low of firing Riech and hiring Saturday, but the subsequent haul from that bad season did not see the high of the Colts return to the playoffs. The big swing on AR was a miss, so QB purgatory remained. The miss put them back firmly on the meh ride. Make no mistake, the new ride is going to be come with more of those ups and downs. It doesn’t feel like we are at the apex, but we are at the point of the ride, where you plunge fast and hard to build momentum for the rest of the ride. Coasters are cool, you just have to survive the plunge, before you get some loops and climbs. We are definitely going to plunge some more and may not see that exciting twist until the new GM and coaches are picked. We may get another rush when we dip into free agency and again when we draft. Here are some other things that will contribute to the volatility of the ride: Not everyone is going to be happy with the GM hire. Those not happy with the GM hire, are likely not going to like the new staff either. Not everyone is going to be happy with free agency. We will either be too active while destroying the salary cap, or not active enough and slipping back into Ballard’s frugal ways. We may or may not like the draft, as that is one that we seldom agree on and it can take a little time to determine whether a pick is good or not. For me, the hard part is going to be trying to enjoy the plunge, or at least get excited about the rest of the ride. As we watch long tenured players leave the building, you know that some of their teammates will now get an opportunity, and it will make room for next year’s acquisitions. I probably will get a little rush when Steichen and Lou get their walking papers, but a twist that sees them retained would put me further into plunge mode. I guess that is what a roller coaster is all about. Some things to keep our interest moving forward this year: The continuation of the purge and just how much Dodd will be allowed to do, while still in that role. It is too bad that Burks is the only young WR we could get a better look at. With Downs gone (likely), we will have to use draft capital or cap space to reload the WR room. Maybe we see Mallory more frequently in the flex role? He’s had flashes, but certainly nothing sustained. There is no reason for Pierce to suit up the rest of the year. If JT can’t get traction behind the makeshift OL, just sit him and plan for a healthy 2027. I wouldn’t play him until the deadline passes and would prefer seeing him dealt. He did essentially sit out and ask for a trade, while also committing the AD sin of celebrating short of the goal line. McGowen probably profiles better with his downhill, hit the first thing that looks like a hole approach. We are going to run a lot the rest of the year. I have no reason to believe that AR will be with the team next year, as it would cost 50+ million to franchise tag him and he has already asked to leave. However, I’d give him the opportunity to bump up his price tag by putting him out there until his next injury occurs. Jones is a shell of himself and seeing him behind a line without Nelson, is a recipe for an injury that could run into next year. Worst case, you have a 3rd string QB who you need to see if is a viable QB2 moving forward. He’s probably not, but his run with the 1’s last year was serviceable. It might be interesting to see what Farmer can do at one of the Guard spots. If Dalton Tucker gets the start, it is evidence that Farmer was not a great pick. It couldn’t hurt to give someone else a look at RT as well. Not much reason to play Warren until he is 100%. We know what we have in our veteran TEs, so keep an eye on that position next Spring. Maybe someone asks about Cox or Ogletree and their expiring contract? Give Adebawore as many snaps as he can handle, so he has a reason to re-sign here. Quit playing the rookie ends at the same time and put one of them opposite Latu more often. I assume that they have talked to Grove and asked his wishes for this year. Moving him and re-signing him next year could be an option if he fits the new regime’s plans. He wouldn’t bring a lot, but he could be somebody’s Booger McFarland. I’d see if I could get a 7th or possibly a 6th by adding our 7th, to find another home for ADG. It is not likely that anyone not named Lou will see him as an asset. Obviously, play the rookie LBs as much as possible. I’m not sure that you get the kind of offer you hope for with Sauce and he should be kept for the next group to decide how he fits their plans. Then there are brass considerations: At what point do you announce that Dodds will or will not be considered for the GM role next year? Is it worth it to see what your position coaches could do in a coordinator or even HC role? If you fired Shane, would you give Reggie the role and let Jim Bob call plays? Reggie has to be like most position coaches, as they see their job as a stepping stone toward being the boss. Giving him that opportunity could be a real plus for him down the road. I would think the team’s situational awareness would double with such a move. He’d certainly have a leg up on Saturday. Just how much will we hear from Carlie over the next few weeks? What will be the message to the fans? “Bear with us, it is not as urgent as we stated earlier this year”? We are relevant right now, only because we are making moves. As soon as that process is over, the best we can hope for is, “They haven’t packed it in.” Unless you do hope they pack it in to have a better 2nd, 3rd,etc.. round pick. I’m mainly hoping that I have a reason not to constantly use the FF button when watching my stream. It may not be long before I go ahead and watch the 1:00 games, even if I run the risk of knowing the outcome of our game, before I watch. A lot of folks have been asking for the roller coaster for a while now. Pull that harness down and hold on!

title: 5 Questions with Stampede Blue: The Colts’ Rebuild is Underway
summary: As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the Indianapolis Colts in Week 8, we exchanged questions with Chris Shepherd of Stampede Blue to learn more about the opposing side. Question 1: The Colts are officially in “rebuilding” mode. Did the firing of general manager Chris Ballard catch you by surprise? And how long a leash […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - NOVEMBER 30: Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor (28) runs up the sideline behind Indianapolis Colts guard Quenton Nelson (56) during and NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Indianapolis Colts on November 30, 2025 at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the Indianapolis Colts in Week 8, we exchanged questions with Chris Shepherd of Stampede Blue to learn more about the opposing side. Question 1: The Colts are officially in “rebuilding” mode. Did the firing of general manager Chris Ballard catch you by surprise? And how long a leash will head coach Shane Steichen be given? After losing to a very bad and previously winless Titans team, in a year when the owner made clear the urgency to win had never been higher, it was no surprise someone was fired. I was a bit surprised it was Ballard. I thought there was a chance it would be offensive coordinator Jim Bob Cooter, for several reasons if for nothing else just to appease the bloodthirsty fans inside of Lucas Oil Stadium. Instead, Owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon did the right thing and fired the guy most responsible for the failures of this team. It was a bit of a good surprise. How long of a leash is a fantastic question. Back in April, Irsay-Gordon sat down to do an interview with the Colts’ internal media department and gave an interesting answer to hiring general managers and head coaches: Mark this down for future reference. As long as Carlie Irsay-Gordon is calling the shots for the #Colts , they'll never hire a GM and head coach in the same year. If Ballard isn't back in 2027, Steichen will be. pic.twitter.com/bbsPEvwtL0 — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) April 11, 2026 I admit my initial reaction to that answer was simplistic and there is a very real chance the Colts move on from Steichen and hire both a GM and head coach in the same offseason. Irsay-Gordon said hiring the GM and HC simultaneously was something they would never do, but they can always hire one and then the other, though not rushing either decision would be difficult. They also have a massive head start in finding their next GM. The issue comes down to the end-of-season hiring window and how short it is. Even with a head start they’ll still need to conduct interviews and find the right fit. Then they would have to move on to finding the right head coach. If I had to guess, I would say the next GM will find himself with an immediate decision to make regarding his head coach. Does he fire Shane Steichen and hire a new staff quickly, or does he run it back for one more year with Steichen in a likely lame duck situation? I don’t think the owner will be the one deciding. Question 2: Were you surprised by the timing of the Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner trades? One could argue that the Colts could have driven up the asking price with two full weeks remaining until the NFL trade deadline. They also don’t have their own 2027 first-round pick (sorry to remind you). A bit surprised on the timing, I thought it would happen after this weekend’s drubbing in Jacksonville but I don’t think it would have changed the return. Buckner and Nelson were ultimate team guys. All accounts were that they both showed up every day, outworked everyone around them, led by example, were loved by their teammates and they never once complained about the absolute disaster that had been happening around them since they arrived in Indianapolis. They worked hard, did all of the right things and were loyal to the organization for years on end and when the time came, all reports indicate that both Nelson and Buckner had a say in choosing their next spot. Given the circumstances, I’m okay with that. At the end of the day football is a whole lot of fun and it’s more fun if your team is good, but it’s not as important as treating people with respect, especially people like Nelson and Buckner, rather than squeezing every last drop of value out of them. Of all of the decisions that have been made by leadership in Indy in the past decade, I don’t think the decisions to sell a round low on those two are the ones that will be remembered as what set the franchise back. With a couple of clicks you can visit Dawgs By Nature and learn everything you need to know about this week’s opponent! Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Question 3: From a team-building perspective, it would be wise to also trade Jonathan Taylor… but he’s on pace to have his jersey hanging in the rafters at Lucas Oil Stadium one day. Do you want to see the Colts trade him for maximum value or keep him for sentimental reasons? I think their motivations are different than that. Thus far, all of the serious trade talks have been for players in contract years. My belief is they’re setting up the next GM to have as much agency over the roster as possible. GM changes usually come with massive roster turnover for better or worse, and if on day one the GM has a stack of re-signings to decide on, there may be one or two players they’re interested in bringing back. There’s a very real chance neither of those players will want to spend his second contract with a rebuilding franchise in the Midwest. So moving them now, instead of losing them then and getting zero return for them, makes a whole lot of sense. As it stands, Taylor is under contract. I think the goal is to give the next GM the opportunity to do with Taylor what they like, but if someone makes a ridiculous offer, sort of like the Bears giving two firsts and a fourth for Jeffery Simmons (fortunately it’s the Titans so they’ll bust those picks, but still, that’s wild), then I don’t think they’ll hesitate to move him. Personally, I hope they do move him. Sending JT somewhere he can compete in meaningful games, combined with the fact that his value will never be higher than right now, is enough for me to want them to. I’m just not sure they’ll get that kind of offer. Question 4: Who are some under-the-radar players that Jaguars fans should know of before Sunday’s kickoff? Let’s go with the two guys who will be replacing Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner. At left guard, the Colts will start rookie Jalen Farmer out of Kentucky. As a run blocker Farmer was an animal at Kentucky but he’s only played three offensive snaps this season so there are a lot of unknowns. OL coach Tony Soprano Jr. was famously quoted as saying, “Draft this guy and I’ll make it work,” and reportedly loved Farmer as a prospect. Soprano has garnered a lot of trust within the Colts building as they have drafted and developed offensive line talent as well as anyone in the league since his hiring. I expect Farmer to have his ups and downs, but on offense I’ll be dialed in on the Colts’ left guard all day. Defensively, Adetomiwa Adebawore will fill in for Buckner at defensive tackle. Adebawore is currently tied for the team lead in sacks with 4.0 despite having only played 36% of the team’s defensive snaps. Obviously his sack numbers won’t scale with his playing time but Ade Ade is an athletic freak of a 3-tech and I’m excited to see what he’ll do with an expanded role- that said, he is in a contract year and Mike Garafolo just told everyone on NFL Network’s The Insiders that Indy is shopping him as well, so who knows if he’ll be active on Sunday. Question 5: Do you expect the Colts to cover as 8.5-point underdogs, and do you have a favorite player prop for the game? Cover? Absolutely not. As far as a prop bet, I’d wager the Jaguars defense scores a touchdown on Sunday. I’d also take the over on yards for most Jacksonville offensive…

title: Chiefs-Broncos: 5 questions with Mile High Report ahead of Week 8
summary: On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs face the Denver Broncos in the late afternoon slot of Week 8 games. We welcome Ian St. Clair of Mile High Report — our sister SBNation site covering the Broncos— for Five Questions with the Enemy. Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device and join the Mile […]
full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs face the Denver Broncos in the late afternoon slot of Week 8 games. We welcome Ian St. Clair of Mile High Report — our sister SBNation site covering the Broncos— for Five Questions with the Enemy . Chiefs Kingdom, bring the noise to the SB Nation app! Join fellow Chiefs fans to react to every explosive play and game-changing moment in real time. Chat live throughout the game Browse with fewer ads Easily jump between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device and join the Mile High Report community through Sunday’s game to get perspectives from both sides of the Week 8 matchup! 1. The Broncos lost 31-10 in Kansas City to open the season but have since won five of six games, including three consecutive victories entering this rematch. What has changed the most about Denver since that Week 1 loss? The defense remembered how to tackle. In all seriousness, just put that horrible showing out of their minds and move on. However, getting humbled can also help level a person or team. The shellacking from the Chiefs was a great reminder that what happened last season has no bearing on the current one. So the Broncos better buckle up. And we’ve seen that in the last six games. The fact they’ve won five of six, with the gauntlet they had to start the season, is a testament to that. 2. Bo Nix produced two explosive touchdowns against Arizona, including a franchise-record 62-yard quarterback run, but he is still completing only 59.2% of his passes and averaging 182 passing yards per game. How would you evaluate Nix’s development through the first seven games? Nix has been bad to start this season. He’s had his moments: the second half against the Jacksonville Jaguars and Los Angeles Rams , the two drives against the Seattle Seahawks in the first half (way more than Patrick Mahomes did against that defense), and then Sunday against the Cardinals. But he’s looked and played like a shell of himself to start this season. However, Nix played similarly to this in his rookie season and last season, so he has had sluggish starts. We’ll see if his performance against Arizona is the confidence builder that gets him and the offense clicking. Of course, all of this is easier to swallow when Denver is 5-2. 3. Seattle held the Chiefs to three points and limited Kenneth Walker III to 36 rushing yards last week. Denver leads the NFL with 21 sacks and could face a Kansas City offensive line starting backup tackles. How much of Seattle’s defensive blueprint can the Broncos reproduce in this rematch? Honestly, just tackling Walker would be an improvement for the Broncos’ defense. But there’s no doubt defensive coordinator Vance Joseph and his assistants will look at what the Seahawks did and find ways to implement that in Sunday’s game plan. What will help Denver is the likely return of Patrick Surtain II, who has been out the last few games, and Jonathan Cooper, who missed the first game of the season. Something to keep an eye on, however, is Talanoa Hufanga has been ruled out , and now Brandon Jones showed up on the injury report with a hamstring. So potentially being down your starting safeties isn’t ideal. But Denver’s defense will be incredibly motivated on Sunday to replicate what Seattle did and make up for the Week 1 performance. 4. Jonah Coleman returned against Arizona and joined J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey in what has become a three-man backfield. Which Denver running back should the Chiefs consider the greatest threat entering Sunday’s game? Running the ball, it’s Coleman. He runs much better than Dobbins right now and is a more dangerous threat with the ball. Payton said after the Cardinals win that Coleman needs more touches, so Coleman should get them on Sunday. As a receiving threat, that’s Harvey, as he showed on the 52-yard touchdown reception. So KC should prepare for more running back screens this Sunday. 5. Kansas City enters the game at 5-1, with Denver right behind at 5-2, making this an important early battle for control of the AFC West and positioning within the AFC playoff race. How do you see Sunday’s rematch playing out, including your final score prediction and how much control the winner will gain in the division race? This is going to be a close game that will likely come down to the fourth quarter. Denver’s defense will play much better than that putrid showing to open the season. I also think Nix and the offense will build off last week against Arizona. The fact that the Broncos are playing at home gives them the edge, and they’ll get the 24-20 victory. That will put Denver in the lead for the AFC West, and with Kansas City’s upcoming schedule, puts it in a great spot to defend the division title.

full_text: (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs will take on the Denver Broncos on Sunday afternoon for the second time this season. In the first game, the Chiefs’ defense held Denver to just two third-down conversions over 12 attempts; Kansas City even stopped the Broncos’ only attempt at fourth down. The Chiefs haven’t been as stout on the crucial down since, including allowing the Seattle Seahawks to convert 11 of 16 third downs last week. Chiefs Kingdom, bring the noise to the SB Nation app! The latest Kansas City Chiefs news Third downs and what else to watch when Chiefs meet the Broncos for second time | The Kansas City Star “We had them in 10 third-and-7 plus,” defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo said. “But we only one four of them. That’s not good.” Maybe Sunday’s road game against the Broncos provides a bounce-back opportunity. Denver ranks 31st in third-down conversions, at 31.1%. Defensive tackle Chris Jones said he’d add to the list of issues against the Seahawks. “You take third downs, and you take tackling,” Jones said. “That kind of makes up the game.” Why doesn’t rookie Cyrus Allen play more? Here’s the uphill climb he faces with Chiefs | The Athletic “He told me to get my eyes up, watching the coverage. ‘Look at the coverage,’” Allen told The Athletic on Thursday in the Chiefs’ locker room. “We had a play that we were running to where I gotta get the other guys open. So, just looking at the coverage and knowing what I got to do to help them guys.” It’s a perfect snapshot of what Allen must consider — and everything he has to think about — as he aims to become a bigger part of the Chiefs offense in his rookie season. Chiefs get Rashee Rice back from injury for Broncos game | ESPN In four games this season, Rice has produced 13 receptions on 16 targets for 190 yards and a touchdown. “He’s such a physical receiver,” Mahomes said Wednesday of Rice. “He does a great job within the zone concepts at getting himself open, as well as being physical versus man [coverage]. Having him back out there will be big for us because it’ll help take some pressure off the other guys to make plays and let them go out there and be themselves. Hopefully, we can have some success.” NFL Week 8 picks: Upset and score predictions, matchup breakdowns for every game | NFL.com Can Vance Joseph’s unit provide that kind of ground defense this Sunday? It’s a tall task, though Denver has shown some improvement against the run during its current three-game win streak, yielding a middle-of-the-pack figure of 4.2 yards per carry during that span. After spending the first six weeks of the season on the Commissioner’s Exempt List, Jonathon Cooper just made his season debut last Sunday, reinfusing the defense with a powerful edge setter. Meanwhile, the Chiefs’ offensive line is highly unstable beyond the Pro Bowl combo of C Creed Humphrey and RG Trey Smith. Here are 4 free agent WRs Kansas City Chiefs should consider signing | Chiefs Wire Darius Slayton A former New York Giant and Indianapolis Colt, Slayton is exactly the type of veteran presence who could immediately make an impact for the Chiefs’ offense as head coach Andy Reid makes mid-season adjustments to his legendary air attack. Curtis Samuel Samuel is a versatile threat who would have no problem earning touches in Kansas City’s offense as both a rusher and receiver. Around the NF L Panthers fire defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero, make other defensive changes after Packers loss | CBS Sports Evero’s unit struggled almost across the board in his four seasons running the Panthers defense. The lone bright spot was Carolina’s pass defense, where they allowed the fourth-fewest passing yards per game (201.1) since 2023. Evero wasn’t anywhere close to having his ideal secondary in the Thursday night loss at Lambeau Field. Cornerbacks Jaycee Horn (quad), Mike Jackson (groin) and Akayleb Evans (knee/triceps) were all on injured reserve in Week 8. Sean Payton goes for his 200th career win on Sunday | Pro Football Talk Payton’s next win will give him 200 for his career, including the postseason. His first crack at No. 200 comes on Sunday against the Chiefs. He has coached 319 games, generating a record of 199-120. He’s 189-110 in the regular season and 10-10 in the playoffs. With two more wins, Payton will catch Dan Reeves and Mike Tomlin for 10th on the all-time list. Four more wins after that will put Payton even with Marty Schottenheimer, at 205. Chuck Noll is No. 8 with 209. Paul Brown is No. 7 with 222. Records show 3 other women accused Packers’ Josh Jacobs of abuse after arrest | ESPN As police investigated whether to file charges against Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs following a May altercation with his then-girlfriend, multiple other women contacted police to detail their own allegations against him. Those accounts were included in evidence regarding Jacobs’ battery case that the Hobart/Lawrence Police Department released Friday night in response to a public records request. Green Bay TV station NBC 26 first reported the records release. Jacobs pleaded no contest Sept. 10 to misdemeanor counts of battery and criminal damage to property. He was arrested May 26, three days after an incident in which a woman said he threw her to the ground. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Kingdom Keys: 3 Keys to a Chiefs victory over the Broncos in Week 8 Kansas City’s defensive ends must remain disciplined. George Karlaftis and the other edge defenders cannot consistently rush beyond Nix and create open escape lanes. Collapsing the pocket means little if Nix can step outside it and turn a broken play into a first down. The Chiefs should make him beat them by consistently throwing from inside the pocket. Nix has completed 59.2% of his passes while averaging only 5.8 yards per attempt, with seven touchdowns, three interceptions and an 80.7 passer rating. And be sure to check out FanDuel Sportsbook , the official sportsbook partner of SB Nation. Chiefs fans’ confidence Chiefs Kingdom’s confidence level dipped dramatically after the Week 7 loss to the Seattle Seahawks . Before the ugly showing, Chiefs fans hadn’t let the confidence meter dip below 89% since the season began. Make a trade, Veach! We asked Chiefs Kingdom this week whether the Chiefs needed to invest in trading for a new wide receiver ahead of the NFL’s November 10th trade deadline. An overwhelming 75% of you replied that yes, the Chiefs need pass-catching help added to their roster. With injuries to Tyquan Thornton and Rashee Rice, a lot has been put on Xavier Worthy, and I think it’s fair to say he hasn’t exactly exceeded expectations so far. As a result, the Chiefs have been forced to rely on unproven guys like Jalen Royals and Cyrus Allen to try to help carry the load. If last week’s loss to Seattle indicated anything, it’s that Kansas City currently has a talent deficit at receiver. So it’s no surprise that unconfirmed rumors abound that the Chiefs are calling around the league about possible trade candidates. What the Chiefs are willing to give up to make a trade happen is a big unknown. We have a little over a week to see if any of this materializes. But at least we know where the fans stand. full_text: (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Each practice day this season, the Kansas City Chiefs release an official injury report ahead of the next game. In Week 8, the Chiefs play the Denver Broncos on Sunday afternoon. Here is the Chiefs’ final official injury report of the week, courtesy of Matt McMullen, Chiefs Senior Reporter, on X : Chiefs Cornerback Mansoor Delane (shoulder) was listed as questionable after suddenly missing practice Thursday and Friday. Head coach Andy Reid confirmed that it is the same shoulder he has dealt with injuries to since training camp and forced him to miss time in Weeks 1 and 2. Cornerback L’Jarius Sneed (knee) was listed as questionable after limited participation in practice for two days and missing on Wednesday with an NIR/personal designation. He is regularly listed as a limited participant due to a lingering knee issue. Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott (knee) was ruled out after three days of limited participation in practice; he was designated to return from the Physically Unable to Perform list on Wednesday . He will continue working in the 21-day practice window before the Chiefs must sign him to the active 53-man roster. Defensive end R Mason Thomas (personal) was listed as questionable after missing practice on Friday. On Friday, Andy Reid said Thomas will meet the Chiefs in Denver and will likely play. Wide receiver Rashee Rice (hamstring/knee) did not have a game status listed after improving to full participation in practice on Friday; he hasn’t played since tweaking his hamstring in Week 4, but he should be making his return to the field in Denver. Tight end Travis Kelce (ankle) did not have a game status listed and practiced in full on Friday after being labeled a limited participant in practice on Thursday. He banged up his ankle in the Week 6 win over the Los Angeles Chargers . The following players were full participants in practice all week: Right tackle Jaylon Moore (concussion) Left tackle Kahlil Benson (ankle) Linebacker Nick Bolton (neck) Center Creed Humphrey (toe) Linebacker Drue Tranquill (elbow) Quarterback Patrick Mahomes (knee) Broncos Starting safety Talanoa Hufanga (ankle) was ruled out after missing practice all week; he hasn’t played since leaving the Week 5 win over the Los Angeles Chargers with an ankle injury. This season, he is tied for the team lead with two interceptions — one he returned for a touchdown — and has three passes defended, one forced fumble and three tackles for loss. Wide receiver Jaylen Waddle (chest) was listed as questionable after limited practice on Thursday and Friday; he suffered his injury in the Week 7 win over the Arizona Cardinals . Pro Bowl defensive lineman Zach Allen (hamstring) was listed as questionable after two limited practices to end the week following an absence from Wednesday’s practice. Allen has 4.5 sacks this year and hasn’t missed any time for this injury so far. After having no designation on Wednesday, running back RJ Harvey (knee) was limited on Thursday, then didn’t practice on Friday and has been ruled out . He has 304 total yards and two touchdowns this season. Starting safety Brandon Jones (hamstring) was listed as questionable after two limited practices to end the week; Jones intercepted Mahomes in Week 1 and has the second-most tackles on Denver’s defense this season. Left tackle Garrett Bolles (hip) is questionable to play after limited participation in practice all week. Bolles hasn’t missed a snap for Denver so far this season, but he was not listed on the injury report last week. All-Pro cornerback Patrick Sutain II (ankle) has not played since suffering the ankle injury in Week 4, but he has practiced in full all week and did not have a game status listed; he will play on Sunday.

full_text: On Sunday, the (5-1) Kansas City Chiefs are on the road to take on the (5-2) Denver Broncos to battle for the division. Let’s see how the game plays out in Madden NFL 2 7. Note: The Chiefs Madden Simulation has predicted five correct Chiefs victories. STOP! If you want to watch the simulation without spoilers, start this video — or if you can’t see it, click here. First quarter Broncos running back J.K. Dobbins jump-started the offense with a 21-yard run to the Chiefs’ 48-yard line. Dobbins continued to find success on the ground, rushing for 52 yards on the opening drive. At the two-yard line, Kansas City’s defense looked to keep Denver out of the end zone. On third-and-goal, Nick Bolton came untouched on a blitz and sacked Bo Nix, ending the drive as Denver settled for three points. Patrick Mahomes felt the pressure on third-and-short but escaped the pocket and connected with Xavier Worthy on the run to pick up the first down. End of first quarter: Broncos 3, Chiefs 0 Second quarter Three plays later, Mahomes found Rashee Rice for a 25-yard gain to get the Chiefs into Broncos territory. On third-and-short, Andy Reid dialed up an inside-zone run for Emmett Johnson, but defensive tackle Zach Allen stopped Johnson in the backfield. Harrison Butker drilled a 44-yard field goal to tie the game. Nix responded by firing a laser to Marvin Mims Jr. for a 30-yard gain. Dobbins followed with an 18-yard rush, continuing to pick up chunk yards against the Chiefs’ defense. He capped off the drive with an eight-yard rushing touchdown, scoring the first touchdown of the game. Mahomes continued to be efficient, completing 10 consecutive passes. However, when he went for lucky number 11 on third down, his pass was batted down, ending the drive. Butker added three more points with his leg to keep the Chiefs within striking distance. The Broncos attempted to add three more points before halftime, but Will Lutz came up short on a 67-yard field goal attempt. Mahomes then connected with Rice to reach the 30-yard line before finding Jalen Royals to get the Chiefs to the 17-yard line, putting Butker in prime field goal range. Butker made the kick to cut into Denver’s lead. End of second quarter: Broncos 10, Chiefs 9 Third quarter After going three-for-three on field goal attempts in the first half, Butker attempted a 66-yarder but missed. The Broncos took over at the Chiefs’ 44-yard line. Mahomes felt pressure from D.J. Jones and was sacked on third down, forcing the Chiefs to punt. On Denver’s next possession, Khyiris Tonga sacked Nix on third down, forcing the Broncos to punt the ball back to Kansas City. The Chiefs were unable to capitalize on the opportunity and punted the ball back to Denver. End of third quarter: Broncos 17, Chiefs 9 Fourth quarter The Broncos’ offense finally started clicking again as Nix picked up three crucial first downs. One of those completions went for 14 yards, with Nix taking a shot at the end of the play. Dobbins found paydirt for the second time that afternoon, going untouched for a 12-yard rushing touchdown to extend Denver’s lead. Mahomes knew the passing game wasn’t working, so he used his legs to pick up a crucial third-and-12 with a 14-yard rush early in the drive. On fourth-and-four, Mahomes tried to pick up the first down with his legs once more. As he reached the ball toward the first-down marker, he took a hit and fumbled. The Broncos recovered the football, ending the Chiefs’ scoring opportunity. At the two-minute warning, Lutz missed another 67-yard field goal attempt. Mahomes was sacked as the clock ran out, sealing the Broncos’ victory. End of the fourth quarter: Broncos 24, Chiefs 9 Notable stats Patrick Mahomes: 23 for 31 passing, 204 yards, 3 rushing attempts, 24 yards. Kenneth Walker: 9 rushing attempts, 39 yards, 2 receptions, 23 yards. Rashee Rice: 9 receptions, 85 yards. Travis Kelce: 5 receptions, 26 yards. Jalen Royals: 4 receptions, 38 yards. Xavier Worthy: 3 receptions, 22 yards. Drue Tranquill: 11 tackles, 1 tackle for loss. Nick Bolton: 8 tackles, 1 sack Khyiris Tonga: 1 sack Harrison Butker: 3 for 4 kicking with a long of 45. Bo Nix: 15 for 21 passing, 211 yards, 1 touchdown. J.K. Dobbins: 15 rushing attempts, 104 yards, 2 touchdowns. Marvin Mims Jr.: 4 receptions, 94 yards, 1 touchdown. Even Engram: 4 receptions, 50 yards. Justin Strand: 9 tackles, 1 tackle for loss. D.J. Jones: 1.5 sacks, 3 tackles for loss. Zach Allen: 1 sack, 2 tackles for loss Will Lutz: 1 for 3 with a long of 28. Next week, the Chiefs are back home at Arrowhead to welcome the New York Jets . Until then, we will see how it is played out inside the EA Universe.

title: Chiefs-Broncos Week 8 game and score predictions from Arrowhead Pride
summary: It’s time for the Arrowhead Pride staff to put their opinions to the test. Before the Kansas City Chiefs travel to face the Denver Broncos — in their second meeting of the year — our writers predicted the final score and result. The 5-2 Broncos have rebounded since being dominated by the Chiefs to open […]
full_text: Credit: Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect It’s time for the Arrowhead Pride staff to put their opinions to the test. Before the Kansas City Chiefs travel to face the Denver Broncos — in their second meeting of the year — our writers predicted the final score and result. The 5-2 Broncos have rebounded since being dominated by the Chiefs to open the season. FanDuel Sportsbook currently lists the Chiefs as 1.5-point road favorites. Denver’s quarterback play under Bo Nix has been a hotly debated topic in 2026, and their defense has not always lived up to the standard set in recent years. But the Broncos are coming off of their best overall performance of the year — a 30-16 win over the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday. We also want to know your score prediction! Vote in the poll on The Feed and share your score prediction ! Jared Sapp ( @TrumanChief ) One of the Chiefs’ biggest priorities should be finding a way to lessen Kenneth Walker’s workload. This is not the week for that. Denver is playing better, but the middle of the defense can still be attacked and will be the Chiefs’ best path to win. This is a week where we can overreact to Week 7 and how inept the Chiefs looked against the league’s best defense while Denver was comfortably beating the Arizona Cardinals. The strengths and weaknesses both teams have shown through the first half of the season are still there. I expect a much closer result than Week 1, but I think the Chiefs can still play smart football and ride a run heavy approach to a close victory. Chiefs 20, Broncos 16 Caleb James ( @CJScoobs ) This matchup will be critical for the outcome of the AFC West, as well as for playoff seeding. Bo Nix is coming off of maybe his best offensive performance of the season while Mahomes is coming off of his worse. That said, Nix has still struggled to create consistency this year, and the Chiefs defense has already gotten the better of him once. I expect the Chiefs to come out with a better offensive plan — but the line must be able to protect for Patrick Mahomes. In the end, it will be interesting to see how much the Chiefs use of Kenneth Walker and the play action passing game affects the Denver defense this week. Chiefs 24, Broncos 17 Mark Gunnels ( @MarkAGunnels ) The Chiefs dominated the Broncos in Week 1, and while I expect Denver to put up a better fight at home, I still don’t trust their ability to stop the run. Kenneth Walker should bounce back after a disappointing performance in Seattle, and if Rashee Rice returns, Patrick Mahomes gets one of his favorite weapons back. On the other side, I just don’t trust Bo Nix and that Broncos offense to consistently sustain drives against Kansas City. Give me the Chiefs to take care of business and put a stranglehold on the AFC West. Chiefs 20, Broncos 17 Maurice Elston ( @MrMauriceElston ) This is a chance for the Chiefs to take a firm grip on the AFC West. A win over Denver would give Kansas City a season sweep and valuable separation from its biggest division challenger. But I don’t expect another convincing win like the season opener. Bo Nix and the Broncos’ offense have found more rhythm, and while I’m not sold on him as a dominant quarterback, he has shown he can make timely plays. Patrick Surtain’s potential return would strengthen Denver’s defense, although Jaylon Waddle’s uncertain availability could leave its receiving corps shorthanded. The Chiefs got punched in the face in Seattle, but I trust their veteran leadership and coaching staff to respond. That starts with getting Kenneth Walker III going and giving Patrick Mahomes better protection. Jaylon Moore’s potential return and the possibility of getting Rice back would help, while I’d like to see more downfield opportunities for the younger receivers. Defensively, I’m looking for more Chris Roland-Wallace in the slot and fewer snaps there for L’Jarius Sneed. Ultimately, I expect Walker to lead the way, Mahomes to bounce back and Kansas City to regain control after its first loss. Chiefs 27, Broncos 17 Matt Stagner ( @stagdsp ) What has really changed since the Chiefs beat the Broncos 31-10 in Week one? The Chiefs followed that win with 4 others vs AFC opponents. They ran into a buzz saw in Seattle for sure — once again exposing the limits of the Chiefs OL and WR depth. Some help seems to be on the way, whether that impacts this weekend’s game or not, we’ll see. Butthis IS still the same Chiefs team from the first 5 weeks. They’ll be able to run the ball again and Mahomes will bounce back with a vengeance. They may not put up 30 points against a good Denver defense, but I’d bet on competence. Chiefs 24, Broncos 17 Dakota Watson ( @D_Watson56 ) A lot is on the line in this one. I don’t see the Chiefs laying an egg like they did last week. But they won’t dominate Denver like they did Week 1 either. Rashee Rice’s likely return will help the offense. I also don’t see the Broncos completely shutting down Walker and the Chiefs’ running game. The defense will play better, although I think our pass rush will remain a major issue against the Broncos’ offensive line. This one will be a close divisional battle, and I think it comes down to the wire. Chiefs 20, Broncos 17 Rocky Magana ( @RockyMagana ) As good as Denver’s defense is, their secondary is not as good as the Seattle Seahawks’. Neither is their run defense. And the biggest fact of all, they don’t have the best wide receiver in the universe as Seattle does. I expect Kenneth Walker to continue to be the best running back in the NFL, and I expect the Chiefs to make Bo Nix look as bad or worse than he has all season. Last week wasn’t a sign that the NFL has figured out the Chiefs. It was never hard to figure out Kansas City’s offense. Stop the run and the Chiefs are in trouble. But that’s easier said than done. And I don’t think Denver can do it. Chiefs 19, Broncos 10 Nate Christensen This game has massive stakes for divisional seeding purposes, but also for the direction of both teams the rest of the year. Denver is trying to prove that Week 1 was a fluke and that their offense is good enough to beat the best teams in the NFL. Kansas City is trying to prove that they can move the ball against a very stingy Broncos defense again, particularly one that will be much more keyed on stopping Kenneth Walker. Unfortunately for the Chiefs, I worry about that. The Chiefs passing offense has looked bad against both Denver and Seattle, which feature top-5 passing defenses. I expect that to continue, and I think Denver does a better job stopping the run to close this game out. I expect the Chiefs defense to keep this close and potentially carry them to a win, but I think Denver splits the series at home. Broncos 17, Chiefs 13 Ron Kopp Jr. ( @RonOnChiefs ) The Seattle loss felt like it was coming from miles away, and this always felt like the real measuring-stick game for the Chiefs through the first half of the season. In Denver, where they lost 22-19 last year and essentially handed the division over to the Broncos. This Sunday, Kansas City can take the reins of the AFC West back, and I see them rising to the occasion. The Broncos’ run defense is the weakness of a strong unit, and I see running back Kenneth Walker bouncing back in a huge way against the team he ran for more than 170 rushing yards against in Week 1. The offense gets back on track this week, especially with right tackle Jaylon Moore back in the lineup. title: Kingdom Keys: 3 Keys to a Chiefs victory over the Broncos in Week 8
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs were thoroughly outplayed in all three phases of last Sunday’s loss to the Seattle Seahawks. The Chiefs must now respond on the road against the Denver Broncos in an important AFC West matchup. Kansas City defeated Denver 31-10 in Week 1, but the Broncos have won five of their last six […]
full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs were thoroughly outplayed in all three phases of last Sunday’s loss to the Seattle Seahawks . The Chiefs must now respond on the road against the Denver Broncos in an important AFC West matchup. Kansas City defeated Denver 31-10 in Week 1, but the Broncos have won five of their last six games and enter the rematch at 5-2. Here are three keys to a Chiefs victory in Week 8: Offensive key: Get Kenneth Walker III going again Denver has one of the league’s better overall defenses, but stopping the run remains its biggest weakness. The Broncos have surrendered 933 rushing yards through seven games, an average of 133.3 per game. Opponents are averaging 4.6 yards per carry against them. Denver has been far more effective defending the pass, holding opposing quarterbacks to a 56.4% completion rate and a 74.2 passer rating while recording 21 sacks and seven interceptions. That should make Kansas City’s offensive approach straightforward: lean on Kenneth Walker III. Walker dominated the first meeting with Denver, rushing for 173 yards and producing a 60-yard touchdown. The Chiefs finished that game with 220 rushing yards, controlled the football for nearly 34 minutes and converted nine of their 17 third downs. Seattle became the first opponent this season to truly slow Walker, holding him to 36 yards on 14 carries. It was also the first time this season that he failed to rush for 100 yards or score a touchdown. Despite that performance, Walker still enters Week 8 with 701 rushing yards, 116 receiving yards and eight total touchdowns. Andy Reid cannot allow one poor performance to move the offense away from what has worked throughout the season. Running Walker will keep Denver’s pass rush from attacking on every down and prevent Patrick Mahomes from repeatedly facing obvious passing situations. The offensive benchmark should be at least 125 scrimmage yards for Walker. The passing game must also provide more support than it did in Seattle. Xavier Worthy caught three of his six targets for only 11 yards, while Jalen Royals was held without a reception on two targets. Denver’s aggressive coverage will challenge Kansas City’s receivers to create separation and win contested catches. Rashee Rice’s potential return would help after he practiced on a limited basis Wednesday and Thursday. Regardless of Rice’s availability, Mahomes’ receivers must be better when Denver commits additional defenders to stopping Walker. Defensive key: Keep Bo Nix in the pocket Denver’s traditional running game has been unproductive. The Broncos are averaging only 3.8 yards per carry, while leading rusher J.K. Dobbins has produced 293 yards at 3.4 yards per attempt. The threat comes when Bo Nix escapes the pocket. Nix has 110 rushing yards and two touchdowns this season. That total includes a 62-yard touchdown run against Arizona last week, when he finished with 73 yards on seven carries. Kansas City’s defensive ends must remain disciplined. George Karlaftis and the other edge defenders cannot consistently rush beyond Nix and create open escape lanes. Collapsing the pocket means little if Nix can step outside it and turn a broken play into a first down. The Chiefs should make him beat them by consistently throwing from inside the pocket. Nix has completed 59.2% of his passes while averaging only 5.8 yards per attempt, with seven touchdowns, three interceptions and an 80.7 passer rating. We finally found a role for Jeffrey Bassa in the Chiefs' defense He played 2 snaps in Seattle, both as a QB Spy. Remember this for the Buffalo matchup pic.twitter.com/CZYX1U8TzS — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) October 27, 2026 Kansas City could also expand Jeffrey Bassa’s role as a quarterback spy. Bassa received snaps in that assignment against Seattle and helped the defense produce two third-down stops in the red zone. His athleticism makes him a logical option when the Chiefs believe Nix may scramble. The plan should be to stop Denver’s running backs on early downs, keep the edges secure and make Nix operate as a pocket passer on third-and-long. X-factor: Make your kicks The Chiefs cannot afford another game in which missed kicks leave points on the field. Harrison Butker missed two field goals against Seattle and has now missed five field goals this season — tied for the most in the NFL — along with an extra point. His 15 missed kicks since the beginning of last season are also the most in the league over that span. Kansas City responded by signing Justin Tucker to the practice squad. Special teams coordinator Dave Toub continues to say that Butker is the preferred kicker and explained that the primary objective is to help him work through his struggles . Tucker provides both competition and a veteran sounding board. He has experienced his own kicking struggles and can communicate with Butker in ways the coaching staff cannot. During Tucker’s workout, he reportedly converted all 30 of his attempts, including seven from beyond 50 yards and a 60-yarder. Butker then made all 10 attempts during Wednesday’s windy practice, with Tucker watching. Whether Butker remains the kicker or Tucker is eventually elevated, the standard is simple: Kansas City must make its kicks. A close divisional game on the road may be decided by three points. The Chiefs cannot leave those points on the board. The bottom line Seattle punched the Chiefs in the mouth, but one poor performance doesn’t erase everything the team accomplished during the 5-0 start. Kansas City must reestablish its identity by getting Walker beyond 100 scrimmage yards and forcing Denver to respect the run. Defensively, the Chiefs must maintain edge discipline and make Bo Nix beat them from inside the pocket. On special teams, whoever handles the kicking duties must convert every reasonable opportunity. If Kansas City can accomplish those three things, it will have an excellent opportunity to respond to its worst performance of the season, complete the season sweep of Denver and regain control of the AFC West race.
