However, Bech’s game status is still unclear after the Raiders released the final injury report for the week and head coach Klint Kubiak held his Friday press conference. Bech, who has been on injured […]
full_text: (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders opened Jack Bech’s 21-day practice window ahead of the Week 8 matchup against the New York Jets . However, Bech’s game status is still unclear after the Raiders released the final injury report for the week and head coach Klint Kubiak held his Friday press conference. #Raiders final injury report for the week: WR Jack Bech is questionable to play. The team will unlikely face #Jets rookie edge David Bailey. pic.twitter.com/ECGBgSGIfi — Ryan McFadden (@ryanmcfadden_) October 30, 2026 Bech, who has been on injured reserve with a broken right forearm since the Week 3 game against the New Orleans Saints, is listed as questionable for Sunday’s game. Kubiak was asked if the wide receiver will be activated before the team’s trek to the Big Apple, but the coach said they have until Saturday to make that decision, according to The Athletic’s Sam Warren . The 2025 second-round pick had five catches for 48 yards and a touchdown in the three games he played to begin the season, while also serving as a notable run blocker on the perimeter. If Bech can’t play, then recently activated wide receiver Dont’e Thornton Jr. could see a good amount of playing time in what is expected to be his season debut. Thornton has been sidelined with a hamstring injury since the beginning of training camp, and Warren also reported that Kubiak said Thornton’s workload in New York is to be determined. In other Raiders injury news, backup edge defender Patrick Johnson (stinger) has been ruled out. That could lead to practice squad edge Cian Slone getting his third call-up in as many weeks. However, Slone has been a healthy scratch during the last two Sundays, and this would be his last call-up before the team has to add him to the 53-man roster if they want to elevate the undrafted rookie a fourth time. Guard Jackson Powers-Johnson (back) was a non-participant in Thursday’s practice but was upgraded to limited on Friday and listed as questionable for Sunday. As for the Jets, their defensive line is pretty beaten up. Defensive tackle T’Vondre Sweat (knee) and edge rusher Joseph Ossai (ankle) have been ruled out, while rookie edge/second overall pick David Bailey (groin) is doubtful. Bailey didn’t practice at all during the week. Additionally, running back Breece Hall (quad) and offensive lineman/former Raider Dylan Parham (knee) are questionable. Hall was limited in practice all week, and Parham was limited for the first two sessions but was a full-go on Friday.
author: Matt Holder

title: How have former Las Vegas Raiders Geno Smith, Dylan Parham looked with New York Jets ahead of Week 8 matchup?
summary: The New York Jets have a couple of familiar faces in quarterback Geno Smith and guard Dylan Parham, adding some intrigue to the Las Vegas Raiders’ Week 8 matchup on Sunday. To preview the game for Raider Nation, Silver and Black Pride reached out to our friends at Gang Green Nation, and MacGregor Wells was […]
full_text: (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New York Jets have a couple of familiar faces in quarterback Geno Smith and guard Dylan Parham, adding some intrigue to the Las Vegas Raiders’ Week 8 matchup on Sunday. To preview the game for Raider Nation, Silver and Black Pride reached out to our friends at Gang Green Nation, and MacGregor Wells was kind enough to answer a few questions about the Jets. Q: Geno Smith had a short and underwhelming stay in Las Vegas last year, but it seems like he’s having a better season this year. What are the reviews on the 2013 second-round pick in his return to New York? A: I think Geno has benefitted from a better situation with the Jets more than anything else. Not that the Jets are some model franchise, but the 2025 Raiders seemed to have a bad offensive line and few options in the passing game other than Brock Bowers, who was hobbled by injuries for a good portion of the season. The 2026 Jets have an average-ish offensive line and multiple weapons to throw to, including Garrett Wilson, 1st-round rookie WR Omar Cooper Jr., who is off to a great start to his career, fellow 1st-round rookie TE Kenyon Sadiq and second-year TE Mason Taylor. For the first time in a very long time, the Jets have a good set of weapons to throw to, and it shows. Geno has been better in 2026 than 2025, but I think that largely has to do with his improved supporting cast. Q: The Jets have another former Raider in Dylan Parham, who signed a two-year, $16 million contract in the offseason. Parham was just an average starter in Vegas, so I’m curious how he’s doing and what he’s brought to the Jets’ offense this year? A: Parham had been doing very well at guard for the Jets before he was injured. He was arguably performing better than any other Jets offensive lineman. However, Parham only played in three games for the Jets before he was injured, and he has missed the last four games, so the sample size is minuscule and the jury is still out on how well he’ll perform in the long run. Q: Garrett Wilson seemingly gave Smith an earful during last Sunday’s loss to the Dolphins, while Fernando Mendoza’s college teammate Omar Cooper Jr. has been very productive in his first two games back from injury. Maybe not right now, but do you think Cooper could eventually take over as the Jets’ No. 1 receiver? What has he shown so far? A: I don’t think Wilson was yelling at Smith. It looked to me like he was yelling at passing game coordinator Seth Ryan. If you take a close look, it looks like Geno is not engaged at all, and Ryan seems to be intently engaged with whatever Wilson was saying. Whether it was Smith or Ryan, Garrett Wilson has not been shy about sounding off when he has felt he was not being utilized properly throughout his career. He is also frustrated over the constant losing he has endured with the Jets every year of his career. It’s possible Wilson will eventually demand a trade, but he doesn’t seem to be there yet. As for Cooper, who knows? I doubt he will ever be a better wide receiver than Garrett Wilson, but I suppose it’s possible. If Wilson is traded at some point, could Cooper be a legitimate WR1 for the Jets? I have no idea. We’ve seen just two games from Cooper, both of which involved 40+ yard receptions. Nobody makes those huge plays on a weekly basis. Cooper won’t either. What will he do if he’s the focus of every team’s top defensive backs? Can he run a full route tree effectively? I don’t know. So far he’s been impressive. We’ll know a lot more by the end of the year, if he stays healthy, regarding his upside and what he can and can’t do well at the NFL level. For now it’s just exciting to have a real weapon opposite Wilson for a change. Q: Speaking of rookies and New York’s first-round picks, what are the early reviews on David Bailey? A: David Bailey has a great motor and a world-class first step. He’s better against the run than advertised, though obviously his pass rush abilities are what pay the bills. He seems to learn quickly. On the downside, for now he’s not a polished pass rusher. He needs to develop the use of his hands and multiple pass rush moves when he doesn’t immediately beat a tackle around the edge with his speed. I think he’s going to be the best Jets pass rusher in decades, but he’s still got a ways to go in his development. Q: Brock Bowers presents a lot of problems for opposing secondaries, and Aaron Glenn typically runs a decent amount of man coverage. So, who do you think Glenn will put on Bowers, or what do you think the strategy will be? A: Let’s be real – the Jets have no answer for Bowers. Few teams do. I’m sure the safeties Dane Belton and Minkah Fitzpatrick will try to cover him at times, and the linebackers Demario Davis and Jamien Sherwood will take a shot at other times. But the safeties are too small, and the linebackers are too slow. Bowers will get plenty of production against the Jets. The key for the Jets will probably be limiting the other Raiders’ weapons to minimal production.
author: Matt Holder

title: Raiders wide receiver Week 7 snap and production review
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders’ lost a 35-21 home game to the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday Let’s review how their wide receivers fared: Tre Tucker Tucker played a season high 82 percent of the offensive snaps. He was targeted a whopping 12 times. He had five catches for 103 yards. He had a 41-yard catch […]
full_text: (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders’ lost a 35-21 home game to the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday Let’s review how their wide receivers fared: Tre Tucker Tucker played a season high 82 percent of the offensive snaps. He was targeted a whopping 12 times. He had five catches for 103 yards. He had a 41-yard catch and he had four catches of 40 plus yards, which is tied for the league high. Tucker has 10 catches for 200 yards and three touchdowns in the past two games. Consistency has been his issue. It’s good to see this continued production. Jalen Nailor: The starter played 75 percent of the snaps. He had two catches for 14 yards on five targets. Nailor has eight catches for 75 yards on 20 targets this season after signing three-year, $35 million deal. Cody White: White played 17 snaps. He had one catch for four yards on three targets. Malik Benson The rookie sixth-round pick played a season low three snaps. He was targeted once without a catch. He has two catches on nine targets for 12 yards this season. Dareke Young: He played three offensive snap. He didn’t have any targets. Conclusion: As has been their recent trend, the Raiders threw more to their tight ends and running backs than their receivers. But it got closer. Kirk Cousins threw to his receivers 21 of 44 targets, which is an increase from the previous three games. Tucker is the clear focus of the current group, but help is coming. Dont’e Thornton has been activated from the injured reserve and Jack Bech’s 21-day practice window from the injured reserve has begun.
author: Bill Williamson

title: Dylan Parham offers reminder about Raiders’ investment on offensive line
summary: Sunday, the Las Vegas Raiders will visit the New York Jets and guard Dylan Parham. Parham left the Raiders this offseason as a free agent to sign with the Jets. Parham was the Raiders’ first draft pick in 2022, taken in the third round. Parham was at the beginning of a commitment from four different […]
full_text: (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sunday, the Las Vegas Raiders will visit the New York Jets and guard Dylan Parham. Parham left the Raiders this offseason as a free agent to sign with the Jets. Parham was the Raiders’ first draft pick in 2022, taken in the third round. Parham was at the beginning of a commitment from four different Raiders regimes to build the offensive line. The Raiders have used eight picks in the first four rounds of the draft on offensive linemen since 2020. They were: John Simpson (fourth, 2020), Alex Leatherwood (first, 2021), Parham (third, 2022), Jackson Powers-Johnson (second, 2024), D.J. Glaze (third, 2024), Caleb Rogers (third, 2025), Charles Grant (third, 2025) and Trey Zuhn (third, 2026). However, only Glaze and Rogers are currently starting for the Raiders. Powers-Johnson, Grant and Zuhn are currently backups while Simpson, Leatherwood and Parham are no longer on the roster. There is a thought that Zuhn may replace Rogers in the starting lineup Sunday at the Jets. So, Rogers could join Powers-Johnson players who lost their starting roles. This is not an ideal payoff for such a strong draft capital investment on the offense line. Part of the problem is that there have been so many different front offices and coaching staffs. They all have different wants and philosophies when it comes to offensive linemen, so that creates the constant need to start over. Second-year Las Vegas general manager John Spytek has been vocal about his affinity for offensive linemen and his selections of Rogers, Grant and Zuhn in the third round shows that. The key is for these young players to develop into depenndable starters so the Raiders can can spread out their premium picks to other areas in the coming years.
author: Bill Williamson

title: Raiders-Jets Week 8: 5 things to watch
summary: The 3-4 Las Vegas Raiders play at the 2-5 New York Jets on Sunday. Kickoff is at 10 a.m. PT. Here are five keys to victory for Las Vegas: Stop the run: The Rams ran right over the Raiders as they compiled 199 yards on the ground last week. That is a recipe for a […]
full_text: (Photo by Sarah Stier/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 3-4 Las Vegas Raiders play at the 2-5 New York Jets on Sunday. Kickoff is at 10 a.m. PT. Here are five keys to victory for Las Vegas: Stop the run: The Rams ran right over the Raiders as they compiled 199 yards on the ground last week. That is a recipe for a defeat. Rob Leonard’s unit must tighten the ship this week. Run the ball: Yes, this has been a focal point every week and every week it seems to be a problem area for Las Vegas. The Raiders have had the worst running game in the NFL this season. Last week, they ran the ball just 17 times. They have to establish the run at some point. Ashton Jeanty said he think the Raiders can run on the Jets because they have some players not interested in tackling. It’s time to live up to those words. Be Better in red zone on both sides of the ball: On offense, in the past two games, the Raiders converted in the red zone just three of 10 attempts. On defense, in the past two games, the Raiders allowed touchdowns on eight of their opponents’ 10 trips to the red zone. That’s another recipe for defeat. That must change this week. Be better than a bad team: The Raiders are 3-0 against teams with a combined record of 3-16. They are 0-4 against teams with a combined record of 17-9 record. The Jets are 2-5. The Raiders are better than the Jets. They need to show it. Take advantage of an Aaron Glenn weakness: Since he took over in 2025, Jets head coach Aaron Glenn’s team have been outscored 106-7 in the final two minutes of the first half. That’s a weird quirk. But it’s real. Go take advantage, Las Vegas.

title: 5 Things I Think I Think About the Miami Dolphins After Week 7
summary: Wait, what? Did the Miami Dolphins respond to arguably their worst loss of the season with their first win? On the road?  You bet your sweet bippy they did. And against the Jets too – if you tell me the Dolphins go 2-15 this season but sweep the Jets, I’d say, “You know, not so […]
full_text: Wait, what? Did the Miami Dolphins respond to arguably their worst loss of the season with their first win? On the road? You bet your sweet bippy they did. And against the Jets too – if you tell me the Dolphins go 2-15 this season but sweep the Jets, I’d say, “You know, not so bad.” Here are five more things I think I think following the Dolphins’ first win. They Did the One Thing Winning Teams Do If there’s one ultimate flex in professional football, it’s this: Running the ball to drain the clock and close out a close game. Everybody in the stadium knows exactly what’s coming: The defense knows, the crowd knows, the broadcast team knows, everybody knows. And it doesn’t matter – the winning team lines up and closes the game anyway. On Sunday, that’s unexpectedly what the Dolphins were able to do against the Jets. Late in the fourth quarter, the Jets scored a touchdown (Mason Taylor?! Again?!) to pull within three points. They then kicked off, hoping to force a stop and get the ball back to tie or win it. The old Dolphins would have played conservative, forcing the Jets to burn their timeouts but giving Gang Green the ball and a chance to win. But what did the new Dolphins do? 3:17 left, 1 st down, 14-yard run from Ollie Gordon. Jets timeout. 3:10 left, 1 st down, 7-yard run from Ollie Gordon. Jets timeout. 3:04 left, 2 nd down, 1-yard run from Ollie Gordon. 2:21 left, 3 rd down, 1-yard run from Ollie Gordon. Two-minute warning. 2:00 left, 4 th down, 2-yard run from Malik Willis. First down. Victory formation. I mean, it wasn’t pure dominance: They needed a two-yard pickup on fourth down to secure the win, whereas ideally you’d lock that in on second or third down. Still, if you want to talk about the growth of a young team, this is Exhibit A with a gold star. Malik Willis Showed Tangible Growth What a difference a bye week makes, eh? Let’s revel in the stat line: 14-of-21 passing 228 passing yards 2 passing touchdowns 0 interceptions, 0 fumbles 37 rushing yards 1 rushing touchdown QB rating of 130.7! So what caused the change? A good night’s sleep? Frank Thomas’ testosterone supplements?* Yes and yes. But also, maybe better decision-making and resource utilization. Instead of going for deep shot after deep shot, against the Jets Willis threw more passes that were short of the sticks, completing a season-high 67% of his passes and keeping the offense on schedule. He also involved his tight ends more, with TE Greg Dulcich leading the team in targets and a season-high 86 yards, and he clearly benefited from having No. 1 receiver Caleb Douglas back. Willis still has more questions than answers right now, of course. But after opening the season with just two touchdown passes against seven turnovers, Sunday felt like the first game that provided a legitimate reason for optimism. I’m eager to see how he performs against the Patriots. *And she’ll like it too! Caleb Douglas Continues To Change the Offense I’m old enough to remember when Jon-Eric Sullivan and Co. caught a lot of flak for selecting Caleb Douglas in the third round and 75th overall. And who knows, maybe time will prove the doubters right. But man, the Dolphins look like a different team with Douglas on the field. It’s not just the traits and production – it’s the game-day savvy that you might not expect from a rookie playing his third game. His biggest play was a long catch-and-run touchdown in the fourth quarter. Douglas recognized a blitz, adjusted his route, caught Willis’ pass, broke a tackle attempt from Minkah Fitzpatrick and raced to the end zone. He also refused to be intimidated when Fitzpatrick got in his face, which is exactly what you want to see from a young receiver. OK, fine, Douglas only has 9 receptions on the season. But when averaging more than 20 yards per catch, it’s fair to say he’s giving this offense a much-needed jolt. The Offensive Line and Running Game Deserve Real Credit When was the last time we had a truly physical offensive line and running game? The Ricky Williams era? I’m not discounting De’Von Achane’s remarkable season last year, but that felt due more to his own speed and elusiveness than a dominant offensive line. Sunday’s performance wasn’t just productive. It was physical. For years, Dolphins fans have begged for an offense that could impose its will rather than relying solely on speed and scheme. Against the Jets, we finally saw a glimpse of that blueprint. Consider: Ollie Gordon rushed 25 times for 103 yards and a touchdown Maybe more importantly, the Dolphins as a team ran the ball almost twice as much as they threw the ball Gordon ran with toughness and attitude, but let’s not forget the offensive line really brought their lunch pails and got to work. The closing sequence mentioned above doesn’t happen without a tough, committed offensive line. Proctor’s injury might be a setback, but if the o-line is starting to gel, it’s not unreasonable to think we may have more games like this in store this season. The Defense Delivered When It Mattered Most OK, it wasn’t perfect. You don’t give up two touchdowns to Mason Taylor and 100 yards and a touchdown to Omar Cooper (side note: Does anyone else think Cooper might be a thorn in our side for years to come?) and claim the defense was exactly on point. That said, when the game hung in the balance, the defense came through. We’re talking: Michael Taaffe’s interception Jordyn Brooks’ 9 tackles, including 2 tackles for loss Chop Robinson’s red-zone sack A goal-line stand that forced a field goal rather than allowing a game-tying touchdown There’s a lot to clean up, and the team definitely needs more talent in the defense as a whole, but they showed up when it counted. It’s a start. So it’s worth appreciating the moment for what it is: The first win of the Hafley era, on a Dolphins takeover of MetLife stadium, no less The first time the Dolphins led at halftime The first time the Dolphins led, period So: Have the Dolphins arrived? Ha! No. The team still had busted coverages, dumb mistakes and an offense that mysteriously disappeared for much of the second half. But for the first time all season, the Dolphins started fast, protected the football, produced explosive plays, responded to adversity, controlled the line of scrimmage and closed out a close game. You know, the things winning teams do. In other words, they spent an afternoon looking a lot like the kind of team they’re trying to become. It’s worth celebrating.
author: Jim Reed

title: Miami Dolphins vs. New England Patriots: Three Reasons Why
summary: Miami Dolphins fans have enjoyed a post-win week that is always extra enjoyable when it comes against the Jets. But the time has come to put away that excitement and focus on another division opponent: The New England Patriots. For a few seasons, the Pats were a doormat, which they honestly deserve after 2 decades […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 25: Malik Willis #2 and Caleb Douglas #7 of the Miami Dolphins react after winning the game against the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium on October 25, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images Miami Dolphins fans have enjoyed a post-win week that is always extra enjoyable when it comes against the Jets. But the time has come to put away that excitement and focus on another division opponent: The New England Patriots. For a few seasons, the Pats were a doormat, which they honestly deserve after 2 decades of dominance. But they rebounded last year with a shocking Super Bowl run. That run could maybe be explained by smoke and mirrors (schedule, backup QBs faced, etc.) but make no mistake, the Pats are not a doormat right now. Does this mean the Dolphins have no chance? Absolutely not. 3 REASONS FOR HOPE THE DOLPHINS ARE BACK HOME This may seem like a cop-out reason. I have used it in previous home games and in fairness, playing at home is an advantage. But Joe Robbie Hard Rock Stadium has typically been a house of horrors for the Patriots. The Dolphins have hosted the Patriots 61 times in franchise history, including playoffs. The Pats have won in Miami 18 times . That’s a 0.295-win percentage. This isn’t simply a result of the Dolphins being good back in the 70s or when Dan Marino was under center. Since 2000 – the Belichick and Brady era up until the Vrabel era – the Pats have won in Miami 10 times in 26 contests (0.385-win percentage). Brady and the Pats won 9 of those, even including 2008 when Matt Cassel was playing for an injured Brady. In 2000, the Pats finished 5-11. They did not have a losing record again until 2020 when they went 7-9. In that span, the Pats averaged 12.2 wins every season, meaning an average of 3.8 losses per season. You could almost bank on one of those 4 annual losses to be against the Dolphins in Miami. Of course, the circumstances are different this season. The Dolphins are rebuilding and the Pats are coming off a SB run. On the surface, this seems like an easy W for the Pats. But in Miami… the Dolphins have as good a chance as any. The Pats just do not like it there. THE OFFENSE MAY BE FIGURING THINGS OUT I don’t want to make too much of the performance against the Jets. It is the Jets after all. But the Dolphins put up 377 yards at 5.5 yards per play against a stingy Jets defense that allows only 4.9 YPP (and that’s after the Dolphins). The Dolphins did it on the road too which is important because the offense has struggled on the road. In 2 home games, the Dolphins average 330 yards per game. In their 3 road games prior to week 7, the Dolphins averaged 247 total yards per game. That average was boosted by a 77-yard garbage time TD against the 49ers. The run game has been the engine driving the offense with Ollie Gordon II taking over for an injured De’Von Achane. He is averaging 4.7 YPC and has scored a TD in each of the last 4 games. Malik Willis is adding to that formula with some designed runs and key scrambles. Willis is 99 yards away from breaking Fiedler’s record for most rushing yards by a QB in a season for the franchise. But Willis also looked like a competent QB passing the ball against the Jets, which was a surprise to me. The Jets have a really good pass defense and given Willis’ struggles in prior games, I was expecting the worst. But he played really well. The Pats defense is decent against the run. They allow 3.9 YPC, which is tied for 12th best. They kept Josh Allen in check in their contest against the Bills with 5 attempts for 4 yards, so they can handle running QBs. But their pass defense is not as daunting, certainly not as good as the Jets statistically. While the Jets allow 6.7 YPA, the Pats are 20th at 7.4 YPA. They have a pressure percentage of 22.2%, which is 18th highest, but they only produce a hurry at a rate of 6%, which is 8th lowest. They blitz at a rate similar to the Jets (36.5 for NE, 36.4 for NYJ). But Miami possibly developed an answer for the blitz against the Jets. Perhaps that carries over. The Pats aren’t a bad defense by any means, but the matchup for Miami isn’t necessarily bad either. THE PASS RUSH WILL GET HOME THIS WEEK I have posted the tweets about Chop Robinson and NextGenStats has him tops in the league with a pressure rate of 23.4%. This graph shows that not only is the pressure rate high, but no one gets to the QB as fast as Chop . The issue is the sacks aren’t there. He’s close but that only counts in horseshoes, hand grenades, and nuclear bombs. This week, he’ll get a OT combo of Will Campbell and Morgan Moses. I don’t have access to all the fancy stats i.e. I ain’tagonna pay for it, but from what I can find, Campbell is having a good season. He’s not allowing pressures at a high rate (I’ve seen numbers like 5.6%). RT Morgan Moses on the other hand is parting the Red Sea for defenders, allowing a pressure rate of 14% . He will have his hands full with Robinson. The Pats have a good IOL in terms of pass protection with center Jared Wilson and guards Ben Brown and Alijah Vera-Tucker all ranked top 20 in pass block win rate. But both AVT and Brown were injured and missed time with injuries. Brown could be back, but AVT is now on injured reserve. Something has to give. I dislike making predictions, but I think Chop has his breakout game for this season with at least 2 sacks. BUT EVEN… if the pass rush doesn’t get home, the pressures could create some turnovers. The Pats are tied for the most INTS thrown with 8. In any case, I have a feeling the pass rush finally gets to it this week. It’s only a matter of time before it does. 3 REASONS FOR CONCERN PASS DEFENSE I don’t need to keep reminding you about the issues with Miami’s pass defense. Everyone knows about the awful completion percentage allowed. The Jets are a mid-level passing offense but still produced against the Dolphins. The Pats are a top 10 passing offense in both total yards, yards per game, yards per attempt, completion percentage, and passer rating. It’s not a question of whether the Pats passing game will produce, but rather how much they will produce. The Pats acquired AJ Brown from Philly and he will be an issue for whatever CB is facing him. But in the 3 games he has played so far, he only has 9 total catches on 20 targets. He may be due for a breakout game, but thus far, he has been quiet. The Dolphins did well against Garrett Wilson last week. The problem will come from RB Rhamondre Stevenson and – cover your eyes Dolphins – TE Hunter Henry. Stevenson is 3rd in targets with 24 and has 20 catches for 204 yards and a TD. He averages 9.4 yards after catch per reception with an average depth of target (ADOT) of 0.8 yards. He’s essentially getting a 1st down every time he catches the ball. Henry will be another TE thorn in the Dolphins’ flesh unless they get something figured out before Sunday. Henry is 2nd in targets with 31. He has 26 catches for 296 yards and a TD. He averaged 6.6 yards after catch per reception with an ADOT of 6 yards. The Pats spread out their targets fairly evenly, but they’ll most certainly attack the Dolphins with those 2 players. Don’t rule out rookie TE Eli Raridon either. He has 12 catches on 16 targets and 2 TDs this season. His target share has started going up. DeMario Douglas is the top target for the Pats with 34. He has 23 catches, 256 yards and 3 TDs. He works primarily in the slot thus will face rookie Chris Johnson most of the game. Johnson has played well in recent games, but he will be tested. Doubs and Hollins will also be factors. Summing it up, the Pats are going to throw the ball and have success. The real question is how much the Dolphins can limit the damage. title: Ollie Gordon: ‘Hafley definitely tried to connect with us more’
summary: The Miami Dolphins reset the franchise this season, from the front office through the coaching staff and onto the roster. The reset has brought with it learning curves, struggles, and growing pains. The team started the season 0-5, with talk that they could be the first team to finish a season 0-17. Last Sunday, they […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 11: Ollie Gordon II #0 of the Miami Dolphins celebrates during an NFL football game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Hard Rock Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins reset the franchise this season, from the front office through the coaching staff and onto the roster. The reset has brought with it learning curves, struggles, and growing pains. The team started the season 0-5, with talk that they could be the first team to finish a season 0-17. Last Sunday, they ended that talk with a solid win over the New York Jets, with every aspect of the team working together and showing their potential. Running back Ollie Gordon II, a second-year player, started the year as a depth player but has thrust himself into a starring role following an injury to De’Von Achane. Earlier this year, he sat down with former Dolphins tackle Terron Armstead on “The Set with Terron Armstead” podcast, and discussed the situation with the team. Released this week, the discussion included a comparison of first-year head coach Jeff Hafley and former head coach Mike McDaniel. “Haf has definitely tried to connect with us more,” Gordon said. “Every team meeting, he’s up in front of us, he is talking. He’s sitting in offensive meetings. He’ll sit halfway through, he goes to defense, he’ll come back. He puts his two cents in, which is good, you need that. He’s not just a one-sided coach. Obviously he was a defensive guy before, that’s his background, but he comes in, he’s like, ‘If I were scheming against y’all, I would do this and this. So I need y’all to make it look like this.’ I feel like that helps alot, especially coming from a defensive guy. “He’s lined up against every offense you can in this league, so it’s like he knows what he is talking about. I definitely feel like he is trying to be more connected to us and make us connected as a team.” Gordon also shared his three “welcome to the NFL” moments: “I feel like one was being on the field with [linebacker] Bobby Wagner when we played the [Washington] Commanders, bro. As a kid, I watched him. I watched the league, you know what I am saying? All of them. I wanted all of them [the Seattle Seahawks ’Legion of Boom’ defense of the 2010s]. [Safety] Earl [Thomas], [safety] Kam Chancellor, [cornerback] Richard [Sherman]. Being able to be on the field at the same time as him, I feel like that was huge. Just like to little me, like ‘Damn, you’re really on the field with Bobby Wagner.‘” Armstead, after pointing out that Gordon did not mention a hit or a specific play, but just being on the field with Wagner as a moment he remembers and made the NFL real to Gordon, said, “I love that, for real. People be acting like they are too proud or got too much ego to be like a fan of somebody. First time I played Terrell Suggs, same thing. Like seeing these guys on the other side that are legends, and still actively playing. Jared Allen, Julius Peppers, I’m like ‘Dog, this is dope.’” View this post on Instagram Gordon went on to his second and third moments, saying, “Two, the Baltimore game, me and my coach [running back coach Eric Studesville] got into it after I slipped…It was one of those where everyone is a grown man in the party. You can’t talk to one person crazy and if you get talked to crazy, you get a reaction from the other person. I feel like, that was my first time really just getting into it with a coach.” Gordon added, “I ain’t going to lie, that was so bad. I think I blacked out. I don’t even remember…We was cool, though, we was cool right after. We talked at halftime. We talked after the game. We was good.” For his third moment, Gordon turned to the team’s Week 10 game last year, when the Buffalo Bills visited Miami. “We ran a little outside zone,” the running back explained, “When I got the ball, [Bills defensive end Joey] Bosa was just looking at me. Bro must have just picked me up and flipped me over. Oh my God. My life flashed before my eyes and when I opened my eyes, I was on the ground.” Gordon went on to add that he thought the hit from Bosa was payback for earlier in the year when the running back scored his first career touchdown, running through the Bills’ defense – including Bosa. What do you think of Gordon’s three “welcome to the NFL” moments? Do you think Hafley is connecting with the players and having the players connect with each other better than McDaniel did?

title: Prove Them Wrong: An Open Letter to the Minnesota Vikings
summary: Dear Minnesota Vikings, As you may be aware, you are the most disrespected 6-0 NFL team that I have seen in my lifetime. Despite the fact that you are 2-0 in divisional games and have a defense that is allowing the league’s fewest points per game at 12.3, people are still calling you frauds. Those […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 2: A detail shot of the Salute to Service logo is seen on a helmet prior to an NFL football game between the Minnesota Vikings and the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on November 2, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Dear Minnesota Vikings, As you may be aware, you are the most disrespected 6-0 NFL team that I have seen in my lifetime. Despite the fact that you are 2-0 in divisional games and have a defense that is allowing the league’s fewest points per game at 12.3, people are still calling you frauds. Those voices have only grown louder over the past few weeks, and now there are comparisons between your starting quarterback and the one you let go to New York. The promises of Kevin O’Connell in locker room speeches saying that this offense is going to improve reverberate off of a concrete wall into thin air. Yes, Kyler Murray is protecting the football and not committing costly turnovers. He has also been inconsistent at times and has missed quite a few throws due to poor timing or inaccuracy. We thought this year was going to be different. Heck, Max Brosmer was 1-1 last year in games where he produced almost zero (if not negative) offensive value. Meanwhile, this season’s offense has to scratch and claw for 60 minutes just to score ONE TOUCHDOWN! We are witnessing the same problems with stagnancy (which seems to be a prevalent theme in your offensive scheme, Kevin) every time we have possession of the football. Every drive feels like ten steps forward with two steps back, culminating in a 50-yard Will Reichard field goal. I don’t even want to watch when you have the ball in between the 40s, because I know you aren’t going to get anywhere near the endzone. For example, this past week, Myles Price set you up with immaculate field position, and what did you do with it? You ran the ball four times and failed to convert on fourth down, turning the ball over on downs. RIDICULOUS. The lack of production on offense is why everybody and their mamas with a microphone and a camera are posting their very loud opinions on the internet. This week you play a divisional rival in the Detroit Lions. This is a chance to prove that your team is elite in all three phases and a true Super Bowl contender. You cannot rely on the defense to hold teams to fewer than 13 points every game. The silver lining is that I believe this defense CAN hold ANY team to 13 points or fewer, but still, you cannot rely on their dominance every week. The tension in my soul wants the confirmation that this offense can score 30+ points when called upon. Nothing would make me happier than for you to shut up all of these armchair analyst CLOWNS who think they know everything about football even though they probably haven’t watched one snap of a Minnesota Vikings game. However, at the end of the day, I am a Minnesota Vikings fan. I know this is a franchise built upon the foundation of excellence on defense. I am also starting to understand why all of these talking heads are so low on you, the Minnesota Vikings. It’s because when they watch you play, they’re bored. They don’t care about history; they just want to be entertained. Nothing is less entertaining to faux media jabronis than elite defense and low-scoring games. Maybe it is a personal problem that has compelled me to write this letter. Why do I expose myself to these opinions on social media and the internet? Part of it is so I can write informed pieces about the narratives surrounding this Vikings team. The other reason is that it fuels my passion. I see the potential, and I know that if this offense can start executing, this is going to be an incredibly scary team. Please, just shut the critics up. Please, please, PLEASE! I now want to speak directly to you, Kevin. You need to get it together. I believe in your ability as a head coach in the NFL; I really do! You have cultivated a winning culture with this franchise, and the results have shown in the regular season. As I am sure you are aware, you have failed to lead this team to a single playoff victory in your tenure at the helm. Your system failed a young quarterback before he failed you (in some eyes), and as a coach brought in for your offensive prowess, you have not delivered on the expectation of efficient and effective offenses. So, what is the deal? Are you calling the right plays and your players just aren’t delivering the results? Are you lacking more explosive playmakers? Are you making the wrong decisions in certain situations, leading to uninspiring results? Do you need to focus more on managing the game and let someone else call the plays? What is it? All I’m going to say is, whatever the issue(s), please fix it. Figure it out so we can all stop asking these questions. To the offense: you need to be better. I’m looking directly at you, Will Fries. You’ve done a nice job cleaning up some of the penalties we were seeing in the first few weeks of the season, but that’s not enough. You need to start scoring some touchdowns. Just know, the whole world is laughing at you and sees you as the downfall of an otherwise dominant team. You frequently start with great field position only to squander it. You have possessed the ball more than any other offense in the NFL, yet you’re in the bottom 5 of points scored (probably lower if you’re only counting touchdowns). Things just aren’t adding up, and you better start materializing the vision of your head coach. You very well know the strength of your team is the defense. Blake, Eric, Jalen, Caleb, Dominique, Dallas, Andrew, Josh, Byron, Isaiah, and Harrison, I see the work you are putting in. Your excellence is not going unnoticed. You are part of an excellent and potentially historic defensive unit. You wreak so much havoc and create so much chaos that opposing offenses don’t know what to do to attack you. Sure, you’ve given up a few big plays this year and some touchdowns. However, you make the adjustments to thwart any offensive game plan. We saw it against Green Bay, New Orleans, and Indianapolis. You let Green Bay score 22 first-half points and then shut them out in the second half. You let New Orleans march down the field on a long drive and score a touchdown in the first quarter, only to hold them to 6 points for the rest of the game. You allowed Jonathan Taylor to break a long touchdown run, only to turn Danny Dimes into Danny Schillings and dominate the rest of the way. You are not the problem here, and I pray you continue to do what you do. Take care of your bodies and stay healthy, because we need you. I will leave you with these parting words. I believe in the 2026 Minnesota Vikings. I have high hopes and expectations for this team. You will be playing meaningful football in January and possibly February. You have the leadership, drive, and determination to bring Minnesota its first Lombardi trophy. You just have to not get in your own way. Believe in yourselves, believe in each other, believe in the Minnesota Vikings’ culture. You have thousands of fans rooting for you, and we will be here with you until the possibly bitter, but hopefully glorious, end. You have my support and the support of many others. I speak for many when I say I love this team and only want the best for you. Until Next Skol.

(Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We’ve got the results of our SB Nation Reacts polls for this week, ladies and gentlemen, so let’s take a look at what our readers had to say about our Minnesota Vikings and the questions we had about them this week. Our first question, as always, was whether or not everyone thought that our favorite team was moving in the right direction. As we’ve said numerous times this week, the Vikings are the last undefeated team in the league at 6-0. But, in a truly fascinating trend, it seems that the more games the Vikings win, the less confident our readers are in their direction. Of those who responded to our poll, just under half. . .49%, to be exact. . .are confident of the direction that the NFL’s last undefeated team is heading in. And as much as I’d love to vehemently disagree with them, honestly, it’s not difficult to see where they’re coming from on this one. The offense just continues to struggle at that whole “scoring points” thing that they’re supposed to be doing, and even though the defense and special teams are doing yeoman’s work out there every week, it’s hard to be confident in this team until they can put together a complete game. At this point, all we can do is hope that something clicks, because we’re rapidly approaching a point in the season where teams just are what they are. Our other question for this week has to do with the league’s best defense. More specifically, who has been the best player on the league’s best defense during their 6-0 start. We gave you several names to choose from, and when it was all said and done, I think our readers made the best choice. Of those who responded, 45% said that linebacker Blake Cashman was the Vikings’ defensive MVP through the team’s first six games, and given the way he’s looked over the past few weeks, it’s pretty difficult to argue with that. He was just named the NFC’s Defensive Player of the Week after acting as a one-man wrecking crew against the Colts this past Sunday, and has been the heart and soul of the defense so far this year. Dallas Turner was a fairly close second, garnering 34% of the vote. Jalen Redmond checked in at the third-place spot with 14% of the vote, with “someone else” picking up 4% of the vote and Byron Murphy Jr. picking up 3% of the vote in our poll. Those are our SB Nation Reacts results for this week, ladies and gentlemen. As always, we want to thank everyone who took the time to cast their votes in our polls for this week and discuss everything in the comments. We’ll have another poll for you next week, so keep your eyes open for that! Check out the FanDuel Sportsbook , the official sportsbook partner of SB Nation .

Injury designation definitions: Probable = the league defines a Probable injury designation as a 75% or greater chance of playing. Historically, 95% of players designated probable are active and played on game day. Questionable = the league defines a Questionable injury designation as being ‘uncertain’ of whether the player will play or not. This replaces the former definition of having a 50% chance of playing. Historically, 70-75% of players with a Questionable injury designation were active and played on game day. Doubtful = The league defines a Doubtful injury designation to mean the player is unlikely to participate in the game. In practical terms, teams use the designation when a player has less than a 50% chance to suit up, and active game appearances from this designation remain rare. Historically only around 6% of players with a Doubtful designation are active and played on game day. Out = will not play. Players with this designation are not active on game day and league rules prohibit them from playing. title: Vikes Views: Who Ya Got? Minnesota Vikings at Detroit Lions
summary: The undefeated Minnesota Vikings will have their biggest challenge of the year as they head to the Motor City to take on the Detroit Lions. It will be strength against strength when the high-powered Lions offense is on the field against the best defense in the league. Series Record: 82-45-2 Road Record: 37-27-1 Largest Win: […]
full_text: Sep 25, 2011; Minneapolis, MN, USA; Minnesota Vikings defensive end Brian Robison (96) sacks Detroit Lions quarterback Matthew Stafford (9) in the third quarter at Mall of America Field. The Lions defeated the Vikings 26-23 in overtime. Mandatory Credit: Marilyn Indahl-USA TODAY Sports | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The undefeated Minnesota Vikings will have their biggest challenge of the year as they head to the Motor City to take on the Detroit Lions. It will be strength against strength when the high-powered Lions offense is on the field against the best defense in the league. Series Record: 82-45-2 Road Record: 37-27-1 Largest Win: 34-0, November 9, 1980 Largest Defeat: 45-7, December 12, 1981 Streak: W2 The Vikings are giving up a league-low 12.3 points per game, 4.9 fewer than the second-best Kansas City Chiefs. The Lions rank 26th in the league, allowing 27.5 points per game. The Lions have the 2nd highest scoring offense in the league with 30.7 PPG. The Vikings are 24th with 20.8 PPG. The Vikings boast the best kick return and punt return averages in the league. Pair that with the best kicker in football, and special teams have become a real advantage. The Lions rank first in offensive success rate on first down (50%), while the Vikings rank 32nd (29.2%). Motown legends The Four Tops will play a halftime show. Justin Jefferson has been a Lions killer throughout his career, averaging 107 yards per game and a 72% catch rate when targeted.. However, he has averaged just 53 YPG in the last four meetings. Unfortunately, we won’t get to see Kerby Joseph reunited with Justin Jefferson this week. The modern rivalry of the NFC North has been fun the last few years. It was nice to have the two annual wins penciled in back in the day, but I do enjoy it now that the Lions are an actual NFL team. It’s a clash of styles for two familiar foes. One of the best offenses in the league will face the definitively best defense in the league. Something has to give on Sunday. Either the Lions prove they can move the ball against an elite defense, or the Vikings continue their march toward becoming the most feared defense in football. Everyone seems to be on the Lions, either because the believe in them, or the Vikings are “due” for a loss. I’m not picking anything based on who is “due” anything. I know the Viking defense is due a turnover twice a game. They’re due another 2nd half shutout. I’m not picking this team to lose until I see them face an offense they can’t stop. We’ll get to enjoy watching them against the two best offenses in the league the next two weeks. I’m taking them to win this week, if I’m right, they’ll be my pick next week too. Vikings 20 – Lions 13

title: How the Vikings Can Neutralize Jahmyr Gibbs and Upset Detroit
summary: How can the Minnesota Vikings beat the Detroit Lions? Simple—exploit Jahmyr Gibbs. On the latest episode of The Real Forno Show, host Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano broke down the Vikings’ key to victory, a wild NFC North trade ahead of the deadline, and why Brian Flores’ defense could be the ultimate difference-maker on […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 11: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions warms up during the NFL game at State Farm Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. The Lions defeated the Cardinals 45-21. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images How can the Minnesota Vikings beat the Detroit Lions? Simple—exploit Jahmyr Gibbs. On the latest episode of The Real Forno Show , host Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano broke down the Vikings’ key to victory, a wild NFC North trade ahead of the deadline, and why Brian Flores’ defense could be the ultimate difference-maker on Sunday. The show opened with blockbuster news: the Chicago Bears acquired DT Jeffrey Simmons from the Tennessee Titans for two first-round picks and a fourth. Forness questioned the fit within Dennis Allen’s read-and-react scheme: “If Simmons comes in and it’s just Jeffrey Simmons, it’s not gonna matter that much.” The Bears still lack edge rushers, raising questions about whether the move translates. Meanwhile, the Vikings have been reportedly aggressive in the run up to the deadline, with names like Maxx Crosby and Jalen Carter circulating. “If you bring in Jalen Carter, that’s become the centerpiece of your defense,” Forness said. “That is the guy that you are building everything around.” He emphasized that such a move wouldn’t be for 2026 alone—it would be a long-term foundational piece, especially with Andrew Van Ginkel and Kyle Van Noy hitting free agency. Forness was blunt on the quarterback front: only Daniel Jones and Kirk Cousins, both familiar with Kevin O’Connell’s system, make sense as trade targets. “You’re not trading for great players at this point. You’re trading for somebody who you hope can steer the ship.” On J.J. McCarthy’s departure, he added: “He got himself traded. The Vikings didn’t do it because they wanted to give up on him. He earned it.” The heart of the episode centered on neutralizing Gibbs in pass protection. Last Christmas, the Vikings forced Gibbs into a career-high 15 pass-protection snaps—over 35% of his total—resulting in seven pressures and a sack. “They made it so Gibbs was basically ineffective because of their blitzing and how they attacked,” Forness explained. With Van Ginkel, Blake Cashman, Ivan Pace Jr., and Dallas Turner matching up on him, the plan is straightforward: make Gibbs block, or take him off the field entirely. Stefano noted the broader impact: “By having him pass block, he’s not out in their patterns either.” Flores’ defense, refined over three seasons, has reached what Forness called his “opus” and a “pile driver onto a steel chair.” Stefano captured the confidence: “Our defense does. They know what they’re doing. The question is, how quickly can Goff figure it out? And I don’t think anybody’s figured it out this season.” Forness agreed: “I do think that this defense is good enough to win a Super Bowl on their own.” Key Points: Gibbs exploitation : Vikings will blitz in the 70–85% range, forcing Gibbs to pass-protect or leave the field Flores’ finalized defense : Three years of refinement into a system nobody has solved Trade deadline : Maxx Crosby and Jalen Carter as long-term defensive cornerstones; Daniel Jones as affordable QB insurance McCarthy’s exit : Talent was never the question—”He got himself traded” Offensive key : Kyler Murray must “take a deep breath, play more relaxed, and trust Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison” Lions’ defensive weakness : 30th in EPA per play, 31st in explosive play percentage allowed Prediction : Vikings favored by 3–3.5; Forness picks Minnesota: “I think they’re gonna be able to take down Goff” Listen: View Link Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: The Vikings’ defense has yet to be solved, and if Flores’ unit can again turn Jahmyr Gibbs into a liability, Sunday could be a statement win. For the full breakdown—trade deadline analysis, quarterback rumors, and complete Xs and Os—listen to The Real Forno Show , a Minnesota Vikings podcast from Vikings 1st & SKOL. Fan with Us!!! Tyler Forness @TheRealForno of Vikings 1st & SKOL @Vikings1stSKOL and A to Z Sports @AtoZSportsNFL , with Dave Stefano @Luft_Krigare producing this Vikings 1st & SKOL production, the @RealFornoShow found at the @BleavNetwork . What do you think? Can the Vikings exploit Gibbs and prove they’re the team to beat in the NFC North, or will Jared Goff finally find the answers?

title: Five Good Questions with Pride of Detroit
summary: While we haven’t gotten that many opportunities to do so this year, this week we’ve gotten the chance to gather some intel on the Minnesota Vikings’ opponent for this week from the folks who run the SB Nation site that covers them throughout the season. I got the opportunity to exchange Five Good Questions with […]
full_text: While we haven’t gotten that many opportunities to do so this year, this week we’ve gotten the chance to gather some intel on the Minnesota Vikings’ opponent for this week from the folks who run the SB Nation site that covers them throughout the season. I got the opportunity to exchange Five Good Questions with Ryan Mathews from Pride of Detroit, SB Nation’s home for everything about the Detroit Lions. You can see my answers to the questions that he sent me over at POD (or on the front page here). Here are the questions that I sent over to him, along with his responses. 1) It seems like every time we talk about the Vikings and the Lions, the subject of Dan Campbell’s aggressiveness on fourth down comes up. This past Sunday, he chose to go for it on a 4th-and-1 from his own 24-yard line in a 17-17 game with five minutes left in regulation, and the Lions didn’t convert. They dodged a bullet when the Packers missed the go-ahead field goal, and ultimately won the game. Are Lions’ fans still fans of Campbell’s aggressiveness or do they feel he veers into recklessness too frequently in these situations now that he’s been the head coach for a while? In the moment, it felt incredibly reckless, even by Dan Campbell’s standards. It was a long yard to gain, and with the way the offensive line was having trouble keeping Packers defenders out of the backfield, the play call felt uninspired at best. But after hearing Campbell’s explanation, it’s hard to argue with his rationale: Detroit didn’t want to punt and run the risk of letting Green Bay eat the clock and score without having a chance at rebuttal. Considering the Lions’ offense was moving the ball all day long, it makes a lot of sense to put the onus on that side of the ball to keep them in the game. However, the issue I took with that particular drive was the sequence of play calls prior to going for it on fourth down. Jahmyr Gibbs arguably reached the line to gain on first down, but Campbell decided not to challenge the play–and in his defense, overturning the spot of the ball doesn’t happen all too often. But after going to Gibbs again on second and third down, the latter being a short pass, it felt like poor play-calling choices if the plan all along was going for it on fourth down that drive. In fact, I took a bigger issue with a different fourth down Detroit went for earlier in the game. At the tail end of the third quarter and from the Packers’ 6-yard line, Detroit was up by three points and decided to go for it on fourth-and-5. Going up six at that point in the game, and forcing Green Bay to find the end zone to take the lead with only a quarter to go felt like a better decision. 2) The Lions’ defense has had significant issues this year, particularly against the pass, where they’re 32nd in the league in both yards allowed and touchdown passes allowed. Do you think this is more of a function of the personnel they have in the back end of the defense or are there other reasons that they’ve had problems stopping teams through the air so far? With the secondary, it’s been a mix; a little bit of this and a little bit of that. Injuries completely ravaged the safety position at the start of the season. Detroit were already without Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, but not long after, both Avonte Maddox and Thomas Harper were sidelined with injuries. Detroit essentially ran out of contingencies after Week 4, and after both injuries and disappointing play took their toll, the Lions were desperate enough to turn to rookie fifth-round nickel cornerback Keith Abney II–he played nearly 60 snaps at deep safety against the Cardinals and did a pretty good job. Good enough he played 34 snaps, this time in more of a box safety role, against the Packers last week despite the return of Brian Branch. Branch’s return last week was a seismic shot in the arm for their defense as a whole. He picked up an interception and was his usual self in run defense, recording three run stops according to Next Gen Stats–tied for second among Lions’ defenders in Week 7. Kerby Joseph did return to practice on Wednesday, but don’t expect him to play in this one. Detroit usually gets their players at least a week before they return them to the field. In short, much of Detroit’s shortcomings on defense stemmed from miscommunications, misunderstanding of personnel, and missed opportunities from the secondary. Cornerback play could have been better, and the Lions were forced to shake things up at CB2 after Rock Ya-Sin’s injury, but much like the safety room, it’s healing and performing much better in recent weeks–even if that means going from 31st in EPA/play on defense in the first four weeks to ranking 18th in EPA/play over their last two games. Throw in some positive turnover differentials and Lions fans couldn’t have imagined seeing this kind of improvement more than a month ago. 3) The Vikings come into this one sporting the best defense in the league by most measures, but the Lions have been able to have a measure of success against them in recent years. How do you think Drew Petzig and company are going to go about trying to attack Brian Flores’ group and trying to solve them this time around? Earlier in the week, Flores had some incredibly complimentary words to share about Jared Goff: “Command of the offense, cadence, his ability to just extract information from the defense with shifts, motions, cadence, and his ability to gather that information and then make the correct reads and throws, is high level.” “Statistically, he’s been one of the best quarterbacks, not even statistically, period. He’s been one of the best quarterbacks in the National Football League over, you know, a good amount of time. And so, yes, he’s grown quite a bit. That’s what you expect, as guys get more time under their belt. I think he’s one of the best in the league and they’ve got a great skill group and he knows how to, you know, distribute the ball to all of them.” It hasn’t all been perfect with Goff and Petzing despite the numbers, and that might sound privileged considering they rank third in EPA/play and second in success rate on offense, but there’s still real room for this offense to work through some of their kinks. It isn’t all perfect along the offensive line as Detroit reintroduces Cade Mays at center, and the ground game is still missing some of those home-run plays from Jahmyr Gibbs. But there is something that Detroit found a lot of success in doing last week: crossing routes and working the middle of the field to open up the shots outside the numbers. Those kinds of long-developing routes require the offensive line holding up in pass protection, and they helped hold the Packers to the 24th-lowest pressure rate in Week 7. The key matchup here, in my opinion, is Goff & Mays vs. Flores. Against the best coach in football, it’s a fair handicap match. Mays got a full load of snaps, hopefully knocked off some of the rust in the process, and is up to the challenge of sorting through the eye candy Flores puts in front of him. 4) Give us one player on each side of the ball for the Lions that fans of the Vikings might not be familiar with that you think will be a big contributor to any success that the Lions are going to have on Sunday. Detroit’s offense is full of household names, so it’s a little more difficult to give you an under-the-radar sort of player who’s expected to be a big contributor on that side of the ball. Here’s the name of a player who will certainly play some snaps on offense as the team’s RB2 and serve as a four-core special teamer: Sione Vaki. He comes on in a lot of third down situations as a pass blocker, but he is liable to get a touch or two just to keep the defenses honest and not completely keying in on what Detroit’s called. For the defensive side of the ball, the aforementioned Keith Abney II has been intriguing over the past couple of weeks. His safety play has been mostly sound, he’s a willing tackler in run defense, and…

summary: The New England Patriots will wait for the weekend before making a final call on No. 1. A.J. Brown headlines the team’s questionable to face the Miami Dolphins after going from a limited participant to missing consecutive practices to end AFC East prep. full_text: Foxborough, MA - October 28: New England Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown at practice on October 28, 2026. (Photo by John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images The New England Patriots will wait for the weekend before making a final call on No. 1. A.J. Brown headlines the team’s questionable to face the Miami Dolphins after going from a limited participant to missing consecutive practices to end AFC East prep. The three-time All-Pro wide receiver is dealing with a knee issue that flared up while also working back from the high ankle sprain that sent him to injured reserve in September. “His status is questionable, like some other players,” head coach Mike Vrabel told reporters on Friday. “We’ll see how he comes in tomorrow and we’ll make a decision.” Running back TreVeyon Henderson, linebacker Christian Elliss and cornerback Carlton Davis III are also officially questionable for Sunday’s 4:25 p.m. ET kickoff at Hard Rock Stadium. OUT Patriots No players listed Dolphins OT Kadyn Proctor (concussion) While no Patriots have been ruled out for the divisional meeting, the Dolphins will be without the No. 12 overall pick in the 2026 NFL draft. Proctor stayed sidelined for three straight practices while in the league’s concussion protocol. The Alabama product has started all six games during rookie campaign and seen 100 percent of the snaps for the offensive line. QUESTIONABLE Patriots RB TreVeyon Henderson (illness) WR A.J. Brown (knee, ankle) LB Christian Elliss (chest) CB Carlton Davis III (neck) Dolphins CB JuJu Brents (neck, concussion) CB Reese Taylor (quad) Brown has played 101 out of 122 offensive snaps since being activated midway through October. The June trade acquisition has caught six passes for 75 yards through those two starts. And with fellow veterans Romeo Doubs and Mack Hollins both on injured reserve , the Patriots stand with three healthy wide receivers on the 53-man roster in DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism III and Kyle Williams. “Just like everything else when you come out of the game or a long week, practice on Monday and evaluate the player. Just wasn’t able to finish practice on Wednesday,” Vrabel said. “So we continue to treat him and we’ll see where he is tomorrow.” In addition to Brown’s recent absences, Henderson was not spotted for back-to-back practices because of an illness. The sophomore running back has logged 203 rushing yards, 45 receiving yards and one touchdown through 57 touches this fall for an active depth chart also featuring Rhamondre Stevenson and Corey Kiner. On the defensive side of the questionable, Elliss has been a full participant with a chest injury for the past two weeks while Davis returned in full this week following a neck injury. The off-ball linebacker ranks atop the Patriots with 51 tackles through seven starts and has tacked on one sack, one forced fumble and a handful of quarterback hits. The cornerback, on the other hand, is on track for his return after missing three games in a row. “We’re really here focused on trying to get a win on the road in the division,” added Vrabel, “and we’ll make a decision on the guys that are questionable tomorrow.”

summary: With the NFL trade deadline coming up on Nov. 10, the rumor mill is starting to work overtime. And one member of the New England Patriots is among the names recently mentioned: defensive tackle Christian Barmore. According to a report by Albert Breer of Sports Illustrated, the veteran defender “could be had” via trade in […]
full_text: With the NFL trade deadline coming up on Nov. 10, the rumor mill is starting to work overtime. And one member of the New England Patriots is among the names recently mentioned: defensive tackle Christian Barmore. According to a report by Albert Breer of Sports Illustrated, the veteran defender “could be had” via trade in the coming two weeks: The Patriots are deep in the AFC race, but veteran DT Christian Barmore could be had, having played only 41.9% of the team’s defensive snaps, falling behind Milton Williams and Cory Durden in the team’s rotation. As noted in the excerpt, Barmore has been on the field for 41.9% of the Patriots’ defensive snaps this season — 13th most on the team overall and third among defensive tackles behind the aforementioned Milton Williams and Cory Durden. In those snaps, he has registered six tackles, three sacks and a forced fumble. His 12 combined quarterback pressures are ranked second among New England’s interior linemen behind only Williams’ 14. Whether or not that production is living up to his $17.1 million salary cap number is up for debate, however. Fact is that New England, currently ranked near the bottom in available cap space, could create significant savings by moving on from the 27-year-old: depending on the timing of a hypothetical trade, as much as $8 million could come off the Patriots’ books this year, plus almost $41 million the next two seasons. Whether that is enough for the team to put Barmore on the trade market will be seen — something that also is true for potential compensation. The Patriots getting the same haul the Titans received for fellow DT Jeffery Simmons, who was traded to Chicago for a package involving two first-round draft picks, is doubtful. The Patriots will travel to Miami this weekend to play the Dolphins.

full_text: After enjoying a weekend off, the New England Patriots are back in action this Sunday. Their opponent coming out of the mini-bye is a familiar one, at least on paper: the Miami Dolphins. However, these are not the same Dolphins that lost both of their games to the Patriots in 2025. Led by new head coach Jeff Hafley, they have overhauled significant portions of their roster and staff. Are they better off as a result? So far, the record doesn’t say so. That said, unlike the Patriots, the Dolphins are entering Week 8 off a victory — their first of the season. Still, according to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Patriots are seen as seven-point favorites entering the game. Will they live up to that status? Or will the Dolphins manage to defend their home turf? Let’s find out what Pats Pulpit’s staff and community think. Even a shorthanded Patriots team playing on the road should therefore be able to come away victoriously, especially after 10 days of rest. title: Patriots vs. Dolphins weather forecast for NFL Week 8
summary: The last time the New England Patriots traveled to Florida, they were soundly beaten 35-6 by the Jacksonville Jaguars. One of the contributing factors to that loss appeared to be the team struggling with the heat and humidity. At least one of the two might not have that big an impact come Sunday’s game against […]
full_text: The last time the New England Patriots traveled to Florida, they were soundly beaten 35-6 by the Jacksonville Jaguars. One of the contributing factors to that loss appeared to be the team struggling with the heat and humidity. At least one of the two might not have that big an impact come Sunday’s game against the Miami Dolphins. According to NFL Weather , temperatures at Hard Rock Stadium will not exceed 78°F during the Week 8 contest between the two division rivals. The National Weather Service , meanwhile, projects highs near 82°F for the day. What will differentiate that game from the Jaguars one, however, is the precipitation. Whereas that Week 3 contest was played in sunny conditions, this one won’t: the chance of rain has been calculated at 80% with showers and thunderstorms an option. In addition, wind gusts of up to 26 mph are projected for the area (although in-stadium conditions may vary). All in all, however, the weather could have an impact on the contest — as could the Patriots’ conditioning. “We have to be conditioned,” said head coach Mike Vrabel this week. “The better that we play, the more we possess the ball, the fresher we’ll stay defensively. Hopefully we get the receivers into a rotation. The backs, we rotate. I don’t think that the offensive linemen will necessarily rotate. We may play a couple guys based on who’s available. That remains to be seen. The edge guys, we rotate. We try to rotate along the defensive line. We like to have our best players available to help us win.” Kickoff between the Patriots and Dolphins on Sunday is scheduled for 4:25 p.m. ET.

title: The importance of during the Saints’ bye week
summary: This bye week for the New Orleans Saints is the most important one in the current era of the franchise. At a time when this team entered the season with so much hope and promise, built on how last season ended, the trust of the fan base is beginning to wane. The team showed flashes […]
full_text: PARIS, FRANCE - OCTOBER 25: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints fumbles the ball during the second quarter of the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Stade de France on October 25, 2026 in Paris, France. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images This bye week for the New Orleans Saints is the most important one in the current era of the franchise. At a time when this team entered the season with so much hope and promise, built on how last season ended, the trust of the fan base is beginning to wane. The team showed flashes of a promising future: a young head coach with previous success as an offensive coordinator, a rookie quarterback who appeared to be a budding superstar, two solid young offensive tackles who looked to be the bookends of what should have been a competent offensive line, and a front office that finally seemed to be turning the page and getting its act together. After the first half of the season, all of that appears to have been misjudged. Now, this team sits with only two wins, the offense that seems lost, and two recent draft classes that are beginning to look like major whiffs. The head coach can’t seem to put together an offensive game plan that allows the team to start games effectively and sustain success for an entire contest. So, this bye week means a lot. As things currently stand, the Saints are still on the cusp of competing for a very weak division. However, if they come out of this bye week with the same offensive issues, an inability to run the football, a team that has managed to score no more than six total first-quarter points all season, and consistent problems with blocking up front, then the statement made by the owner two weeks ago, which still looms over this team like a cloud, will only ring hollow in the ears of the Who Dat Nation faithful. If the Saints come out of this bye week without making changes to the coaching staff, they will absolutely have to demonstrate meaningful changes on the field. And if they don’t, trust will be broken, and apathy will begin to set in. The last thing any professional sports franchise should want is for its fan base to become apathetic toward the team. At least frustration stems from passion, and that passion can drive change and progress. Apathy, on the other hand, only leads to the team being ignored and fans finding better ways to spend their time and, most importantly, their money. This upcoming week will be incredibly important, and the results of the work, sacrifice, and development of this roster and coaching staff will be evident from the opening moments of the next game. Hope is gone. Faith is low. Trust is slipping away. The Saints must approach this bye week with a sense of urgency and make the necessary changes to restore confidence in this team and organization.

title: Saints Draft Position: NFL Week 8
summary: The New Orleans Saints lost another game, and sadly, it really didn’t change much in the draft order. Like these past two seasons, the bad teams keep losing, and it’s keeping the Saints away from a single-digit pick, so in the bye week, the Saints are set to select at pick 10 in the NFL […]
full_text: WEST LAFAYETTE, IN - OCTOBER 10: Minnesota Golden Gophers offensive lineman Greg Johnson (65) warms up on the field during the college football game between the Purdue Boilermakers and Minnesota Golden Gophers on October 10, 2026, at Ross-Ade Stadium in West Lafayette, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints lost another game, and sadly, it really didn’t change much in the draft order. Like these past two seasons, the bad teams keep losing, and it’s keeping the Saints away from a single-digit pick, so in the bye week, the Saints are set to select at pick 10 in the NFL Draft. Here are some players the Saints could select at 10. OG Greg Johnson Looking at top guard options, Greg Johnson is the guy in the first round, although 10 may be a little bit of a reach, guard is becoming more and more important in today’s NFL, and the Saints need a starting RG. If they do not move on from Cesar Ruiz before the deadline, it’s going to happen in the offseason. Although I do like Jeremiah Wright, there’s no reason to believe he can start next season, and I don’t want the Saints to rely on that to happen. The other caveat to this selection is the coaching staff. If Kellen Moore, this coaching staff, and the front office are still in place, I don’t want the Saints to make this selection. They have good offensive linemen that are regressing under them already, so I wouldn’t expect a rookie offensive lineman to have much success. However, it’s the perfect selection for a new coaching staff and GM who hopefully knows the trenches, and a new head coach who can elevate this rookie. DL Xavier Gilliam The caveat put in place for the Johnson pick should be here as well. The Saints haven’t done well lately at drafting defensive linemen. Doesn’t matter if it’s a defensive tackle or edge rusher, it doesn’t work out. So, if a new staff is put in place, Xavier Gilliam would be a really good option. He is incredibly athletic, extremely quick off the snap, can win against offensive linemen with power and different pass-rush moves, and is equally dominant against the run. Gilliam is a player you will see throughout any game blowing up plays in the backfield, but he also makes the right decisions and has a consistent impact when he’s not creating incredible moments. The Saints do not have a DT anywhere close to the player Gilliam is on their roster, and putting him next to Chase Young could really elevate this entire defense.
