title: Draft prospects for the NY Giants in Week 9 of college football
summary: Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 9 of the 2026 College Football Season. The Giants are on their bye week this week and are guaranteed to control the NFC East regardless of what happens, so we’re all free to sit back and simply enjoy a weekend of football without […]
full_text: Miami defensive tackle Justin Scott recovers a fumble against Pittsburgh. | ISI Photos via Getty Images Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 9 of the 2026 College Football Season. The Giants are on their bye week this week and are guaranteed to control the NFC East regardless of what happens, so we’re all free to sit back and simply enjoy a weekend of football without stakes As usual, we’re using college football and the NFL Draft as a lens through which to look at the New York Giants. In particular, we’re going to look at the Giants’ needs as we perceive them, and focus on players who could fit those needs. Texas Tech vs. Arizona ESPN – Noon Don’t look now, but Arizona is quietly making noise and could force their way into the College Football Playoffs. Texas Tech is more highly regarded right now, but Arizona is a fun team to watch. Keep an eye on freshman linebacker Dash Fifita, younger brother of Arizona QB Noah Fifita. Dash is coming off a game against Iowa State with 2.5 tackles for a loss and 2.0 sacks… At 5-foot-7, 190 pounds. He won’t be draft eligible for two more years and might not be a draftable prospect due to his size, but he’s fun. For our purposes, however, I want to turn to the Texas Tech defense. Player spotlight: A.J. Holmes Jr. (iDL, Texas Tech) Holmes jr. transferred to Texas Tech a year ago, and was a productive member of that disruptive defensive front which carried them into the playoffs. He’s having a fantastic year as “The Guy” on Texas Tech’s defensive line. So far he has 6.5 tackles for a loss and 6.5 sacks (leads the Big 12) though 7 games, as well as 23 total tackles and a forced fumble. Holmes Jr. is listed at 6-foot-3, 300 pounds, but plays with solid leverage and anchor, as well as impressive explosiveness and power. He excels at firing out of his stance and using heavy hands to rock blockers backward before shedding and using his agility and burst to make a play on the ball. He would likely be best in a 1-gap system at the next level, and could fit the Giants as a 3 or 5-technique depending on their personnel package. As things stand now, Holmes Jr. is probably a second round pick, but he could work his way into the “1st – 2nd” range if he continues to produce as a disruptor. (8) BYU vs. Arizona State Fox – 3:30 p.m. Most of the nation will be watching BYU to see if they can rebound after their 39-31 loss to UCF a week ago. BYU catapulted themselves into the national spotlight and the Playoff conversation with their upset win over Notre Dame two weeks ago, but couldn’t avoid the letdown game the following week. For our purposes, however, we’ll be taking a look at the Sundevils. Arizona State has produced some interesting prospects over the last couple years, notably Cam Skattebo, WR Jordan Tyson, and now QB Sam Leavitt (currently at LSU). We’re going to stick to the offensive side of the ball and one of the fastest risers in recent weeks. Player spotlight: Reed Harris (WR, Arizona State) Both Harris and fellow WR Omario Miller could be of interest to the Giants, and both could be solid Day 2 picks. We’re going to focus on Harris, because he’s having a better year and his physical profile could be more appealing to the Giants. Harris is a transfer from Boston College and is an imposing presence on the field. He’s listed at 6-foot-5, 220 pounds and looks every bit of it. He appears to have solid speed and agility for a big receiver and plays with plenty of power. He has a massive catch radius as well as the ability to drag defenders as a ball carrier. There would likely be some overlap between Harris and Malachi Fields, however redundancy isn’t necessarily a bad thing. The Giants have increasingly used Malik Nabers in the slot and he’s responded well, getting nearly as many yards from the slot as out wide, despite having far fewer snaps as a slot receiver. Adding a second big wide receiver could allow the Giants to use Nabers as a slot receiver even more often, or create size mismatches with smaller corners. North Carolina vs. (1) Miami ABC – 7:30 p.m. We’re checking in on the ACC in the evening slate. The matchups between Ohio State and USC or Texas and Mississippi State may be more compelling, but the Hurricanes have a number of defensive players that could interest the Giants. Likewise, QB Darian Mensah could be one of the linchpins early in the draft, and sophomore WR Malachi Toney is simply a human highlight reel. Player Spotlight: Justin Scott (iDL, Miami) The Giants might not want to spend a first round pick on a defensive tackle — or the board may not line up for them even if they do. But, as noted up above, this is shaping up to be an impressively deep defensive tackle class. We’ve already talked about Miami defensive tackle Ahmad Moten, and his teammate is a high-upside player as well. Scott has a versatile frame at 6-foot-4, 305 pounds with enough length and strength to play any gap alignment in an even or odd front. He boasts an explosive first step and should be a dangerous gap-shooter in a one-gap defense, while also having a powerful lower body to take on blockers in the run game. In addition to great explosiveness and power, he also has the kind of wide-open motor and competitive toughness we’ve come to expect from this Miami defense. That combination should appeal to the Giants’ coaching staff, and Scott could easily step into Shelby Harris’ spot as a 3, 4i, or 5-technique. There’s currently some speculation that Scott could work his way into the first round conversation thanks to his traits. However, this could be a very deep defensive tackle class and there are prospects with similarly impressive traits who also have significant production to their name. As of this writing, Scott has 21 tackles but only 1.0 tackle for a loss and 0 sacks on the season. Unlike many of the defensive tackles the Giants have drafted lately, Scott is still young and won’t turn 21 until January. It’s possible that he could slide in a deep class and be available to the Giants somewhere in the second round.
author: Chris Pflum

title: NY Giants John Harbaugh violated norms, called Titans ownership about Jeffery Simmons
summary: New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh took the extraordinary step of calling Tennessee Titans ownership directly in an effort to acquire star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, according to a startling report from Jonathan Jones of The Athletic. Per Jones, that breaks with “traditional NFL trade-talk norms” where general managers deal directly with each other. […]
full_text: John Harbaugh | Getty Images New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh took the extraordinary step of calling Tennessee Titans ownership directly in an effort to acquire star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, according to a startling report from Jonathan Jones of The Athletic . Per Jones, that breaks with “traditional NFL trade-talk norms” where general managers deal directly with each other. Jones reported that Harbaugh contacted Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk after Giants GM Joe Schoen had been told by Titans GM Mike Borgonzi that Simmons, a 29-year-old four-time Pro Bowler and 2025 First-Team All-Pro, would not be traded. Strunk apparently gave Harbaugh the same message. That obviously changed when the Chicago Bears made a Godfather offer to the Titans of two first-round and a fourth-round draft pick. Per Jones, one GM said Harbaugh’s call to Strunk “violates a code amongst primary football decision-makers, that they will only deal with each other.” Valentine’s View Whether Harbaugh violated NFL traditions or not, the move tells you a couple of things about the Giants. This is clearly Harbaugh’s show. We have told you that before, but this is absolutely evidence that Harbaugh is front-and-center in every major decision, and that he will do whatever he believes necessary to get something done. Even if that steps on toes. The Giants are clearly intent upon seizing the opportunity they have in the NFC East. Forget building. Harbaugh wants the Giants to be the best they can be right now, and if there is a star player out there like Simmons or running back Jonathan Taylor who can help make that happen, the Giants will try to get it done. Whether going for it right now is the correct approach, after the Giants have spent most of the last 15 years floundering you have to appreciate the boldness. I think it is also important to note that Simmons and Taylor, who is now reportedly available , are players who would be more than short-term, 2026 upgrades. One other note in terms of surrendering draft capital. Whether it is too early for a Jaxson Dart vs. J.J. McCarthy debate, the Giants clearly understand that if they spend draft capital now, they possess two desirable, 23-year-old quarterbacks and they can use one in the offseason to recoup premium draft picks.
author: Ed Valentine

title: Colts willing to trade RB Jonathan Taylor, per report
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are now willing to trade star running back Jonathan Taylor, per a report from Adam Schefter of ESPN. Schefter adds in his report that the New York Giants are among the teams thought to have at least “some level of interest” in trading for Taylor. Schefter also lists the Seattle Seahawks, Denver […]
full_text: Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are now willing to trade star running back Jonathan Taylor , per a report from Adam Schefter of ESPN . Schefter adds in his report that the New York Giants are among the teams thought to have at least “some level of interest” in trading for Taylor. Schefter also lists the Seattle Seahawks, Denver Broncos, Minnesota Vikings, Green Bay Packers as teams believed to be interested in trading for Taylor. It’s no secret that while new Giants head coach John Harbaugh likes the trio of Cam Skattebo , Tyrone Tracy , and Devin Singletary , he has coveted a “bellcow” running back. The Giants reportedly pursued Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III in free agency and it was likewise reported that star Notre Dame running back Jeremiyah Love was tied with Arvell Reese at the top of their board. It was widely believed that the Giants would have drafted Love at fifth overall if he was still available. One of the issues with the Giants’ backfield is that while they lack an explosive option out of the backfield, and Taylor has been one of the NFL’s most explosive runners. Last year he was tied for sixth in the NFL with 16 designed runs of 15+ yards, and was third in “breakaway” runs. He also led the NFL with 18 rushing touchdowns to just two (2) fumbles last year. Our own Ed Valentine wrote earlier this week that the Giants should capitalize on their opportunity to win the NFC East this year and go all-in on the 27-year old Taylor. After a report that head coach John Harbaugh personally called Tennessee Titans ownership in an effort to get defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons , who landed with the Chicago Bears, you can expect the Giants to be aggressive in pursuit of Taylor. The move would likely cost significant draft capital, possibly a first round pick to replace the one the Colts traded to the New York Jets. That’s real consideration oncern in a 2027 draft class that’s shaping up to be very talented and deep at a number of positions of need for the Giants. Acquiring Taylor would also require significant cap space and financial maneuvering. However, the argument is that Taylor is among the very best runners in the NFL and could complete a true “three headed monster” with wide receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely. And frankly, if Taylor becomes the apple of Harbaugh’s eye, it becomes Joe Schoen’s job to do everything in his power to acquire the running back. So what do you think Giants’ fans? Do you think the Giants are serious contenders for Taylor? And should they be?
author: Chris Pflum

title: NY Giants defensive review: Kudos, Wet Willies, and thoughts on every player
summary: The New York Giants defense under coordinator Dennard Wilson has become an aggressive unit that is playing well despite the loss of Brian Burns, questions on the defensive line, and churn in the secondary due to injuries. Let’s go position-by-position with Kudos, Wet Willies, and thoughts on every player. Defensive line D.J. Reader — Dexter […]
full_text: Abdul Carter | Getty Images The New York Giants defense under coordinator Dennard Wilson has become an aggressive unit that is playing well despite the loss of Brian Burns, questions on the defensive line, and churn in the secondary due to injuries. Let’s go position-by-position with Kudos, Wet Willies, and thoughts on every player. Defensive line D.J. Reader — Dexter Lawrence is an elite player who has returned to form this season with the Cincinnati Bengals. It isn’t worth crying over spilt milk, though. Reader has been everything the Giants could have hoped for in a replacement. Maybe more. Pro Football Focus, in fact, ranks Reader as the best defensive tackle in football so far this season with an elite 90.4 grades. Lawrence (87.6) is No. 2). Want to see a major difference in grading systems? Pro Football and Sports Network, which puts much more weight on pass rush, has Reader as its 53rd-ranked defensive tackle, with Lawrence at No. 2. Regardless of all of the number gobbledygook (now that’s a cool Halloween word), Reader has been outstanding for the Giants. They just need to get him some help. Grade: Kudos Shelby Harris — The fact that Harris is the Giants’ second-best defensive lineman tells you why the position is an issue, and a priority for the team to address before the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline. The 35-year-old, in his 13th NFL season, is not the player he once was. Statistical sites, in fact, tell us that Harris is clearly having what is by far the worst season of his career. Pro Football Focus tells us Harris is No. 102 of 126 qualifying defensive tackles, and that his 49.2 grade is the first would be the first time in his career he has graded below 60.0. Pro Football and Sports Network shows a similar degradation in Harris’ play. Harris is still playing a ton of snaps (238 thus far, 54%), and doing what he can. At this point in his career, though, the Giants appear to be asking too much of him. Grade: Kwillie Darius Alexander — One reason the Giants are asking so much of the aging Harris is that Alexander, a 2025 third-round pick, has not given them enough. PFSN ranks Alexander 119th among 121 qualifying defensive tcles this season, and PFF ranks him No. 102 of 147 qualifiers in their grading system. Alexander’s talent and athleticism tell you he should be much more than he has been. Grade: Wet Willie Bobby Jamison-Travis — The rookie sixth-round pick did not see action until Week 6 against the New Orleans Saints. He played well against the run vs. the Houston Texans in Week 7, giving reason to hope he can contribute, but 42 total defensive snaps is not enough to give a legitimate grade. Grade: Incomplete C.J. Okoye — The Giants acquired the 6-foot-6, 365-pound 24-year-old from the Baltimore Ravens, where he had played for John Harbaugh, for the low price of a 2028 seventh-round pick. They hoped Okoye would take a step forward in his development and become a solid rotational run defender. It hasn’t happened, and Okoye has played just 87 defensive snaps (14.5 per game) across six games. A man as big and strong as Okoye shouldn’t be pushed out of a hole by blockers as easily and as often as Okoye is. Grade: Wet Willie Chauncey Golston — The veteran defensive end had earned a big role on defense before a neck injury short-circuited his season. Grade: Incomplete Edge defender Abdul Carter — The No. 3 overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft has spent the season reminding everyone why the Giants drafted him so high a year ago. His sack numbers (2.0) just don’t yet reflect how good the 23-year-old has actually been. Carter has been a nightmare for opposing blockers this season, and is one one three qualifying edge defenders with elite Pro Football Focus grades of 90.0 or higher. With a 90.3 mark, he joins Will Anderson (90.8) and Aidan Hutchinson (92.2). PFSN penalizes him for the lack of sacks, ranking him a ridiculousy low No. 58 among 122 qualifiers. Abdul Carter is tied with Will Anderson Jr. for 3rd in the NFL in total pass-rush wins, but that hasn't led to an overly impressive pressure rate or sack total. Couple of thoughts on why Carter's still been an impactful pass rusher and the pressures + sacks should come below pic.twitter.com/e6s9wdYsio — Ben Linsey (@benlinsey_) October 26, 2026 Carter had a rocky rookie season, marked by maturity issues. This season, he has stepped up as both a player and as a vocal locker room leader. Grade: Kudos Kayvon Thibodeaux — The No. 5 pick in the 2022 NFL Draft is always a lightning rod for disagreement when it comes to trying to assess his play. The pure numbers would tell you that Thibodeaux, starting after Brian Burns’ unfortunate season-ending injury, has been terrible and the Giants should either trade him before the upcoming deadline or happily let him walk in free agency at season’s end. He is 12th on the team in tackles (15), doesn’t have a tackle for loss or a sack, and has just one quarterback hit. But, there are other more advanced and less visible to the naked eye measures that tell you there are plenty of ways in which Thibodeaux has been quietly effective. Kayvon Thibodeaux in the last 3 games Pass Rush Win Rate: 18.3% – 7th in the NFL (among EDGE's) Run Stop%: 9.2 – 4th in the NFL (among EDGE's) Stops: 6 – 1st in the NFL (among EDGE's) pic.twitter.com/cENtBdKC50 — Marshall Green (@MarshallGreen_) October 26, 2026 Two things can be true at the same time, and in this case probably are. Thibodeaux is a good player, and if he were a third-round pick he would probably be looked at as a fantastic find at that point in the draft. Quietly effective, though, is not what you are hoping for from a No. 5 overall pick. Grade: Kwillie Brian Burns — I feel terrible for Burns. He is a pro’s pro, a nice guy, and a locker room leader who approaches and plays the game the right way. In eight NFL seasons, though, Burns has never had the good fortune of playing for a team that has made the playoffs. This Giants team has the chance to do that, and his season-ending knee injury means Burns won’t have a chance to help make that happen. Grade: Incomplete Trace Ford — The second-year former undrafted free agent gets credit for perseverance. The Giants cut him in 2025, and he spent part of the season on the team’s practice squad. They cut him again this year, and he again landed on the practice squad. Burns’ injury opened an opportunity for him to be a game-day elevation, and he parlayed that into a spot on the 53-man roster. Ford has shown some potential with 10 tackles and three hurries over four games and 70 defensive snaps. Grade: Kudos Inside linebacker Arvell Reese — I don’t care how good David Bailey, Jeremiyah Love, or Carnell Tate turn out to be, how did the New York Jets, Arizona Cardinals, and Tennessee Titans let this guy fall to the Giants with the fifth pick in the 2026 NFL Draft? Arvell Reese with one of the best HUSTLE plays you’ll ever see out of a LB. The Giants rookie LB is built like and plays like an absolute CYBORG 😳👽 pic.twitter.com/NM3QZjyjS9 — Rookie Watch (@RookieWatxh) October 26, 2026 “Man, how good has he been? He’s been awesome. He’s been phenomenal since the day he got here,” GM Joe Schoen said during his bye week press conference. “And that’s probably why Coach and I, even in that [draft] video, we were shocked he was there. So, he’s just a quiet kid that goes about his business and he’s all ball all the time. “That play he made the other day where he should have had the sack on (Houston Texans quarterback) C.J. (Stroud) and then turns around and hauls tail all the way down the field and puts the guy flat on his back while punching for the ball. I mean, you don’t see many people with his size that can move like that. And then just, that’s internal. That’s just want to. To go towards the quarterback and then turn and run, you can’t coach that. You either got that or you don’t. And his effort and the way he plays and flies around, I mean, you see him on film, he’s moving at a…
author: Ed Valentine

title: New York Giants mailbag: Abdul Carter’s impact, J.J. McCarthy, Tae Banks, more
summary: Bob Letchstein asks: It seems like part of the reason that Abdul Carter’s sack numbers aren’t higher is because he is frequently held. He gets pressure very quickly but offensive linemen tend to clothesline him around the neck and bend him backwards. The refs did call holding on two consecutive plays in the Texans game […]
full_text: Bob Letchstein asks: It seems like part of the reason that Abdul Carter’s sack numbers aren’t higher is because he is frequently held. He gets pressure very quickly but offensive linemen tend to clothesline him around the neck and bend him backwards. The refs did call holding on two consecutive plays in the Texans game but it’s been happening all season and most of the time it’s not called. Do you think the refs are not always seeing it or are they choosing not to call it so the game isn’t stopped after every play? Ed says: Bob, it is commonly said that NFL referees could call holding on every play. That is probably true. In my view, Carter gets held frequently because his speed and ability to bend so often put blockers at a disadvantage. Carter leads all edge defenders in quick pressures (pressures under 2.5 seconds) with 16, per NextGen Stats. Officials are human. They will never see everything, or get every call correct. As it is, officials are calling 16.85 penalties per game, per NFLpenalties.com . That is the most since that site began tracking that data in 2009. I would much prefer fewer penalties to be called, especially the ticky-tack calls that don’t need to be made. Steve Cariello asks: I wanted to see what you know about Jack Kelly and what may be holding him back from stepping into a larger role on defense, given the injuries to Edmunds and Burns. It felt like the kid had a lot of promise in training camp, but I feel like we haven’t heard about him since then. Any insights? Ed says: Steve, the answer to what is holding Kelly back is pretty simple. Arvell Reese is the No. 5 overall pick, and he is a star. Despite the injury to Tremaine Edmunds, Micah McFadden is a proven commodity and a capable starter in the NFL. McFadden was next in line. As for the Brian Burns injury, that really has nothing to do with Kelly. Burns is an edge defender. Kelly is an inside linebacker at the NFL level, not a guy who is going to get snaps on the outside unless it is an emergency. Now, what could happen is that McFadden plays well the rest of the season and decides to go to a team that can offer him a starting job next season and a richer contract than he could get from the Giants. That would move Kelly to the No. 3 inside linebacker role. Adam Jacobs asks: Hi, Ed. Hope you have had another great week recapping the game, as there was a lot to love about the results. I am curious about your take on the following. The Giants, as was expected, were not very highly thought of coming into the season, based on the last decade or so. At what point do you think the public opinion of the team comes around to the point that we are much better than everyone thought coming in? The team showed a lot of grit last year, but the difference this season is the execution, especially on the O line and the secondary (at least to me). The team still has flaws, but that doesn’t seem to matter since we have a 4-2-1 record coming into the bye week. Do you think the overall opinion of the team trends upwards, or is it a matter of the public thinking the Giants are the best of a middling division? Ed says: Adam, it isn’t really a matter of the public thinking that the Giants are the best of a middling division. Right now, they are the best of a middling division. After watching what the Giants have been for most of the past 15 years, NFL observers are having a hard time wrapping their minds around what the Giants are doing. Especially without Jaxson Dart, Brian Burns, and a host of other players they had planned on having. Respect is earned. The Giants are beginning to get some, but they are going to have to keep earning it. Rob Laraia asks: Who is the NY Giants quarterbacks coach because when Jaxson Dart was on the field he looked like he had progressed further along than a second year man, and now JJ McCarthy after a few weeks in the Giants looks a whole new QB without the INT oopsies. Granted that can change but he looked poised and calm. So really curious who is working with them; the QB coach, Harbaugh, Nagy, or whoever is turning them into high-caliber QBs? Ed says: Rob, Brian Callahan is the quarterbacks coach. He was head coach of the Tennessee Titans in 2024 and part of 2025 before being fired. Callahan has extensive experience with a number of top quarterbacks. Callahan works most directly with the quarterback, but Matt Nagy, senior offensive consultant Greg Roman, and John Harbaugh all have a hand in dealing with quarterbacks. Seth Weissman asks: My question is about the Cam Skattebo penalty. Could you please explain to me what the refs expect him to do when he has the ball? All he did was run hard up the middle, like he was taught to do as a kid. Calling unnecssary roughness on a running back while he is running the ball makes absolutely no sense to me. If the call was made because he was running low and his helmet hit the defender’s, then why not call it on the defender who clearly could have tried to tackle Skattebo without using his own helmet? I understand that the league wants to protect the players, but the rules have to make sense … don’t they? Ed says: Seth, if I had a good explanation for that one I’d be happy to give it to you. Players are not supposed to lower their head and use the crown of the helmet to initiate contact. Technically, that rule applies to both offensive and defensive players, but Sunday was the first time I can recall an offensive player being flagged for it. In this case, the defender did not use his own helmet. Skattebo just trucked him. I don’t know what a ballcarrier is supposed to do there. If you stay upright you are putting the ball, and yourself, at risk. This was John Harbaugh’s comment about the play on Monday: “I understand the idea, but I also understand human physiology and anatomy and the way the body works. Skatt runs low. You have to run low. You have to run low to protect the football. You have to run low to protect your body. You can’t run in there and give tacklers your chest. When you run low, your head’s down there, too. You can’t move your head off your shoulders. It’s a physical impossibility. I’m quite sure Skatt’s not trying to use his helmet as a weapon, as a battering ram. It’s not the way he’s thinking. He’s leading with his shoulder. That’s what he’s trying to do. He’s trying to keep his head in a good, strong, upright position. But his pads are down there low. He runs low to the ground. That’s a good thing, that’s football. That’s the way you’re supposed to run. That’s how you protect yourself and the football. So, I didn’t have a problem with the technique personally at all, but we haven’t heard from the league. Maybe they’ll be able to enlighten us a little bit on it in terms of what they want us to teach, and that would be great.” Louis Rolston-Cregler asks: Banks played lights out against Nico Collins in a matchup that quite frankly I expected him to struggle mightily. Is it crazy to think that we need to extend him before he has a chance to hit the open market? I believe Hood and Adebo are the only CBs signed past this season and I’m sure Adebo will be gone unless he takes a massive pay cut? I’m sure we’ll address the position via the draft but at this point it seems like keeping Banks should be a priority. Thoughts? Ed says: Louis, no, it’s not crazy to think the Giants need to give Deonte Banks a contract extension. Sometimes those things happen during the bye week, but I am not expecting an extension for Banks or anyone else to happen at this time. That said, I don’t think the Giants are going to let Banks hit the open market. Not when it looks like he has finally turned into the top-shelf cornerback they drafted him to be, and that every team craves. Giants fans, go big on game day! title: NY Giants trade candidate: Titans RB Tony Pollard would provide an upgrade
summary: The New York Giants appear to be targeting running back and defensive tackle help at the 2026 NFL trade deadline. The top two defensive tackles, DeForest Buckner and Jeffrey Simmons, are already off the board. So, the Giants will likely have to look for more incremental, short-term help there. The top running back, and probably […]
full_text: Could Tony Pollard join the Giants? | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants appear to be targeting running back and defensive tackle help at the 2026 NFL trade deadline. The top two defensive tackles, DeForest Buckner and Jeffrey Simmons, are already off the board. So, the Giants will likely have to look for more incremental, short-term help there. The top running back, and probably the biggest fish remaining in the trade market pool, is Jonathan Taylor of the Indianapolis Colts. Taylor doesn’t sound like a player who wants to be traded , and the price might be prohibitive for a team like the Giants that is not in a championship window. So, when it comes to running backs, where should the Giants turn for an upgrade? Potential trade target: RB Tony Pollard If the Giants want to upgrade their running back room and a Taylor trade isn’t going to happen, the view here is that Pollard should be the next target. Why it would work Pollard is not the bell-cow back that Taylor is, and he would not give John Harbaugh the “Derrick Henry or Saquon Barkley circumstance” he would like to have. He would, though, give Harbaugh an upgrade over Tyrone Tracy and Devin Singletary to team with Cam Skattebo in a two-headed timeshare. Pollard, 29, has never averaged fewer than 4.0 yards per carry in eight seasons since being a fourth-round selection by the Dallas Cowboys in the 2019 NFL Draft. He is currently averaging 4.3 yards per carry for the Tennessee Titans and is on pace for a career-best 1,171 rushing yards, which would be his fifth consecutive 1,000-yard season. Pollard is also a useful receiver, having caught at least 30 passes in each of the last five seasons. Pollard is in the final year of a three-year, $21.75 million contract with the Titans. The Giants would only be responsible for the prorated portion of his $6.74 million 2026 base salary. Over 10 weeks, that would be $3.74 million. Why it wouldn’t work The 1-6 Titans are terrible. It would seem to make sense for them to get something in return for a 29-year-old running back who is likely headed to free agency at season’s end. Maybe, though, it doesn’t. As bad as they are, the Titans are still trying to develop 2025 No. 1 overall pick Cam Ward into an effective NFL quarterback. That is not going well. Trading away their best running back and more or less neutering their run game isn’t going to help their young quarterback. If the Giants make a bid for Pollard, they would likely want the cost to involve one of the two sixth-round picks they have in 2027, or a fifth- or sixth-round pick in 2028. With the potential to create a bidding war, and the idea of supporting Ward for the remainder of the season, the Titans could hold out for better picks. Or, not trade Pollard. The only currently tradeable mid-round pick the Giants have in 2027 is a third-rounder. They have no fourth-rounder (traded for Malachi Fields) and no fifth-rounder (traded for J.J. McCarthy). The locker room might be another factor. We saw how tight-knit the running back group of Skattebo, Tracy, and Singletary is at the end of the victory over the Houston Texans. I don’t believe the potential for disrupting that chemistry would prevent the Giants from making a trade for Pollard, but it is something they should consider.

title: The Deonte Banks renaissance: Former first-round pick finally playing like one
summary: Everyone loves a redemption arc. New York Giants cornerback Deonte Banks became the talk of the NFL media when he locked down star X receiver Nico Collins in the Giants’ win over the Houston Texans. Banks had Collins in a vault in Week 7, spending much of the afternoon in man coverage on Collins and […]
full_text: New York Giants cornerback Deonte Banks breaks up a pass intended for Nico Collins | Getty Images Everyone loves a redemption arc. New York Giants cornerback Deonte Banks became the talk of the NFL media when he locked down star X receiver Nico Collins in the Giants’ win over the Houston Texans. Banks had Collins in a vault in Week 7, spending much of the afternoon in man coverage on Collins and giving up just two catches for 6 yards. For much of the NFL world, the performance seemed to come out of nowhere, but there have been clues that it has been coming. Banks was named the NFC Defensive Player Of the Week for Week 4 following his walk-off Pick 6 against the Arizona Cardinals. But the pieces have all been there for Banks to become a top flight cornerback from the very beginning. But as our friend Mark Schofield is fond of saying, development isn’t always linear, and Banks’ development has been anything but. The promising prospect and rookie To start, Banks is a truly elite athlete with one of the best combinations of size and speed of any cornerback in the NFL. Banks’ 9.99 score ranks second in the RAS database and his ability to physically match up with almost any receiver is the foundation for his game. Even as a raw rookie, Banks ability to generate tight coverage was evident, as noted by our own Nick Falato when recapping the Giants’ 2023 draft class after that season. Nick wrote at the time: Banks played 840 defensive snaps for the Giants, recording 56 tackles, two interceptions, six passes defended, and a solid 57.6% reception rate. He did, however, commit 8 penalties, which was 13th-highest of all cornerbacks. … Banks ranked 23rd best in reception rate of cornerbacks who played at least 50% of their team’s defensive plays. … Banks has all the necessary athletic traits to thrive in man coverage, and he had a good overall rookie season, by my estimation. He also displayed very good awareness with zone and match principles. Whoever replaces Martindale as defensive coordinator will approve of having Banks on the roster. With the retention of Jerome Henderson, I expect Banks to continue his development as a number one corner in the league. GRADE: B+ The Giants hoped that Dennard Wilson would replace Martindale in 2024, but Wilson opted to replace Shane Bowen as the Tennessee Titans’ defensive coordinator instead. That led to Brian Daboll hiring Bowen to be the Giants’ defensive coordinator, bringing a fairly significant shift in defensive philosophy. The Bowen years and decline Banks went into the 2024 season as the Giants’ CB1 and was asked to follow top receivers around the field, but he struggled in that role and didn’t take the anticipated steps forward. He didn’t record a single interception in the 14 games he played and didn’t appear comfortable in the zone coverages Bowen called for much of that year. That isn’t to say that Banks didn’t develop or take steps forward in 2024. He finished with 12 passes defensed in 2024, one more than in 2023 despite playing one fewer game. He also finished 11th in the NFL in forced incompletions and 12th in incompletion rate, per PFF. It was obvious in 2023 and 2024 that Banks’ elite athleticism allowed him to excel in forcing tight window throws, and he was able to put himself in position to disrupt those passes. However, his technique still hadn’t caught up with his athletic traits and his play at the catch point was inconsistent at best. Making matters worse, Brian Daboll fired defensive backs coach Jerome Henderson, who was Banks’ biggest supporter and the loudest voice holding him to account for lapses in effort. The combination of upside and and frustrating factors made 2025 a “ Make Or Break ” year for Banks. The pieces were all there for Banks to take a step forward, however the circumstances had changed such that he might not be able to do so. The Giants ultimately chose to go with Cor’Dale Flott as the starting cornerback opposite Paulson Adebo. That said, Banks wasn’t benched completely and Bowen called a curious timeshare that had Banks on the outside in some situations. And once again, Banks was sticky in coverage. When he landed on the injury report midseason he was averaging the second-least amount of separation among corners playing significant snaps (trailing only Sauce Gardner) and had the seventh-lowest target rate among qualifying corners (both via NextGenStats). However, Banks’ play at the catch point continued to lag behind and he was allowing a 70% catch rate and his play continued the disappointing trajectory we saw start in 2024. Personally, I put the blame on the Giants’ coaching staff and Bowen in particular. I noted after Bowen was fired that the decline in most of the Giants’ defensive personnel last year suggested that coaching was the root cause for the lack of development for many players on that side of the ball. Rebound and redemption It was widely expected that Banks would be one of the players on his way out after John Harbaugh was hired to replace Daboll. There was, however, a glimmer of hope that Dennard Wilson’s “Baltimore Style” defense could give him an opportunity. And Harbaugh did indeed give Banks a clean slate in the spring. Banks made the most of that, taking to Wilson’s aggressive scheme as well as the coaching he was getting from cornerbacks coach Addison Lynch and defensive pass game coordinator Donald D’Alesio. “We make these tapes called ‘get better tapes’”, Lynch said. “We tried to just show him his consistency was his deal. He wasn’t consistent getting lined up fast, wasn’t consistent with his feet. So, he’s improved his consistency, now his play has improved, now his confidence is up, and he can keep this rolling into the season.” “Right now we’ve built the trust, and he’s being consistent in his technique. That’s all we really needed from him to prove that he can do. Now he’s showing up day in and day out, he’s being a pro, he’s putting in extra work, so he’s motivated to do the right things, and I think he’s headed in the right direction.” Banks split time with Greg Newsome opposite Paulson Adebo in the spring and impressed. That translated to more opportunities early in training camp, and Banks made the most of every rep. He clawed his way up the depth chart until he was listed as a “co-starter”, and finally jumped Adebo as the Giants’ starting cornerback opposite Newsome. Fans, and even members of the media who watched Banks throughout training camp, expressed skepticism that he could be an effective starter. It was widely expected that the Cowboys would try to pick on Banks, which would lead to more failures at the catch point. Instead, Banks started and played well until he stepped on a first down marker and left the game with a calf injury. Banks would miss the next two games, but his return in the Cardinals game showed that his play in Week 1 wasn’t a fluke. So, what’s changed? Realizing his potential It’s pretty clear that Wilson’s scheme and defensive philosophy fit Banks much better than Bowen’s did. Even when the Giants’ defense is playing zone coverage, Wilson is employing man-match rules and calling MEG (Man Everywhere he Goes) for Banks. Much of Wilson’s defense is built on using “step coverage” (ie, cornerbacks being just a step away from receivers) to force tight window throws. That’s been the strength of Banks’ game since his rookie year, and just being allowed to be an athlete has raised his comfort level considerably. That said, the biggest change in Banks has been his consistency. As Lynch said in the offseason, the coaching staff and Banks have put a significant amount of work into playing with more consistency, and consistently doing the little things well. Practicing with a greater attention to detail has led to him being able to do those things in high leverage situations without having to think or second-guess, which in turn has led to more confidence. There’s a clear difference in how fast and decisively Banks is playing.…

title: Previewing the Jets’ opposition: Las Vegas Raiders
summary: The Jets and Raiders represent two franchises that have been trying to rebuild for a long time, without much success. Having picked first and second in the 2026 NFL draft, the teams meet on Sunday with each trying desperately not to fall out of contention yet again. While the Jets could easily be better than […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - OCTOBER 25: Tonka Hemingway #97 of the Las Vegas Raiders celebrates with teammates after a sack against Matthew Stafford #9 of the Los Angeles Rams during the first quarter at Allegiant Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jets and Raiders represent two franchises that have been trying to rebuild for a long time, without much success. Having picked first and second in the 2026 NFL draft, the teams meet on Sunday with each trying desperately not to fall out of contention yet again. While the Jets could easily be better than their current 2-5 record, the Raiders stand 3-4 having won their first three only to then lose four straight. When these teams last met, in 2023, Las Vegas beat the Jets 16-12 in a frustrating game that dropped the Jets below .500. Whoever loses this one will be similarly frustrated. Let’s break down the Raiders’ roster going position by position: Quarterbacks The Raiders got rid of Geno Smith during the offseason and replaced him with someone even older, the 38-year old Kirk Cousins. So far, Cousins is off to a productive start and the Raiders have the number four passing game in the NFL as he leads the league with 16 touchdown passes. However, while the Raiders have been marching up and down the field and are 2nd in the league in terms of red zone visits, they are down in 29th for touchdown conversion percentage in the red zone. They were 1-for-5 down there in Sunday’s loss to the Rams. Of course, the biggest quarterback story for the Raiders is currently on ice, as the number one overall pick Fernando Mendoza won’t get a chance to show the Jets what they missed out on unless Cousins is hurt or benched during Sunday’s game. His first start probably isn’t too far away though, and he did complete six of eight passes in garbage time action so far this season. The number three is Aidan O’Connell, who beat the Jets as a rookie in the aforementioned 2023 game. Offensive Line The Raiders’ offensive line was awful last year, although two of the players they got rid of – Dylan Parham and Jordan Meredith – are actually faring quite well with the Jets. Former Raven Tyler Linderbaum was brought in at center to stabilize things, signing a massive $81 million deal. The jury is still out on this deal because, while the offensive line is definitely improved, his own performance has been somewhat underwhelming. He leads the team with five offensive penalties in seven games. The Raiders also brought in Spencer Burford on a low-cost one-year deal and he’s currently starting at left guard. Burford is best known for blowing a costly assignment in overtime during the 49ers’ recent Super Bowl loss. The other three players listed as starters are all returning from last year’s group: Kolton Miller at left tackle, DJ Glaze at right tackle and Jackson Powers-Johnson at right guard. However, Powers-Johnson was recently benched for Caleb Rogers with the suggestion being that he doesn’t fit the system and could be traded at the deadline. He is also listed as questionable having missed practice time due to a back issue. Glaze led the team in offensive snaps last year, as the one constant on a line that kept changing personnel. Miller is the team’s highest paid offensive player, but has given up a team-high four sacks. The rest of the bench comprises guard Bryce Cabeldue, tackle Charles Grant and third round rookie guard Trey Zuhn III. Grant was a third round pick who had one start as a rookie last season but Cabeldue and Zuhn have played less than 50 offensive snaps between them in regular season action. Zuhn sees some time as a sixth lineman in jumbo packages, though. Running Backs Last year’s top pick Ashton Jeanty continues to see a lot of the ball and rack up production by volume even though he hasn’t been all that effective with a 3.1 yards per carry average. Having come within 25 yards of a thousand-yard season as a rookie, he’s ramped up his passing game production this year and has accounted for 640 yards from scrimmage with four total touchdowns. Jeanty made headlines during the week when he suggested that unnamed Jets players didn’t like to tackle. That was ironic given that he is 25th out of 26 qualifying backs in terms of forced missed tackles so far this season according to Pro Football Focus. Fourth round rookie Mike Washington Jr. has shown some early promise in a reserve role, though, as he is averaging almost five yards per carry. Dylan Laube is the number three back and Connor Heyward is listed as the fullback, although he will also line up at tight end. Pass catchers The Raiders’ best pass catching weapon is pro bowler Brock Bowers. The tight end missed two games but is still tied with Jeanty for the team lead in receptions on 31, for 455 yards and three scores. His fellow tight end Michael Mayer also has 31 catches. Leading the team in receiving yards and touchdown receptions, though, is Tre Tucker with 474 yards and four scores. No other Raiders wideout has double figures in catches, although Cody White has made his eight catches count, with three of them being touchdowns. Jalen Nailor is the other starter along with Tucker, but has just 75 yards on eight catches for the season. Last year’s second round pick, Jack Bech, would presumably be playing a significant role if he weren’t on injured reserve, though, and he has been practicing this week so he may be about to return. His official game status is questionable. Dont’e Thornton, Malik Benson and Dareke Young are also on the roster at wideout and Ian Thomas is the number three tight end. Benson was drafted in the sixth round in April. Defensive Line As ever, the Raiders’ biggest threat on either side of the ball is all-pro defensive end Maxx Crosby. However, it’s the other two edges in the Raiders’ three man rotation – Malcolm Koonce and Kwity Paye – who are tied for the team lead on three sacks each. Crosby certainly hasn’t been slacking, though. His 16 quarterback hits are more than twice as many as any other player on the team. At defensive tackle, Adam Butler and Tonka Hemingway are listed as the starters. However, ex-Jet Folorunso Fatukasi has actually started all seven games. With third round pick Keyron Crawford on injured reserve, depth on the edge comes from Patrick Johnson, although he’s out of Sunday’s game with a stinger. Thomas Booker and JJ Pegues provide further depth inside. Linebackers The Raiders signed linebacker Nakobe Dean to a $12 million per year contract in the offseason and he’s been a settling influence on the defense in the same way Linderbaum was supposed to be for the offense. Dean is tied for the league lead with three forced fumbles and has 68 tackles, 1.5 sacks and an interception. The other starter at linebacker is former first round pick Quay Walker, who has a team-high five tackles for loss, while Tommy Eichenberg sees action in base packages. Cody Lindenberg and Segun Olubi provide depth off the bench. Olubi started two games for the Colts back in 2023. Defensive Backs The Raiders’ 3-0 start was significantly influenced by fifth round rookie Hezekiah Masses, who intercepted three passes in the first three games. However, since that time, Masses has found himself back in a reserve role as he has given up four touchdowns and five defensive penalties with the defense now statistically one of the league’s worst. Eric Stokes, who signed a three-year, $30 million extension during the offseason and Darien Porter are now starting on the outside after Porter had previously seen his starting role taken away by Masses. In addition, Taron Johnson is one of the most reliable slot specialists in the league. At safety, the Raiders drafted Treydan Stukes in the second round and he’s been starting alongside veteran Jeremy Chinn. Isaiah Pola-Mao sees time in three-safety sets. The Raiders also drafted Jermod McCoy and Dalton Johnson in the middle rounds to add some depth at…

title: Stop Looking for the Next Ben Johnson
summary: Every Jets coaching search starts the same way. Find the next hot coordinator before anyone else does. Find the next Ben Johnson, the next Liam Coen. It sounds smart. It isn’t. The Jets are 2-5, Aaron Glenn is 5-19, and the team has three first-round picks and well over $100 million in cap space coming […]
full_text: Every Jets coaching search starts the same way. Find the next hot coordinator before anyone else does. Find the next Ben Johnson, the next Liam Coen. It sounds smart. It isn’t. The Jets are 2-5, Aaron Glenn is 5-19, and the team has three first-round picks and well over $100 million in cap space coming in 2027. This is the most important hire the franchise has made in a decade, and the worst thing they can do is treat it like a lottery ticket. Here’s the problem with chasing the next star coordinator: you only know who he is after it works. Coen had one year as an offensive coordinator in Tampa when Jacksonville took him. Johnson spent a cycle turning down jobs before Chicago landed him. Both look like geniuses now. Jacksonville went 13-4 last year and Chicago took the NFC’s No. 2 seed. But at the time, plenty of teams passed on both, and plenty of other “next big things” went nowhere. If you can’t clearly see who that guy is by now, you’re guessing. Guessing on your head coach in the same offseason you draft your franchise quarterback is the definition of stupid risk. So stop guessing, and shrink the job down to the one thing that actually matters: building a quarterback. Not culture. Not a defensive identity. Not a big name who wins ten games around whoever’s under center. The 2027 quarterback is the franchise for the next decade, and the head coach’s job description should start and end with him. The rest of the roster, the line, the secondary, the depth, Darren Mougey has already shown he can fix with picks and cap space. The good news is that QB development is the one thing you can actually check. Shane Steichen called the plays for Justin Herbert’s Rookie of the Year season, for Jalen Hurts’ 2022 jump to MVP runner-up, and for Daniel Jones’ revival in Indianapolis, where Jones was an MVP candidate at 8-2. Dan Pitcher has been in the room with Joe Burrow every day of Burrow’s career. And in college, nobody has a better eye and hand for quarterbacks than Oklahoma State’s Eric Morris. He was Mahomes’ offensive coordinator at Texas Tech, and he found Cam Ward as a zero-star recruit at Incarnate Word and coached him at two schools on his way to becoming the No. 1 overall pick. Now he’s done it again with Drew Mestemaker, a kid who never took a varsity snap at quarterback in high school and is now the top QB on a lot of 2027 boards after developing at lightning speed. Those aren’t projections, they’re track records. You can argue about clock management or a head coaching record, and you should hire around those weaknesses, but you’re not guessing about what these guys do best. And here’s what the hot-coordinator crowd misses: get the quarterback right and the next Ben Johnson comes to you. Coaches chase quarterbacks. The Chargers had Justin Herbert, and when their job opened, Jim Harbaugh took it. A Jets team with a young franchise quarterback on a rookie deal, a stacked draft haul and a GM who knows how to build assets becomes one of the best jobs in football the next time it opens. That’s how you land a star coach: you build the thing star coaches want to coach. The Jets have tried it the other way. They’ve chased the hot name, the culture guy and the defensive mind, and they’ve started over with a new quarterback again and again. This time, flip the order. Hire the coach who builds quarterbacks, draft the quarterback, and let everything else follow. Get that right, and the Jets won’t be hunting for the next Ben Johnson. He’ll be calling them.

title: Three Things I’m Looking at in the Jets vs. Raiders Game
summary: It’s another week of Jets football, and I’m here to turn your frowns upside down. Remember last week I said it was a fact that the Jets could lose to the Dolphins and still make the playoffs. Even though some of you commented to challenge that fact, I’m here to remind you that crazier things […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 12: Josh Jacobs #8 of the Las Vegas Raiders runs the ball during a game against the New York Jets at Allegiant Stadium on November 12, 2023 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s another week of Jets football, and I’m here to turn your frowns upside down. Remember last week I said it was a fact that the Jets could lose to the Dolphins and still make the playoffs. Even though some of you commented to challenge that fact, I’m here to remind you that crazier things have happened . The Jets have a pulse, objectively and mathematically are still in the dog race for the playoffs, and still need your cheers to will them on. For those of you saying, ‘whoa, this guy’s been all negative, bashing Glenn, and now he’s suddenly positive,’ I need you to realize it’s never been about positivity or negativity this whole time. I’m not an atom; I’m a football analyst who prides himself on objective football discussion. Are you ready to objectively discuss our football team of choice!? Great, because I have a lot to say. The 2-5 Jets face the 3-4 Raiders, and both teams are coming off consecutive losses. Someone’s losing streak ends this Sunday; we just don’t know which team yet! Coaching will certainly play a key part in this matchup. Vegas averages 26.1 points per game (6th in the NFL) against a Jets defense that allows 21.4 (13th in the NFL). On the other side of the ball, the Jets score 19.6 points per game (6th worst in the NFL), and the Raiders allow 28.1 (4th worst in the NFL). Half Full, or Half Empty? It physically pained me to type the Jets’ scoring ranking – how can a team that employs Garrett Wilson, Omar Cooper Jr., Kenyon Sadiq, Adonai Mitchell, Mason Taylor, and the league’s second-most prolific rusher since Week 4 (Braelon Allen) struggle so badly to score points!? The short answer is coaching. The longer, more important answer is more complicated than a single word, but it still comes down to Frank Reich. Let’s look at the opposing WR1, Tre Tucker, for example: In seven games played, he’s never had a game with fewer than four targets. Garrett Wilson is coming off a game where he was targeted just three times. In his last four games, Garrett Wilson has been targeted 24 times for 16 catches and 1 touchdown. In Tucker’s last four games, he’s been targeted 32 times for 18 catches and 3 touchdowns. This is Tre Tucker we’re talking about – not JSN, not Ja’Marr, not Puka. Tre Tucker is out-targeting Garrett Wilson in this recent stretch. This isn’t unique to Tre. Malik Washington on the Dolphins has 26 targets in his last 4 games, Carnell Tate on the Titans has 31 targets in his last 4 games, and Chris Olave on the Saints has 35 targets in his last 4 games. Like Wilson, all of the receivers named in this paragraph are the clear number one option on a bad team that doesn’t have many wins. Yet, despite all this attention from opposing defenses, these WR1s still get targeted while an elite talent like Wilson gets buried. Targets aside, the Jets have a serious problem scoring after the opening drive. The only time the Jets have scored more than once in the first half was in Week 1 (10 points). Every game since, the Jets enter the halftime break with 3 or 7. Of course we can go back to the dead horse of the 2-minute drill, but there are lots of minutes in between the opening drive and the last two minutes of the half. So far, no consistent scenario has kept happening. In some games, the offense looks completely inept for the rest of the half (the Bears game), but other times the Jets move the ball fairly well before stalling (Patriots). Failed 4th down conversions, missed FGs, or turnovers ruin what were pretty good drives. The Jets are also abysmal at scoring touchdowns in the red zone. The Jets are the only team in the NFL to reach the red zone 20+ times this season and have fewer than 10 red zone touchdowns. Their 45% red zone touchdown rate is second-worst in the NFL, behind only the Cardinals (42.9%). So let’s wrap this up with a few conclusive points: the Jets need to target Garrett Wilson way more. The Jets are the third-worst scoring team in the first half and have the second-worst red-zone TD percentage. Vegas is the perfect team to face for each of these issues. They allow the third-most first-half points per game in the NFL (14). Their secondary has been destroyed all season, leaving a clear path for a Garrett Wilson statement game. Lastly, the Raiders allow red zone TDs a whopping 78.1% of the time, the 4th-highest rate in the league. Of course, if you’re the Raiders defense, this would be considered the perfect offense to ‘get right’ against. One of these units has to get it right this game, and there is just too much healthy talent on this Jets offense for me to side against them! Loose Ends The defense’s abysmal performance last Sunday was largely overshadowed in the media discussion by the terrible coaching decisions, but I cannot give them a pass. Allowing a team that never scored 25+ points to score 28 and dominate from the opening drive was pretty egregious, but perhaps the most egregious stat was allowing random NFL tight end Greg Dulcich to catch five passes for 86 yards on Sunday. Coming into that game, he hadn’t had a 60+ yard game for over three years, but leave it to the Jets to help opposing players get their groove back. The previous week, Hunter Henry had a key third-down conversion on third and 13, along with a touchdown. Is the opposing tight end now a weakness for the Jets defense? Let’s hope not, because this week they are facing the absolute best of the best in Brock Bowers. Bowers has battled injury, but his combination of physical attributes and route running has helped him live up to the pre-draft hype and become one of the best tight ends in football. He’s had at least eight targets and 70 yards in every game and has three touchdowns so far this season. I can’t help but wonder: if the Jets let Dulcich run wild, what happens when Kirk finds his big target in the middle on Sunday? Payback or Validation This is another situation where both teams have a chance to ‘get right’ and finally stop struggling against a team that is also struggling. Perhaps Klint Kubiak, the brilliant second-generation coach, realized this early in the week during his preparations and shared it with Ashton Jeanty, who was happy to reveal his excitement to the media. I definitely wouldn’t say these Jets are “afraid to tackle”; they’re 5th in total tackles while having the 9th-fewest missed tackles in the league. They are, however, a porous run defense that keeps getting gashed by a running back with a pulse. Ollie Gordon II kept the onslaught going with a 100-yard, 1-touchdown performance last week. Even in obvious running situations with Miami trying to waste clock and end the game, the Jets defense was powerless to stop them from moving the chains. The Raiders’ rushing attack (and Ashton Jeanty specifically) has been absolutely horrid this year. Only two teams in the league average fewer than 80 rushing yards per game: the Raiders (74.7) and the Packers (60.6). Jeanty is the only player in the league with 100+ carries to not have 400+ yards (328). His 3.1 yards per carry is truly bottom-of-the-barrel and shameful for a running back. With the world talking about Jeanty’s comments and the Jets supposedly seeing them as “bulletin board material,” will they get payback, or will Jeanty’s comments be validated? For the Jets, they finally face a team struggling to run the ball and have a golden opportunity to shut down runs early to keep the Raiders behind the sticks. For Jeanty, who’s looking at a unit missing the 300-pound monster T’Vondre Sweat, he’s looking for his first game with 4+ ypc since Week 1. Just like the Jets’ stagnant offense facing the Raiders’ struggling defense, one of these two units is guaranteed to get back on the right track this Sunday. Let’s go Jets!

The injury occurred during a team drill on a day that is considered a light practice. He’ll undergo more tests Saturday, but initial X-rays showed significant damage, a team source told ESPN. Depending on what the additional tests reveal, it’s possible Payne, who’s in the final year of his contract, will be done for the season. It’s yet another blow for the Commanders, who are 1-4-1 in a pivotal third season for coach Dan Quinn. Eagles at Commanders Game Preview: 5 questions and answers with the Week 8 enemy – BGN The Philadelphia Eagles are riding a five-game losing streak entering Sunday Night Football against the Washington Commanders, a team they beat in the season opener. Can the Birds win a game for the first time since September 20? In order to preview this Week 8 NFC East battle, I reached out to our enemies over at Hogs Haven. NFC East Mixtape VOL. 202: Can Dallas build? | PHI/WAS | Giants Outlook – NFC East Mixtape It feels like the NFC East has been whittled down to two teams, and only one of them is playing this week in the Dallas Cowboys. Meanwhile… the Philadelphia Eagles and Washington Commanders are about to play one of the least exciting Sunday Night Football games we have ever seen. Who wants it more? Who wants it least? And while the New York Giants are off this week times are very exciting for them. Big Blue View’s Ed Valentine joins RJ Ochoa and Brandon Lee Gowton for an update on how things are going with the G-Men. You can see that we have a BRAND NEW NFC East Mixtape YouTube Channel so make sure to subscribe as the show will live here exclusively in video format. AND you can also listen to the show! On Blogging The Boys and/or Bleeding Green Nation podcast feeds as well as the SB Nation NFL Show feed! Washington Commanders vs Philadelphia Eagles Week 8: Five Questions with Bleeding Green Nation – Hogs Haven On defense, the Eagles are healthier, primarily dealing with injury to LB Jihaad Campbell, who has been ruled out of week 8. Despite their health, the Eagles defense has declined precipitously in 2026 to be the 5th-worst pass defense by yards allowed and the 6th-worst rush defense by yards allowed, as well as ranking poorly in advanced stats. One theory behind the defense’s decline is that they are getting beat up from being on the field all the time due to the collapse of the offense. Through Week 7, the Eagles defense has been on the field for 67.3 plays/game, 4th-most in the NFL. Certain players have had a harder time than others, with slot CB Cooper DeJean suffering from a high missed-tackle rate and notable drop in coverage quality. I asked Brandon Lee Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation five questions to better understand the state of the Eagles and what to look for in this game. Why the NFL didn’t flex the Eagles vs. Commanders out of ‘Sunday Night Football’ – SB Nation For 20 years, the NFL has made Sunday Night Football on NBC the marquee prime-time game of the weekend. Flexible scheduling was one of the selling points of SNF on NBC, with the league having the ability to swap out lackluster games for higher quality matchups. For several years, SNF has had its flex scheduling window opened in Week 5 instead of the back-end of the season. And yet, the 2-5 Philadelphia Eagles and 1-4-1 Washington Commanders were not flexed out this weekend, even though there are far more compelling and flex-worthy games on the Week 8 Sunday schedule. Is this just another case of NFC East bias? Well, it’s a little more complicated than that, and it’s largely the NFL’s own doing. Eagles-Commanders Preview: Will Saquon Barkley Tough It Out? SHOULD He? – PHLY Eagles Podcast Saquon Barkley returned the practice field just in time to put his status in play for the Eagles’ road matchup against the Washington Commanders on Sunday night. EJ Smith is joined by Deniz Selman and Brandon Lee Gowton to discuss whether the star running back should push through the hamstring and back injury he entered the week dealing with, whether Jeremiah Trotter Jr. should take over for Jihaad Campbell, and how this year’s team compares to previous lost Eagles seasons. In Roob’s Observations: Has the league figured out Vic Fangio? – NBCSP COULD HOWIE DRAFT A QUARTERBACK? As it stands now the Eagles would have the sixth pick in next year’s draft, and they’ve only drafted that high twice in the last 25 years, taking Lane Johnson fourth in 2013 and Carson Wentz second in 2016. Before that you go back to Corey Simon sixth in 2000 and Donovan McNabb second in 1999. Before that? Kenny Jackson fourth in 1984. So four top-6 picks in the last 42 years. What direction would Howie Roseman go if the Eagles draft that high? We can rule out receiver, running back, tight end, linebacker, corner or safety, which leaves trenches and quarterback. Edge or o-line never surprises you with Howie, but you don’t get many opportunities to draft top-10 quarterbacks, and if the Eagles are concerned with Jalen Hurts’ long-term health, and it’s something they won’t talk about, quarterback makes a lot of sense. You probably wouldn’t get Oklahoma State’s Drew Mestemaker at 6, but C.J. Carr of Notre Dame and Darian Mensah of Miami are in play if there is concern about Hurts being healthy enough to play in 2027 and beyond. Howie has drafted three quarterbacks in the first three rounds as a GM, and all three played a key role on a Super Bowl championship. Nick Foles and Jalen Hurts were Super Bowl MVPs and Carson Wentz went 11-2 before getting hurt in 2017. There is no No. 1 seed without him. It’s hard to imagine having to move on from a Super Bowl-MVP quarterback at 28 years old, but there are so many unknowns with his condition and treatment that it’s possible. Hurts’ contract status only complicates matters because with limited guarantees beyond this year it’s hard to imagine him playing for the Eagles in 2027 without a new or re-worked contract. But are the Eagles ready to give him a new deal when he’ll miss most of this year after a middling five games? So many questions and not a lot of answers. title: Eagles opposing player to stop, Week 8 edition
summary: The Eagles are a mess. They are the unproud owners of a five-game losing skid, the longest losing streak in the NFC and currently the second-longest streak in the NFL behind the winless Los Angeles Chargers. The Eagles sit in third place in the hapless NFC East, not that it is any great distinction, one […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jayden Daniels #5 of the Washington Commanders carries the ball during a game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Eagles are a mess. They are the unproud owners of a five-game losing skid, the longest losing streak in the NFC and currently the second-longest streak in the NFL behind the winless Los Angeles Chargers. The Eagles sit in third place in the hapless NFC East, not that it is any great distinction, one game up on their next opponent, the one-win Washington Commanders, this Sunday night on national TV. If you’re wondering how low the Eagles can go, they are 5.5-point underdogs against the one-win Commanders, who even with one victory hold a larger upside this season than the sinking, listless Eagles. The Eagles are currently ranked 31st in offense, averaging 264.9 yards a game, and 29th in scoring, averaging an NFC-low 18.1 points a game. Defensively, the Eagles are not much better, ranked No. 27 in the NFL, giving up an average of 371.3 yards a game, and 25 points a game. The Eagles are coming off their worst performance of the season, giving up a season-high 416 total yards that translated into a season-high 38 points in the 38-21 to the Dallas Cowboys on Monday night. One weapon the Commanders have that the Eagles do not have is Jayden Daniels, despite the fact that he is 0-7-1 in his last eight starts and will be without Eagle killer Terry McLaurin, out for the season after surgery on Friday to repair the torn patellar tendon in his left knee. Even without McLaurin, the Commanders will be the better team. Defensive tackles Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis were awful against Dallas. They were nowhere to be found. They had no quarterback pressures and were knocked off the ball the whole night. The Cowboys ran 65 plays and the vaunted Eagles’ defense had zero tackles for a loss. Carter, the highest paid defensive tackle in the NFL, ran from adversity and declined to talk to the media after the game and continued with his denial of putting out a maximum effort against Dallas this week leading into the Washington game. At least Eagles’ defensive coordinator Vic Fangio was accountable—as he should have been. When asked about a lack of effort, Fangio denied seeing any lack of effort, although he did say, “I didn’t do a good enough job coaching. We didn’t play the run, obviously, well enough. When you do that, it kind of affects everything. I didn’t have them ready to do that the way we need to. We just didn’t play it well.” Numerous sources in and around the Eagles have told Bleeding Green Nation recently that they still trust and believe in Nick Sirianni and Fangio. That the pair still have the locker room. They still somehow believe that Sirianni and Fangio can turn around this disaster, because they have done it before. That they still have faith the Eagles will be playing in vital November and December games. But where there was once unbending support for learning-on-the-job offensive coordinator Sean Mannion and offensive line coach Chris Kuper may be bending. It has changed to doubt as the Eagles keep sinking.

title: Eagles-Commanders Final Injury Report: Saquon Barkley WILL play
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles issued their third and final injury report of the week on Friday in advance of their Week 8 game against the Washington Commanders. The big news is that Saquon Barkley is listed without a game status. He will play on Sunday night. Barkley returned to practice on Friday — albeit in a […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Saquon Barkley #26 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on as he walks through the tunnel against the Washington Commanders during an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles issued their third and final injury report of the week on Friday in advance of their Week 8 game against the Washington Commanders. The big news is that Saquon Barkley is listed without a game status. He will play on Sunday night. Barkley returned to practice on Friday — albeit in a limited capacity — after being listed under did not participate on Wednesday and Thursday. There’s no question that Barkley wanting to play and help his team try to turn the season around is admirable. But the team should protect him from himself and sit him down if he’s not nearly healthy enough to play and remain in the game. Which is reasonable to think that’s the case considering he wasn’t even able to fully participate in a practice this week! While overcompensating for his hamstring injury, Barkley injured his back on his first rushing attempt in Week 7 and then played sparingly through obvious discomfort the rest of the game. What’s the point of that? What if he gets further injured? That’s not only a setback as it relates to this season, which very well might be cooked anyway, but potentially long-term as well. It could also prevent teams from making offers not only ahead of the NFL trade deadline but in the offseason, too. Even if you’re not of the mind he should be traded at any point, you should want him healthy for next year! I just think playing him is a short-sighted decision with much more downside than upside. The Eagles ruled five players OUT: DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Jihaad Campbell, Britain Covey, and Jonathan Jones. Smith and Wicks did not practice this week ahead of their second straight game missed; the Eagles will once again be without their top two wide receivers. With Covey also out, the Eagles only have four healthy wide-outs on the roster: Darius Cooper, Makai Lemon, Hollywood Brown, and Elijah Moore. Against the Cowboys last week, Cooper played the most snaps of any Eagles WR while Lemon was right behind him. Despite this, Cooper only saw three targets while Lemon saw eight. The team will probably look to force-feed their rookie first-round pick again in this matchup. To be determined if they’ll look to elevate a fifth receiver from the practice squad. Their options there: Erik Ezukanma, Xavier Gipson (who also has returning experience), and Quentin Skinner. Campbell will miss the first game of his career. Jeremiah Trotter Jr., who was already eating into Campbell’s playing time, will start in his absence. Smael Mondon is the only linebacker on the roster behind Trot Jr. and Zack Baun. Jones has been the Eagles’ top backup cornerback on the outside. His absence might mean that Kelee Ringo (or Jakorian Bennett or Mac McWilliams) is the next man up if Quinyon Mitchell or Riq Woolen miss snaps. The Eagles ruled one player QUESTIONABLE: Jakorian Bennett. Bennett fully participated in practice all week. He’s still in his 21-day practice window to return from injured reserve. The Eagles have until 4:00 PM Eastern on Saturday to activate him from IR in order for him to play on Sunday. They’ll need to open a roster spot to do so. Players notably listed without a game status: Barkley (as previously noted), Zack Baun, Landon Dickerson, Dallas Goedert, Drew Kendall, Tyler Steen, Arnold Ebiketie, Smael Mondon, Michael Carter II, Nolan Smith, Jonathan Greenard, Jalyx Hunt, Moro Ojomo, and Marcus Epps . They all appeared on the injury report this week. Nolan Smith is notably set to return after missing Week 7 due to a concussion. Michael Carter II is also set to return after missing the Eagles’ last two games. Hunt and Ojomo will play but they were limited in practice all week. They’re clearly not 100%. Bigsby is eligible to return to the roster after Week 8. Shipley is eligible to return to the roster after Week 9. Pierce is eligible to return to the roster after Week 12. Hurts, Sam and, Wilson are out for the season. RESERVE/NON-FOOTBALL INJURY S Tucker Large WASHINGTON COMMANDERS INJURY REPORT (FRIDAY) Washington ruled one player OUT: starting defensive lineman Javon Kinlaw. He ranks second among Commanders defensive tackles in snaps played this season. The Commanders ruled four players QUESTIONABLE: starting defensive tackle Daron Payne, rotational defensive tackle Jer’Zhan Newton, fill-in starting receiver Treylon Burks, and No. 2 tight end John Bates. Payne is a new addition to the report; he was listed as limited with a foot injury on Friday. Not good for the Commanders’ defense if he can’t play. Newton was limited in practice all week. Guessing he won’t suit up. But the Commanders could use him to take some snaps since Kinlaw is out and Payne is now questionable. Burks went limited-DNP-limited over the past three days. We’ll see if he plays. The Commanders are already missing some of their other top receiver options. Bates was limited on Friday after not practicing the previous two days. He might have a chance to suit up. Washington notably has starting left tackle Laremy Tunsil, leading receiver Terry McLaurin, and leading rusher Jacory Croskey-Merritt on injured reserve.
