title: Eagles at Commanders Game Preview: 5 questions and answers with the Week 8 enemy
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles are riding a five-game losing streak entering Sunday Night Football against the Washington Commanders, a team they beat in the season opener. Can the Birds win a game for the first time since September 20? In order to preview this Week 8 NFC East battle, I reached out to our enemies over […]
full_text: Nov 10, 2024; Landover, Maryland, USA; Washington Commanders head coach Dan Quinn (L) congratulates Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels (5) after a touchdown drive against the Pittsburgh Steelers during the first half at Northwest Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Geoff Burke-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Philadelphia Eagles are riding a five-game losing streak entering Sunday Night Football against the Washington Commanders, a team they beat in the season opener. Can the Birds win a game for the first time since September 20? In order to preview this Week 8 NFC East battle, I reached out to our enemies over at Hogs Haven . The amicable Andrew Y kindly kindly took the time to answer my questions about this upcoming battle. Let’s take a look at the answers. 1 – In our Q&A exchange ahead of Week 1 , you said that the Commanders are “ one of the most boom-bust teams in the NFL.” There’s clearly been more bust than boom so far. What’s the biggest reason why? In short, I would say: injuries, two rookie coordinators figuring out how to call plays, and poor preparation and in-game decision making that I mostly blame on HC Dan Quinn. I should also throw in that GM Adam Peters deserves some blame for botching the Center situation in the offseason by starting week 1 with career backup IOL Nick Allegretti as our starting Center. On the plus side for Peters, he found a serviceable Center off the scrapheap in Lucas Patrick who has started at Center since week 3. In terms of injuries, the Commanders’ week 5 injury report had 23 players on it. I don’t remember seeing another injury report that long! Many of those players are on the mend and likely to play this week, but some key remaining absences are LT Laremy Tunsil (out for the year), RB Jacory Croskey-Merritt (the best pure rusher on the roster), WR Terry McLaurin (torn patellar tendon, may never be the same player again), and DT Javon Kinlaw (one of our better penetrating IDL). In terms of the coordinators, we knew it was going to be risky having two coordinators who have never called plays in the NFL before and that is bearing out. On defense, DC Daronte Jones is trying to implement the complicated and almost unique Brian Flores defense from Minnesota. The defense is difficult to implement because it requires players to be very versatile, with even DTs occasionally dropping into coverage and CBs blitzing the QB. Even in Minnesota, the Flores defense was ranked 16th in yards allowed in its first two years before being ranked 3rd last year and 1st this year, and I think a lot of the improvement is due to players getting better at understanding their responsibilities. In addition, Daronte Jones is a first-time NFL playcaller and I think is showing a bit of slowness in adapting to mid-game changes by the opposing offense. On the other side of the ball, OC David Blough is a first-time playcaller with only two years of coaching experience and it’s occasionally showing. He has a good playbook, but plays are taking too long to get called, players are taking too long to get set, and Blough hasn’t been adapting well enough to blitzes by building hot routes into his plays. In terms of Dan Quinn, it’s a lot. Even though the Commanders are somewhat middle-of-the-road in terms of number of penalties, they are exceptional at getting penalties that erase big plays. The Commanders have the most yards erased by penalty in the NFL right now, and I think that comes down to coaching and ultimately, Dan Quinn. In addition, Quinn’s in-game decisions have cost this team games. If he had called for a field goal on the last play in overtime against the Giants, it’s almost certain the Commanders would have won that game. Most importantly though, he’s supposed to be a defensive head coach, yet the Commanders defense has been atrocious the entire time he’s been here. The defense is better under Jones, but it’s still the 9th worst defense in terms of points allowed. 2 – The Commanders decided not to fire Dan Quinn during their bye. How much longer do you think he has left? Reports have been pretty unanimous that owner Josh Harris would rather not fire a coach mid-season, so I think Dan Quinn should be safe until the end of the season unless it looks like the team has quit on him (which it hasn’t). For all his other faults, Quinn has traditionally been great at maintaining the locker room and keeping players motivated, so I don’t think they’re likely to quit on him. At the same time, I think the team would have to not only win the division, but also win a playoff game to keep Quinn around until next year. So I think the most likely outcome is that Quinn gets fired at the end of the season. 3 – Should Washington sign Jayden Daniels to a contract extension this offseason? Will they? Yes and yes. Although Jayden has made a few high-profile gaffes in situational awareness in recent games, he’s the biggest reason the Commanders are in those games to begin with. He’s adapted to a new (very different) offense really well and is playing from the pocket and even protecting himself better with his choices. He’s showing the passing ability you would want from a QB and is an amazing scrambler to boot. My only major concern with Jayden is whether or not he can stay healthy. However, he missed very few games in college and almost all of his games missed in the NFL (both last year and this year) have been due to his left elbow. I’m hoping he has just had a bit of a complicated left elbow problem that will ultimately get fixed. From what I understand, the ligaments in his left elbow may not have healed from last year, which is a low-probability, but very real risk whenever someone dislocates their elbow. It can be fixed with a replacement of damaged or torn ligaments with cadaver ligaments, which I expect Jayden to get after the season is over. 4 – What’s the biggest matchup in the Commanders’ favor and the biggest matchup against their favor? In terms of favorable matchups, WR Antonio Williams won his matchups against CB Cooper DeJean in week 1, so I expect that matchup to get exploited again. The Commanders also did a pretty good job in week 1 of limiting the Eagles run game outside of Jalen Hurts scrambles and I expect them to do it again. The Daronte Jones/Brian Flores scheme is particularly good at stopping the run. The biggest matchup against the Commanders is probably the Eagles DL against the Commanders run game. The Commanders have not been able to move the ball effectively on the ground outside of Jayden Daniels’ scrambles. I think the issue is partly run blocking, partly abandoning the run in playcalling, and partly that very little capital has been invested in the RB room. 5 – Who wins this game and why? With the Commanders currently listed as 5.5-point home favorites, what’s your score prediction? Maybe 23-17 in favor of the Commanders. In Week 1 when these teams played, the Eagles offense relied heavily on Jalen Hurts scrambles to move the ball in critical situations. Tanner McKee doesn’t seem to have the same scrambling ability. The Commanders also let in a lot of interior pressure in that matchup with Nick Allegretti playing at Center. With Lucas Patrick there now, the pass protection should be improved.
author: Brandon Lee Gowton

title: Eagles Film Preview: Philadelphia’s passing plan must punish the Commanders’ blitz
summary: Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite. I also record a video version for Patreon, where I break down […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 04: Tanner McKee #16 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks to pass during the third quarter of the game against the Washington Commanders at Lincoln Financial Field on January 04, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite . I also record a video version for Patreon , where I break down the plays in greater detail and where you can further support my work. I think the Commanders’ defense is a little better than its numbers suggest. The secondary has some talent, and Daronte Jones can create problems with his pressure packages. However, the lack of a reliable four-man pass rush is killing this defense. For the Eagles, this matchup comes down to whether they can handle the blitz. If they can, there should be opportunities to score. Pass Defense The Commanders are allowing around +0.15 EPA per dropback, ranking 26th, but I don’t think that tells the whole story of their secondary. Looking at the individuals, there is more talent here than those results suggest. The problem is getting everyone to play the same coverage correctly while asking them to hold up for too long. Moving to a new system has brought some predictable communication issues. Some plays each week show defenders with different understandings of how a route should be handled. The red-zone example below looks like Cover 4, but the two sides don’t seem to be operating with the same rules. The underneath defender carries a route on one side, while the cornerback on the other passes a receiver off to nobody. Those are the opportunities the Eagles need to create and exploit. Motion, changes in formation and route combinations that force defenders to exchange responsibilities should be part of the plan. There are capable coverage players here, but making them communicate and adjust gives you a chance to expose the mistakes. If you just line up and throw isolation routes, I’m not sure the Eagles are good enough to win. Washington Defense All22 Thread. 1) Moving to a new system, it's no surprise that they have had a few issues with communication in the secondary. I think they are a talented secondary individually, but they seem to make a few mistakes every week, like the one below, that cost… pic.twitter.com/6wpeMU7Lmu — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 29, 2026 Jones comes from the Brian Flores school of defensive football, and you can see the influence in the disguises and unusual pressure looks. Sometimes it’s fascinating. Sometimes I think they are asking their players to do too much. The Tampa 2 disguise below is a good example. A cornerback follows the receiver across the formation, suggesting man coverage, before the defense rotates into zone. I like that part! However, Frankie Luvu is lined up over the A gap and then has to become the deep middle defender. That is an enormous amount of ground to cover, especially for someone whose best work comes moving toward the quarterback. The disguise is supposed to make the quarterback hesitate, but it can also create a difficult assignment for your own defender. The Eagles need to read the movement after the snap and attack the space before that defender can get there. Tanner McKee will have to distinguish the initial picture from the coverage they actually play. 2) I think they are also guilty of trying to do too much at times. Daronte Jones comes from the Brian Flores school of thought, so expect to see some funky blitz looks. Sometimes, I think they try to do too much. This starts off pretty cool, with the CB following the WR across… pic.twitter.com/TUjRasUANd — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 29, 2026 The biggest issue, though, is the pass rush. They simply don’t generate enough pressure with four. The Commanders blitz on 47.4% of dropbacks, the second-highest rate in the league, yet their overall pressure rate is only 34.4%, ranked 18th. That is a lot of extra rushers for a fairly ordinary amount of disruption. The individual numbers reinforce the film. Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson are the main edge threats, but neither has consistently taken over games by winning his matchup. Daron Payne contributes pressure inside, but this isn’t a front that reliably wrecks the pocket without help. When the initial rush stalls, quarterbacks have time to wait for routes to develop and find the gaps between defenders. That is why I’m reluctant to blame all the passing production on the secondary. There are coverage mistakes, but there are also snaps when the coverage has done enough, and the quarterback is still standing comfortably in the pocket. I do think Quan Martin is a weak link when playing deep. His recognition of crossing routes needs to be better, and he can be slow to react and affect the throw. There are opportunities to manipulate his positioning and attack the space around him. Mike Sainristil has also had a terrible season, but his role has changed. With Trey Amos back, Sainristil played only seven defensive snaps in their last game. The Eagles shouldn’t expect the same opportunities to target him that they had in Week 1. Amos, Rasul Douglas, and Amik Robertson give this secondary a more credible group of corners, and Douglas and Robertson have both shown plenty of good individual coverage. 3) However, the biggest issue this defense has is the pass rush. That's why the defense isn't very good. They simply cannot get pressure with 4, which leads to more blitzes. They give up a lot of passing yards, but I do believe it's down to the pass rush rather than the… pic.twitter.com/lblsoD2Ext — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 29, 2026 The Commanders play a lot of two-high coverage, particularly Cover 2 and Cover 4. Their two-high rate is 69.6%, second highest in the league, and they are predominantly a zone defense. That doesn’t mean the Eagles should abandon the idea of throwing vertically. There are opportunities downfield. The classic Cover 2 hole shot, between the cornerback and the safety along the sideline, has been available. Posts and Go routes have also produced high-value plays against them. The Eagles need to recognize the coverage and take those chances when protection allows. Again, the pass rush is a huge part of the explanation. In the example below, the Commanders send five, and the quarterback still gets a beautiful pocket. You can debate the spacing in the secondary, but at some point somebody up front has to make the quarterback uncomfortable. 4) They play a lot of two-high coverages, especially Cover 2 and Cover 4. They give up the sideline on the classic 'hole' shot between the safety and cornerback a lot, but I still look at the pass rush here rather than the secondary. Washington sends 5, and you could not have a… pic.twitter.com/8z9j1o8Jfd — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 29, 2026 This defense is at its best when it blitzes. Extra pressure gives them a better chance to disrupt the play before the coverage is stretched. If I were in the Commanders’ defensive meeting this week, I would plan to blitz the hell out of the Eagles. I would make this offense prove it can identify the pressure and consistently get the ball to the right place. Given the Eagles’ problems answering pressure this season, I would be stunned if the Commanders didn’t lean heavily into that approach. I think we see a 50%+ blitz rate. This will not be like the Cowboys game. Expect overloads and defenders dropping from unexpected places. An edge defender showing rush can become an underneath coverage player, while a linebacker or defensive back replaces him. The offensive line, quarterback, and receivers need to understand the same answer. Getting the protection right is only part of the job if nobody is…

title: Eagles Film Preview: Commanders’ offense gives Philadelphia’s defense a chance to bounce back
summary: Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite. I also record a video version for Patreon, where I break down […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Zack Baun #53 of the Philadelphia Eagles tackles Jayden Daniels #5 of the Washington Commanders in the second quarter of a game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite . I also record a video version for Patreon , where I break down the plays in greater detail and where you can further support my work. The Commanders have a decent offense and a very good young quarterback, but I came away wondering how much more Jayden Daniels could do with better support. Injuries have depleted the talent around Daniels, so the Eagles aren’t facing Washington at their best. For this preview, I focused my film study on the four games Daniels played. Pass Game Remember all the offseason discussion about the Commanders becoming an under-center offense? Well, that hasn’t really happened. David Blough has introduced more of it than we saw under Kliff Kingsbury, but the Commanders still operate from under center on only around 27% of their plays. More importantly, they don’t look particularly good doing it. This offense looks far more comfortable in shotgun and empty, spreading the defense out and letting Daniels see what is happening in front of him. It sounds familiar, doesn’t it?! The lack of production from under center is pretty striking. Looking through their passing plays, I found no explosive completions of 20-plus yards from under center and only one under-center throw that generated at least +1 EPA. The intended relationship between the run game and the play-action passing game just hasn’t produced enough. They will show some interesting receiver insert action and crossing routes behind linebackers, but the under-center menu is heavily tilted toward runs and play action. They barely ever just drop back and throw. Defenses aren’t being asked to defend a particularly broad range of possibilities. Sound familiar?! (On a serious note, I want to write an offseason piece about young OC’s trying to force QB’s under center when it doesn’t suit them, because I think it’s a theme of this season). Washington' Offense All22 Thread. 1) After losing Terry McLaurin for the season, this is a team without a great deal of weapons. Stefon Diggs is their best weapon, and the Eagles already know how much of a threat he can be. They move Diggs around everywhere, and he's still an… pic.twitter.com/dV8oKkh9Wc — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 29, 2026 Stefon Diggs is the biggest remaining receiving threat. The Eagles already know how much trouble he can cause after the first meeting. He remains an outstanding route runner, and the Commanders move him around to find favorable matchups. He’s spent a lot of time in the slot, but I wouldn’t expect him to stay in one place all evening. His ability to change pace, manipulate leverage, and separate gives Daniels a dependable option in an offense that badly needs one. McLaurin’s absence makes the rest of the receiver rotation much more important. Antonio Williams should get more opportunities, and there are some encouraging examples of him working on choice routes and intermediate concepts. However, I would also keep an eye on Treylon Burks. He doesn’t get a huge number of targets, but I thought he looked pretty good in the games I watched. He can get downfield, threaten vertically, and make plays on crossing routes. I loved Burks coming out of college, so there is absolutely some bias here! Still, there is talent to work with, and this offense needs somebody to take on a bigger role. 2) Treylon Burks doesn't get a lot of targets, but he's actually looked pretty good in the games I've watched. He was a 1st-round pick for a reason, and he can get downfield and win vertically. They love these crossing routes, and Daniels normally excels at throwing them.… pic.twitter.com/9qrGA7ZSjs — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 29, 2026 The receivers benefit from playing with a quarterback who is much more advanced than the “one read and run” label that athletic quarterbacks inevitably get. Daniels wants to win from the pocket. He will stand in against pressure and release the ball before a receiver has finished his break. This opposite-hash comeback to Williams below is an excellent example. That throw requires anticipation, timing, and confidence in where the receiver will be. It’s a fantastic throw from a very good young quarterback. I do think there are stretches when Daniels is a little too conservative, particularly early in games. Kurt Warner has highlighted that, and I agree to an extent. However, watching the second half against the 49ers shows what he can do when he starts letting it rip. He also had a few accuracy misses in the games I watched, so I wouldn’t describe every aspect of his passing as consistently excellent. But the quality of his better plays is obvious. 3) Speaking of Williams! This is an outstanding throw from Daniels. Opposite-hash comeback with anticipation. Phew, He's an excellent young quarterback. Because of his running ability, many wrongly assume he's a 1-read, run-only QB. He can run, but he wants to win from the… pic.twitter.com/LLu3tOcxVG — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 29, 2026 The thing that impressed me most was how quickly Daniels eliminates what isn’t available. You regularly see him start on one side, recognize that the defense has taken it away, and work back across the field within the timing of the play. He isn’t automatically looking for an escape route when the first read is covered. He can get to his backside routes and deliver the ball with anticipation. That matters for the Eagles’ linebackers because the Commanders like attacking the middle of the field with crossing and dig routes. Daniels is comfortable finding those windows, and Chig Okonkwo gives him another receiving option inside. The linebackers can’t chase the first underneath route they see or get pulled too far forward by a run fake. 4) The thing that impressed me more than anything about Daniels was his ability to eliminate what isn't there quickly. He gets through his progressions very quickly for a young QB. He does this very frequently. He can eliminate what isn't there (you can see him start right here)… pic.twitter.com/cjiCMftDy9 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 29, 2026 However, the passing game has a significant weakness: its answers to pressure. There are too many plays when the protection is stressed, and the routes don’t give Daniels an accessible immediate answer. Overload pressures, particularly bringing four defenders from one side, have caused repeated problems. The offense can end up asking the quarterback to survive while receivers are still working downfield. This is something I want Vic Fangio to attack. We haven’t seen enough of those aggressive overload looks from the Eagles, and this matchup makes sense to mix them in. The Commanders have taken 14 sacks as a team, with eight coming against blitzes and eight coming on third down. Obvious passing situations and pressure have caused real problems. 5) However, Daniels and the whole offense have a massive problem. They are struggling against the blitz big time, as many offenses are this year. They just don't seem to have answers built in against pressure. Even when they do, Daniels doesn't always take them. Here's the… pic.twitter.com/3RvBFmpyOT — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 29, 2026 Daniels has to take some responsibility too. It would be too generous to blame every pressure failure on Blough. There are snaps when a quick throw is available, and Daniels doesn’t get to it quickly enough. In the example below, he spends too long considering the vertical route…

title: Eagles News: Philadelphia has reportedly told teams that Moro Ojomo is not available for trade
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! I don’t buy that the Eagles won’t trade Moro Ojomo and actually plan to re-sign him instead. This reporting reads to me like Howie Roseman outwardly maintaining that stance in hopes that other teams will increase their offers for the impending […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JULY 30: Moro Ojomo #97 of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts during training camp at Jefferson Health Training Complex on July 30, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! I don’t buy that the Eagles won’t trade Moro Ojomo and actually plan to re-sign him instead. This reporting reads to me like Howie Roseman outwardly maintaining that stance in hopes that other teams will increase their offers for the impending free agent defensive tackle. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Albert Breer: How Two Former Roommates Put the Jeffery Simmons Trade Together – SI Philadelphia Eagles — The Eagles have gotten calls on DT Moro Ojomo, a rising star in a contract year. And that makes sense, given that the team has already paid Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis at his position. Still, the team has told others that Ojomo is not available, and has at least given off the vibe that it’ll try to re-sign him, despite having Carter and Davis already on big deals. That said, other contract-year players like Hollywood Brown, Tariq Woolen and Dallas Goedert could be had. A Saquon Barkley trade seems less likely, especially with Barkley banged up. Eagles Injury Report: Saquon Barkley among key players missing from practice again – BGN Barkley is tracking to miss Sunday’s game. If he can’t play, the Eagles are left with one healthy running back on the active roster: Jaydon Blue. Blue was called up from the practice squad on Wednesday. Playing for the Dallas Cowboys as a rookie last season, Blue logged 38 carries for 129 rushing yards (3.4 average) in addition to one reception for five receiving yards. The Eagles also have Elijah Mitchell, whom the team temporarily elevated to be available to play in Week 7, on the practice squad. Jaydon Blue and Elijah Mitchell. Not exactly the most inspiring backfield for the Eagles to work with! Fantasy football start/sit advice for Week 8 at QB, RB, WR, TE – SB Nation Start — Dallas Goedert, Eagles vs. Commanders — The Eagles are hard to trust, but Goedert gets an excellent matchup here against the Commanders. On the season they’ve allowed the second-most touchdowns, the fifth-most yards and the second-most fantasy points to the position. In Week 1 Goedert caught 4-of-5 targets for 77 yards and two touchdowns against this same team. That was with Jalen Hurts of course, but Tanner McKee is targeting Goedert, as he has 17 receptions over their last three games. Unfortunately those receptions haven’t led to a lot of fantasy scoring, but this week I like his chances to find the end zone. Eagles-Commanders preview: 5 things to watch – PhillyVoice At center, the Commanders cut Tyler Biadasz this summer. Biadasz certainly wasn’t a world-beater but was a solid enough starting center. They then moved Nick Allegretti to center, full-time. Allegretti wasn’t really even a good guard (or a starting one at that), and yet the Commanders opted to put more responsibility on his plate. That was ill-advised. Allegretti missed time during training camp, played poorly during the regular season, and has since been replaced by 33-year-old Lucas Patrick. At RT, 2025 first-round pick Josh Conerly has cut down significantly on his sacks allowed. He has been an improved player. Sam Cosmi is a good RG. This is a bad offensive line, but it might not matter since the Eagles have failed to pressure opposing quarterbacks. As noted above, they have just 8 sacks as a team. Only one team has fewer. Game Review – DAL 38, PHI 21 – Iggles Blitz Tanner McKee seemed more confident and aggressive. The coaches had a better gameplan for him and it gave McKee a better chance of being successful. He should continue to improve as he gets more experience. If he plays the rest of the season we should have a good idea of whether he’s worth bringing back to be the backup QB. I know the current version of him isn’t a guy you’d want, but I do think he’ll get better. As far as him ever developing into a future starter, I think that ship has sailed. My biggest frustration with him on Monday night was decision-making and accuracy. There were times when he had good opportunities available and went elsewhere. Worse was him missing some open guys. McKee must get better with his footwork and mechanics to improve his accuracy. He also needs to be smarter about situational football. McKee did draw defenders offside on two plays. NFL Week 8 preview: Picks, predictions, schedule, betting odds, fantasy tips – ESPN Betting insight: Since 2000, home favorites off a bye are 1-9-1 ATS against teams on short rest after Monday night. Washington’s defense gives Philadelphia a chance despite the injuries. McKee keeps finding Dallas Goedert, and the Commanders struggle against TEs. They also allow touchdowns on 81.8% of red zone trips. I don’t trust Washington to pull away from this depleted Eagles offense. Saquon Barkley on the trade block? What an Eagles sell-off could look like – The Athletic Buyer’s perspective: A running back who is approaching 30 is risky, even one as good as Barkley, who has dealt with injuries this season. His production may have peaked in 2024, during his 2,000-yard season. Still, Barkley’s contract mitigates some of the risk for a potential buyer. He only has $2.5 million guaranteed in 2027. A buyer could view Barkley as a rental for the rest of this year, then cut him in the offseason before his option bonus is due Sept. 1. If Barkley is healthy, he could be a difference-maker for a contender that needs backfield help. The Vikings are one possible team. […] Seller’s perspective: Trading Barkley guts the locker room of its most (available) influential voice on offense. That’s worth considering for a team trying to identify its next generation of leaders. However, Barkley is battling the health challenges he wanted to defy at age 29. Barkley’s stinger, hamstring and back injuries raise red flags. If the Eagles trade Barkley, they can avoid $52.4 million tied up in future option bonuses. Do the Eagles think Barkley’s production in 2027 and 2028 will be more valuable than the investments they could make otherwise? After Dreadful Cowboys Loss, Where Do Eagles Go From Here? Answering Philly’s Biggest Qs – FOX Sports So the idea that Sirianni is safe just because of his stellar record doesn’t hold up to scrutiny, especially since two of those years felt like wasted chances in Philadelphia. And don’t forget, there was some thought he might have been in danger after the Eagles’ first-round exit last year. “They don’t tolerate failure there,” the NFL executive told me. “It feels like every year they don’t win a title, they’re at least thinking about firing their coach. And if you’re about to start over anyway, this might be the perfect time to change it all.” “I never got the impression that they loved him there anyway,” the scout added. “You can’t argue with winning, though. But once that’s gone, all bets are off.” NFL Week 8 picks: Upset and score predictions, matchup breakdowns for every game – NFL.com Why Dan picked the Commanders: Things are getting worse at a troubling clip for Nick Sirianni’s Eagles, who were once 2-0. They have the league’s second-longest active losing streak (five games) and a -745 differential in total yards (second-worst in the NFL and worst by the Eagles through seven games since 1999). Yes, they have entered worst of the century levels of bad, at least by their standards. The Commanders didn’t win in October, either, but they enjoy a significant rest advantage entering Week 8. Washington is coming off a bye, while Philadelphia is playing on a short week after being blown out by the Cowboys on Monday night. Dan Quinn should have ample time to get his players ready to kick a division rival when it’s down. Then again, the following from NFL Research makes me wonder if the Commanders can…
author: Brandon Lee Gowton

title: Steelers vs. Browns: Week 8 game picks
summary: First place in the AFC North is up for grabs as the Pittsburgh Steelers host the Cleveland Browns. Both teams enter the day at 5-2, with Cleveland holding a 1-0 head-to-head advantage over Pittsburgh. Will they beat the Steelers on the road in a regular season game for the first time since 2003? Our staff […]
full_text: (Photo by Frank Jansky/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images First place in the AFC North is up for grabs as the Pittsburgh Steelers host the Cleveland Browns. Both teams enter the day at 5-2, with Cleveland holding a 1-0 head-to-head advantage over Pittsburgh. Will they beat the Steelers on the road in a regular season game for the first time since 2003? Our staff weighs in. Mike Nicastro : The Steelers haven’t lost to the Browns twice in a season in almost three decades, but this year presents a unique challenge. Teams traveling internationally over the last two seasons are just 1-7 when returning to face a team that did not travel overseas the prior week. That one win was the Broncos last season, when they scored 33 4th quarter points against the Giants to win by 1 point. Fatigue will play a factor, but having home field will help significantly. This is still a Browns team that lost to the Jets on the road, and just went to the wire with the Titans. Won’t be surprised if its ugly, but Pittsburgh rides the run game again into their bye. Steelers 20 Browns 17. Ryan Parish : The Steelers were the better team in 3 out of 4 quarters the last time these teams met a few weeks ago. Both teams have found a groove since, and they enter the contest at 5-2. Winner leaves the game atop the AFC North. I’ve had a running bit in these predictions that will not change until it stops working. Browns 24-Steelers 23. Austin Bechtold: The Steelers haven’t lost to the Browns at home in the regular season since I was two. I can’t fathom it happening with how the Steelers defense is playing right now. I’ve been wrong about Patrick Graham and doubted his scheme to a degree early in the season, but if he calls a great gameplan Sunday I’m sold. Aaron Rodgers is playing his best football since 2021. The Browns aren’t the old Browns and I think are better than people are giving credit for. The Steelers do what it takes, and will be in sole possession of first place in the AFC North on Sunday. Steelers 24-18. Ryland Bickley : This is a series that has been defined by home teams winning as of late, and with the Steelers on a hot streak and playing in Acrisure this Sunday, I don’t expect that to change. Cleveland’s man coverage scheme should once again prove a challenge for the Pittsburgh offense, but the Steelers defense has taken some strides since the last matchup. Steelers 27, Browns 20 . Joey Bray : When these teams take the field on Sunday, the Pittsburgh Steelers will be exactly one month removed from suffering another loss to the Browns in Cleveland on Thursday Night Football. Since that game, the Steelers have won three straight. I can’t say for certain how much the team has grown since then, as they still have concerns in the secondary on defense and struggles in the red zone as an offense. Unlike last time where the browns jumped out to a big lead early, I think this game will be a close one throughout. The Browns are a much better football team that anyone anticipated entering the season. Todd Monken deserves a ton of credit for the way he has continued to put Deshaun Watson and the offense in positions to win. However, all five of their wins have come on game winning drives, a trend that is unlikely to continue. I’ll take Pittsburgh to get their revenge on Cleveland and go into the bye week with sole possession of first place in the AFC North. Steelers 21, Browns 20 . Jarrett Bailey: I said ahead of the Saints game that I don’t know if the Steelers are a team I’d bank on winning four games in a row, yet here we are after a three-game win streak. The whole “Cleveland hasn’t won in Pittsburgh since 2003” doesn’t necessarily mean much to me in terms of results. Although it does seem to matter when these two teams play in Cleveland that the Steelers turn into the worst versions of themselves. I do think the Steelers win, but I’m not going to take this Browns team lightly. Steelers 20, Browns 16. Let us know what you think in the comments . full_text: The Seattle Seahawks’ Friday injury report is akin to a trick-or-treating outing with some candy, some raisins and plenty of scares. Starting on the unsettling side, the Seahawks are looking at playing the Chicago Bears on Monday night without starting left tackle Charles Cross, who was injured last week, and edge rusher Uchenna Nwosu. Cross and Nwosu both did not participate in practice on Thursday, and the same held true on Friday. The loss of Cross should equal plenty of time for swing tackle Josh Jones, while Nwosu’s loss could be massive for a pass rush that has gotten inconsistent pressure with four rushers. Nwosu is excellent at slowing quarterbacks who leave the pocket, so look for the Seahawks to blitz on Monday against Caleb Williams. While Seattle got welcome good news about Leonard Williams, who returned to practice in full after being limited on Thursday with an Achilles injury, all is not well with their defensive tackle room. Fellow star defensive lineman Byron Murphy was added to the injury report with a back injury that kept him limited on Friday. Backup to both of them, Brandon Pili, also missed Friday’s practice with a back injury. Seattle will more than likely be without wide receiver Rashid Shaheed, who missed his second straight day of practice on Friday. The team will surely lean on Tory Horton to step up to fill the void felt, both on offense and on special teams. Back on the positive side of things, the Seahawks offense looks to be getting a boost in the running back room ahead of Monday night. Rookie Jadarian Price was a full participant in practice after returning from an IR stint. Price’s return couldn’t come at a better time, as Zach Charbonnet was limited with a knee injury and backup Velus Jones Jr. missed Friday’s practice entirely with a hamstring injury. Linebacker Drake Thomas’ return to the lineup appears imminent as he was a full go in practice after he missed several games with an ankle injury. The linebacking core continues to be in flux as Tyrice Knight was limited, while Chazz Surratt was a full participant and Patrick O’Connell missed Friday’s practice. Here is the full Seahawks report. title: Former Seahawks assistant takes over Panthers defense after Ejiro Evero firing
summary: A familiar face will be pulling the strings for the Carolina Panthers’ defense when they face the Seattle Seahawks in Week 17.  After the Panthers fired defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero, in the wake of their 27-19 loss to the Green Bay Packers on Thursday night, they named former Seahawks defensive line coach Todd Wash as […]
full_text: A familiar face will be pulling the strings for the Carolina Panthers’ defense when they face the Seattle Seahawks in Week 17. After the Panthers fired defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero , in the wake of their 27-19 loss to the Green Bay Packers on Thursday night, they named former Seahawks defensive line coach Todd Wash as interim coordinator. Wash coached Seattle’s defensive line from 2011-12, before leaving with Gus Bradley for the Jacksonville Jaguars to become their DL coach and run game coordinator — and later being elevated to defensive coordinator. The 58-year-old has been with the Panthers since 2023, and is a part of a brass heavy on Seahawks ties. In the front office, general manager Dan Morgan got his start as a scout under John Schneider. The coaching staff, meanwhile, is led by former Seahawks QB coach Dave Canales. Darrell Bevell is an associate head coach and long-time tight ends coach Pat McPherson serves that role under Canales after 13 years in Seattle. In his second go-round as a defensive coordinator, Wash will be tasked with helping to turn around a defense currently 27th in points allowed and 23rd in yards allowed.

title: Why the Seahawks are allowed to have five comp picks in 2027 NFL Draft
summary: The Seattle Seahawks technically have just five picks in the 2027 NFL Draft as things stand right now. By the early part of spring, they should have 10 picks after their five compensatory selections are awarded. After the Quenton Nelson trade, one of our commenters brought up that the Seahawks should only get a maximum […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks technically have just five picks in the 2027 NFL Draft as things stand right now. By the early part of spring, they should have 10 picks after their five compensatory selections are awarded . After the Quenton Nelson trade, one of our commenters brought up that the Seahawks should only get a maximum of four compensatory picks, which is something I want to address and clarify! It’s a partially correct statement but with a caveat. Free agency comp picks max out at four Compensatory picks for free agents do have a limit. Next season, the Seahawks are slated to have comp picks for the following FA departures: Kenneth Walker III Boye Mafe Coby Bryant Riq Woolen Dareke Young’s contract was too low to be classified as a compensatory free agent (CFA) and Seattle didn’t sign a single CFA free agent. NFL rules limit the maximum number of compensatory picks awarded through free agency to four. That the Seahawks were a -4 in compensatory free agents lost is purely coincidence. Even if the Seahawks didn’t retain Rashid Shaheed and Josh Jobe and lost six CFAs while signing none, Seattle would’ve instead been awarded the four highest valued comp picks by round. The Nolan Teasley comp pick is separate Seattle’s fifth comp pick is a 2027 third-rounder for Nolan Teasley, who left the Seahawks assistant general manager role to become the Minnesota Vikings GM. Teasley is biracial— his father is black —and therefore he qualifies as a minority candidate hiring. Under the Rooney Rule, teams who lose a minority candidate to a head coach or general manager position—or, more accurately, a primary football executive—receive third-round compensatory picks over the next two drafts. For the Seahawks, they will get third-rounders from the Teasley hire in the 2027 and 2028 drafts. Those picks are completely separate from the comp pick formula, so it is possible to have five compensatory picks in a single draft. In 2022, the San Francisco 49ers had five comp picks split into two minority candidate hires (the first of two third-rounders for Mike McDaniel, plus the second of two third-rounders for Robert Saleh) and three CFA formula picks. Teasley’s third-rounder is set in stone, whereas the free agent comp picks will be settled into specific rounds at the end of the season.

title: What kind of Seattle Seahawks fan are you?
summary: (Editor’s note: The following is a guest discussion post by Field Gulls commenter Kasey McKillip) I don’t mean how passionate you are, how many games you attend, or whether you regard a loss as a personal affront requiring several hours of silence. I mean something more revealing: when you encounter a number, which Seattle Seahawk […]
full_text: (Editor’s note: The following is a guest discussion post by Field Gulls commenter Kasey McKillip) I don’t mean how passionate you are, how many games you attend, or whether you regard a loss as a personal affront requiring several hours of silence. I mean something more revealing: when you encounter a number, which Seattle Seahawk appears in your mind? When you see 54, do you immediately think of Bobby Wagner, or does Grant Feasel get a look in? When you see 3, is it Russell Wilson without a moment’s hesitation, or have you already moved on to Nick Emmanwori? Richard Sherman would seem to have 25 pretty well locked up, unless you harbour an inexplicable affection for Robert Blackmon. And 24? Come on. Is there even a discussion? Marshawn Lynch played just 83 regular-season games for Seattle, but longevity has never been the only way to measure a football player. Some people occupy a roster spot. Others occupy a permanent location in your imagination. The same principle applies to 37 and Shaun Alexander, 29 and Earl Thomas, and 31 and Kam Chancellor. These aren’t merely numbers attached to men who played football. They are shorthand for entire periods of your life, complete with victories, disappointments, arguments and the occasional moment when you were convinced the Seahawks were about to ruin your entire weekend. Then there’s 89, which presents a legitimate dilemma. Brian Blades or Doug Baldwin? Both are perfectly defensible answers. You could make a case for either, and the interesting part isn’t necessarily which player you choose. It’s what your choice reveals about the games you watched, the teams you remember and the particular version of the Seahawks that lives inside your head. Number 4 is another curious case. Perhaps you remember Trent Dilfer’s time in Seattle. Perhaps, like me, your mind now goes straight to Michael Dickson, whose punting has somehow made a position most people barely think about into something worth watching. And 16? It will take some getting used to seeing somebody else wear it. Tyler Lockett leaves behind the kind of legacy that makes a jersey number feel less like an item of sporting equipment and more like an inherited family possession. Because that’s what these numbers become. Players are temporary custodians, doing their best to represent a number before eventually passing it along. Every new player adds another chapter, whether that chapter becomes legendary, forgettable or something that only one person in your friendship group remembers. Perhaps 1 takes you back to the seasons when Warren Moon was in Seattle. Maybe 5 conjures Charlie Frye. These aren’t necessarily the names that appear in highlight packages or feature prominently in conversations about the franchise’s greatest players. They’re simply the names your memory has decided to keep. And that, I think, is the beauty of following a football team for years. The longer you watch, the more complicated these associations become. Numbers accumulate histories. Memories overlap. A jersey can connect you to a championship, a terrible season, a favourite player or an afternoon spent watching a game with someone who is no longer around. Some numbers, of course, have been retired altogether: 45 for Kenny Easley, 71 for Walter Jones, 80 for Steve Largent and 96 for Cortez Kennedy. Their achievements have made the numbers inseparable from their names, leaving the Seahawks with no intention of asking someone else to fill those jerseys. Which brings me back to the original question. What kind of Seahawks fan are you? The answer might have very little to do with how loudly you cheer. It might be found in the numbers you recognise, the players you remember and the names that surface before you’ve even had time to think. Join the conversation! title: DeForest Buckner joins growing list proving 49ers don’t burn bridges
summary: Dre Greenlaw, Deebo Samuel, Kendrick Bourne, and now DeForest Buckner. The San Francisco 49ers now have four players who left, either in free agency or via trade, and eventually made their way back to Santa Clara. You might see one or two players return to their original team, but not at the rate the 49ers […]
full_text: MIAMI, FLORIDA - FEBRUARY 2: DeForest Buckner #99 of the San Francisco 49ers stands on the sideline before the game against the Kansas City Chiefs in Super Bowl LIV at Hard Rock Stadium on February 2, 2020 in Miami, Florida. The Chiefs defeated the 49ers 31-20. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Dre Greenlaw, Deebo Samuel, Kendrick Bourne, and now DeForest Buckner. The San Francisco 49ers now have four players who left, either in free agency or via trade, and eventually made their way back to Santa Clara. You might see one or two players return to their original team, but not at the rate the 49ers have. There are two ways to look at this. The first is that the 49ers are a first-class organization. While wide receiver Mike Evans wanted to play with Brock Purdy , George Kittle sold him on it with all the things the 49ers do differently . It was either more modern technology, personalized nutritionists instead of a team nutritionist, or other small things that cost a lot of money and don’t show up on a salary cap sheet. The second: the grass isn’t always greener elsewhere. That’s not to say there aren’t grievances from the 49ers’ returning players. Dre Greenlaw had some choice words for Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton, but it’s not so much an indictment that other teams are worse, just that the 49ers do something right. Greenlaw left for a three-year, $35 million deal in Denver. This resulted in eight games and a release after one season. A r elease he felt was handled poorly . Then there’s Samuel. He was traded to the Washington Commanders and got a crowd-pleasing 17 carries. This is after he averaged around 45 a season over his previous four years with the 49ers. Same player, different usage. The time away was so short that Samuel said he felt like he never left . And finally, Buckner. The latest addition of returning players . The Chicago Bears were reportedly interested in the defensive tackle in this week’s NFC arms race. Buckner himself wanted San Francisco . Reports said Buckner was unhappy with the extension offer —which is fair. If there really were burned bridges back in 2020, would he really be gunning to go there? Doubtful. And that second point is even more valuable for rookies to keep in mind when their contracts expire. Sure, they can go for the big money—and they should—but they also now have three players in the building (minus Bourne, who returned for 2025 only) who went after a better deal or a different role and know what it’s like to leave the 49ers—sometimes frustrated. This isn’t an argument to say players need to take whatever cheap deal the 49ers offer because they are the 49ers. Sometimes letting players go is the 49ers’ mistake. While the 49ers used the savings from Buckner’s deal to extend Arik Armstead and Jimmie Ward, the trade itself—a first-rounder from the Indianapolis Colts—backfired because Javon Kinlaw—the pick meant to replace Buckner—did not work out. It’s helpful for veteran leadership and a talking point for the younger players. The 49ers have had some good drafts both in 2025 and 2026, and those young players can look to three people in the locker room who were drafted by the 49ers, left, and returned—and know what leaving the team is like as well as why they came back. Then they can look to George Kittle, among others, as to why he stayed. It also offsets the grievances of one Brandon Aiyuk. Aiyuk’s offseason antics of never wanting to do business with the 49ers create an impression of an insufferable organization. One that all players should avoid. And players talk; they take notice. Free agents and draft prospects can all look at Aiyuk and think something is wrong with the 49ers. Aiyuk looks more and more like a severe minority when you see Buckner, Greenlaw, and Samuel coming back and playing hard. Playing devil’s advocate for his side of the 49ers feud gets more and more difficult when you see other players having no problem returning—even after the 49ers couldn’t pay them what they wanted initially. If the 49ers were such an evil organization, how can you explain all three of them coming back? Again, Buckner said it was San Francisco or nowhere. I’ll never argue against a player getting paid. There’s too much fine print in a contract in a league referred to as “Not For Long” for them not to get the best deal for them and their family. That said, the fact that the 49ers keep the door wide open should they want to return—and players accept—says something about the organization. And the players themselves can tell rookies and second-year players what to expect when they sign on the dotted line with another team. Sometimes that’s more valuable than a film breakdown.

I just needed somebody to kind of veer me back on the path, right?” The king of the jungle also keeps an eye on his teammates’ happiness as well as their success on the field. “I try to keep a good feel of the locker room and the guys that I feel like might need that kind of a push,” he said. “If all of a sudden they’re a little off, I can kind of ask questions to make sure they’re good. “I can tell them things that helped me in the past, and maybe there is something they can hold on to.” No veterans did that for Warner when he was a rookie in 2018 because “let’s be honest, athletes weren’t talking much about mental health back then,” he said.” 49ers’ John Lynch opens up about Kyle Shanahan partnership, trade outlook “”And so, that’s why you’ve got to have a lot of different ideas, if you feel like you need something. And you also have to be able to say, ‘No, I like our team. We’re going to roll with this.’ And next year’s draft is real important, too. That’s the lifeblood of these teams. So, you always want to have enough assets to improve your team via the draft, because that’s the best way.” 49ers’ Renardo Green addresses Kyle Shanahan sideline confrontation, game slowing down “When you just done played so much ball, been in so many situations, been around so many great minds, and then, think about it, I do play around a whole bunch of great players,” Green said. “You just learn and pick the game up, and from that point on, it’s like, now you’re just processing everything, and it’s just happening—it’s just slow. Everything just happening slow.” I graded every single DeForest Buckner snap this season. Here’s what he’ll bring (back) to the 49ers. (Paywall) “I really wanted to get a sense of what Buckner’s plan of attack is. Overwhelmingly, he relies on a stab/swim combo. It can look a little different depending on the scenario, where he sometimes doesn’t need the stab, or he gets attached, reacts, and then pulls out the swim. His real secondary move is power. His height should make it far trickier to pull off, because he has to lower himself to really get into the chest of offensive linemen. But he’s so crafty, strong, and leverage conscious that he’s extremely effective when he uses it (it’s also a slight alternative to what offensive linemen expect). He’ll occasionally mix in the ole Reggie White hump move, too. When he wants to split a double team and knows it’s coming, he also tries to get skinny and rip through, but that hasn’t been exceedingly effective in the six reps he tried it out. The occasional cross-chop is fun though….He’s an exceptionally difficult pass rusher to handle and requires double teams on most snaps. If I had a criticism, it’s that stumpier guards like Peter Skoronski and John Simpson gave him a little bit of trouble…. …The interesting thing about watching Buckner wasn’t that he had run game weaknesses. Those were clear, as I show in the video above. But based on the narrative, I would have expected him to be a worse run defender than what I saw. Is he gettable? Sure. I’ll get into that shortly. But he had some tremendous, singlehanded run stuffs, and generally looked like a positive player in the run game.” John Lynch on Mike Evans’ Achilles injury: ‘I think the idea is you’ve just got to quiet that thing down’ “Mike’s been working tirelessly.” On KNBR, Lynch said, “He’ll continue to do that. He’s on a great plan, and I think the idea is you’ve just got to quiet that thing down. We dealt with that with Christian [McCaffrey] last year — remember, he had that bilateral. We talked about that a lot, and fortunately, with Mike, it’s just on the one side.”

title: Inside Brock Purdy’s passing numbers this season
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are enjoying their bye week while calling around and keeping tabs on potential trade partners and players. Although it isn’t technically the second half of the season, the bye week marks a nice point in the season to look back at the past seven weeks for Brock Purdy. With seven weeks […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) The San Francisco 49ers are enjoying their bye week while calling around and keeping tabs on potential trade partners and players. Although it isn’t technically the second half of the season, the bye week marks a nice point in the season to look back at the past seven weeks for Brock Purdy. With seven weeks of sample size paired with the efficiency and offensive output, narratives have been spun praising and knocking down Purdy’s performance. It’s hard to argue the level of play from Purdy this season hasn’t been an upgrade over past years, but the same tired narratives about Kyle Shanahan and his system and the “Avengers” persist. Unfortunately, no matter how well Purdy plays, people will cling to the Shanahan and playmakers argument for eternity. The truth is, everyone needs help from playmakers, and the system absolutely matters. Think about all the people who blame coaching and the lack of playmakers for certain Patrick Mahomes or Josh Allen performances. If those guys need help, then everyone does, right? Taking a look at some key metrics for Purdy through seven weeks as a passer, outside of QBR or passer rating, tells another side of the story of 2026, thanks to PFN Fantasy . Purdy’s average time to throw is 2.99 seconds, which is good for fifth in the league. The offensive line has played well this season, but this number is indicative of Purdy scrambling more than others, as evidenced by four of the quarterbacks ahead of him on this list. Mahomes and Drake Maye are tied for first at 3.17 seconds and are followed by Caleb Williams and Bo Nix. As far as “first read” throws go, Purdy is fourth in the NFL at 67.5%. Matthew Stafford is first at 77.4%, with Jared Goff at 72.7% and Jordan Love at 69.6% right behind him. Stafford and Love play in similar offenses to Purdy, with timing and precision as a passer being at the top of the list. Joe Burrow is right behind Purdy, and Zac Taylor is part of the same tree. Looking at “designated receiver” throws, which are screens, shovel passes, jet sweeps, and forward passes, Purdy has a modest 7.5%. I would argue that Purdy’s ability as a passer negates the need for these types of plays, as opposed to past quarterbacks and in years past for Shanahan and the offense. “Second read” throws are an interesting number to note. Purdy has a 7.5% of second-read throws. For reference, that is the third-lowest percentage, with only Love (2.2%), Malik Willis, and Tyler Shough at lower numbers, and Willis and Shough have zero throws to the second read. Again, citing the timing and precision needed in Shanahan’s offense, this shouldn’t be viewed as a negative all the time. When the offense is operating normally, the throws are out quickly to a receiver who is open and in the spot he’s supposed to be in. What about the good old “checkdown” narrative? The issue is people not understanding the difference between designed throws underneath as a way to gain YAC and a checkdown. A checkdown is after the quarterback has looked downfield and found his outlet. Not when it’s a designed throw. Either way, in 2026, Purdy has a 12.5% checkdown rate. When you have Christian McCaffrey, it’s not the worst idea to put the ball in his hands. Finally, Purdy’s scramble throw rate is 10%. Part of Purdy’s hot start to the season and his overall approach is to extend plays and make something happen off-script, which is a welcome sight for Shanahan at times. Again, the quarterbacks who top this list are Mahomes, Nix, Williams, Willis, and Snoop Huntley. Only Huntley is under 20 percent, with the other four in the high 20s. Hopefully, these numbers help paint a better picture of what Purdy is asked to do and what he adds to the 49ers offense. The bye week is at the perfect time for San Francisco as Purdy’s weapons are returning healthy, with the potential of adding another weapon at receiver. Purdy has played very well in 2026, and here’s to hoping people can discuss his play honestly now and going forward.
author: Jason Aponte

title: John Lynch on Mike Evans’ Achilles injury: ‘I think the idea is you’ve just got to quiet that thing down’
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are hopeful to get a handful of reinforcements back at practice next week. One of those players expected to return in the near future is Mike Evans, who missed Week 7 with multiple injuries. It didn’t make sense to play Evans on a short week with the bye coming up. According […]
full_text: (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are hopeful to get a handful of reinforcements back at practice next week. One of those players expected to return in the near future is Mike Evans, who missed Week 7 with multiple injuries. It didn’t make sense to play Evans on a short week with the bye coming up. According to general manager John Lynch, “Mike’s been working tirelessly.” On KNBR, Lynch said, “He’ll continue to do that. He’s on a great plan, and I think the idea is you’ve just got to quiet that thing down. We dealt with that with Christian [McCaffrey] last year — remember, he had that bilateral. We talked about that a lot, and fortunately, with Mike, it’s just on the one side.” Lynch continued, saying, “he’s dealt with it some throughout his career, but it got to a point where it was really inhibiting his ability to play. At that point, you’ve got to take him out and try to quiet the thing down. Making good progress on that. We need to continue, and Mike will be tireless in his efforts to do that.” Lynch wouldn’t commit to saying Evans would be back at practice next week. He did say, “Mike, he’s a pro. Mike’s going to attack that, and it’s hard for Mike to miss. He doesn’t like doing it, but he also understands the big picture: That we need him right, and we’ll make sure that he is before he returns.” The 49ers face two subpar defenses in the Raiders and Vikings in Weeks 9 and 10, before the schedule turns into two to three playoff teams in the Vikings, Seahawks, and Giants. If you need to give Evans another week or two, then so be it. Ideally, it’s only one. You should be able to get by the Raiders without Evans. Dallas’s defense is lousy enough that maybe even the Cowboys, too—although you’ll need to score against that offense. But the Vikings present a unique challenge, and the Seahawks are the Seahawks. We’ll see how patient the 49ers are with Evans, and if he misses any more time at all. They have to be smart and understand Evans was signed to do what he’s been doing all season, but that won’t matter if he’s not on the field come January.

title: Do the 49ers have the resources for another trade deadline splash?
summary: The 49ers have already filled one significant need ahead of the trade deadline, making a move that made perfect sense in reuniting with defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. San Francisco sent a fourth-round pick to the Indianapolis Colts to bring back the player who was selected by the 49ers with the seventh overall pick in the […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 11: General Manager John Lynch of the San Francisco 49ers gestures after the game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on October 11, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 49ers have already filled one significant need ahead of the trade deadline, making a move that made perfect sense in reuniting with defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. San Francisco sent a fourth-round pick to the Indianapolis Colts to bring back the player who was selected by the 49ers with the seventh overall pick in the 2016 draft. That is a very reasonable price for a player who has four sacks and who was tied for 10th in pressures among defensive tackles entering Week 8. But it leaves the 49ers with limited capital with which to address their remaining issues as they plot a run at the Super Bowl. In an ideal world, the 49ers would probably like to add another wide receiver and an edge rusher to their 53-man roster before the Nov. 10 trade deadline. However, with only six picks remaining in the 2027 draft , they may not have the resources for another splash trade. The 49ers still hold their first, second and third-round picks next year. They also have their fifth-round pick and a sixth-rounder acquired from the Baltimore Ravens and a seventh-rounder acquired from the Kansas City Chiefs. San Francisco has put a lot of emphasis on getting younger in recent years, and each of their last three drafts have netted them players who have either established themselves as starters or made a significant impact playing in a rotation. As such, the 49ers may be reluctant to use too many of their remaining 2027 selections in another trade, especially as they do not have the luxury of projected compensatory picks on which to fall back. Of course, that does not necessarily prohibit the 49ers from making another move. Veteran edge Khalil Mack has been named as a potential target and, as a 35-year-old edge rusher on a 0-6 team in the final year of his contract, it likely would not take much to prise him from the Los Angeles Chargers. But if the 49ers want to make a more eye-catching move by pursuing a wide receiver like Garrett Wilson or a dominant edge such as Maxx Crosby, it could cost them multiple first-round picks and several more selections in next year’s draft. At 6-1 after a largely impressive effort on both sides of the ball through seven games, the 49ers look to be in a position to push their chips into the middle of the table with an all-in trade. However, they will be well aware of the risk of doing so, and the potential damaging knock-on effects of having limited draft picks if such a move does not work out. By trading for Buckner, the 49ers have once again shown they are willing to do the deals to try to put the team over the top in the hunt that for that elusive sixth Super Bowl title. Yet the Niners also need to think carefully about the future and, given the position a blockbuster trade could put them in come next April, San Francisco’s next swing before the deadline may have to be more conservative than many will want.
author: Nicholas McGee

title: The Niners are not expected to trade for a star receiver, per insider
summary: The San Francisco 49ers started their bye week with a splash, trading for DeForest Buckner to add another veteran to their defensive tackle room. The move wasn’t too costly, as the 49ers sent a 2027 fourth-round pick for the 32-year-old defensive tackle, who is in the final year of his contract. On Thursday, we saw […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 19: Head coach Kyle Shanahan of the San Francisco 49ers leaves the field after a win against the Washington Commanders at Levi's Stadium on October 19, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers started their bye week with a splash, trading for DeForest Buckner to add another veteran to their defensive tackle room. The move wasn’t too costly, as the 49ers sent a 2027 fourth-round pick for the 32-year-old defensive tackle, who is in the final year of his contract. On Thursday, we saw the Chicago Bears make a major move, trading two first-round picks and more for Tennessee Titans star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, positioning themselves as a top contender in the NFC alongside the 49ers. This deadline could end up being a busy one, with the Super Bowl race feeling quite open overall. The 49ers are at the top of the board, as they’re the current Super Bowl favorites. And they might not be done yet after the Buckner deal, with potential needs at edge rusher, wide receiver, and even cornerback. However, a trade for a star wide receiver doesn’t seem likely, according to NBC Sports Bay Area’s Matt Maiocco. Speaking on KNBR, Maiocco addressed the possibility of the 49ers going after Garrett Wilson or another star receiver following the Bears move for Simmons. “The player that I’ve heard the fans are clamoring for that would be along the lines of a Jeffery Simmons would be maybe on the other side of the ball: wide receiver Garrett Wilson, where you would have to give up a lot because he’s under contract for a while,” Maiocco shared on Thursday. “But he’s also under contract for a while at a salary up around $30 million a year.” Instead of a splash like that, the insider suggested a smaller move like San Francisco’s trade for Keion White last year that allows the 49ers to keep their draft capital and remain balanced. “I think that what the 49ers could do would be something similar to what they did last year in getting Keion White,” Maiocco continued, “where you don’t necessarily know too much about the player, but he’s on a fixed salary for this year and the next, and maybe he’s fallen out of favor or doesn’t fit a new coach’s scheme. “So, I could see where something like that would happen, but with as many high-priced players as the 49ers have on the team now, currently, and who remain under contract to the team for years to come, I don’t see them adding another 30-plus or $25 million player and giving up the first-round draft picks. I think the 49ers value those first-round draft picks.” Earlier in the season, I was against the idea of the 49ers going after a wide receiver on the trade market. After all, following their returns from injury, the 49ers are expected to have Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel, De’Zhaun Stribling, Christian Kirk, Jordan Watkins, and Jacob Cowing as their roster room. Is it an elite room? No. But that group of players could be good enough for the 49ers high-octane offense, with Evans as the clear No. 1. The big question is health, and whether Evans needs a better complementary piece, such as Brian Thomas Jr. It feels like the top priority for the 49ers next is an edge rusher. Perhaps the 49ers go the cheap route there again and look to develop a younger player, but that room definitely feels like an area to add ahead of the deadline.

title: NFL trade deadline: Will the Buccaneers be sellers in 2026?
summary: Welcome to the the midway point of the NFL season. This is the fun time where teams that are good are supposed to go out and add to their roster, while the bad teams have fans and pundits saying they need to start unloading talent to acquire draft picks and begin the preparations for next […]
full_text: Photo by Cliff Welch/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to the the midway point of the NFL season. This is the fun time where teams that are good are supposed to go out and add to their roster, while the bad teams have fans and pundits saying they need to start unloading talent to acquire draft picks and begin the preparations for next season because this season’s hopes and dreams are finished. So which team are the Tampa Bay Buccaneers? Bad? Yes. Out of contention? No. The decision of whether or not to be sellers cant be talked through without mention of the NFC South. Since the departure of Tom Brady, the NFC South has been NFC South-ing at a high level. The division has only had one double-digit victor since 2021 and hasn’t won a postseason game since 2023. This year’s rendition of the South, has Tampa Bay in third place with just two wins after seven games— The difference between the third place Buccaneers and the second place Falcons? This Sunday’s game. Carolina remains out in front, however, Tampa has the current tiebreaker over Carolina and all of ther other division games to go. The ineptitude of the NFC South makes Jason Licht’s decision difficult. It would be sincerely simple for Tampa to throw in the towel at 2-5 if they were in the NFC West, the NFC North, or even the NFC East. Each of those divisions would have the Buccaneers in third or tied for last needing to work all the way to a winning record in order to compete. That is just not necessarily the case in the NFC South— There’s a fairly decent chance a team with a record closer to, perhaps even below, .500 snags the divison crown. The Buccaneers would need quite a turn around down the stretch to finish with a winning season, but seven wins? That feels possible and because those seven wins are a possibility, it may hold Jason Licht back from moving any major pieces at this year’s deadline.

title: NFL predictions: Titans-Bengals matchup could get ugly
summary: Each week I write a preview post on Fridays. Earlier in the week, I was thinking about the mismatch that the Cincinnati Bengals offense poses for the Tennessee Titans defense. That was when Jeffery Simmons was still on the Titans. Now that Big Jeff has been traded to the Chicago Bears, that mismatch is astronomical. […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 25: Quarterback Joe Burrow #9 of the Cincinnati Bengals throws a pass against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images Each week I write a preview post on Fridays. Earlier in the week, I was thinking about the mismatch that the Cincinnati Bengals offense poses for the Tennessee Titans defense. That was when Jeffery Simmons was still on the Titans. Now that Big Jeff has been traded to the Chicago Bears, that mismatch is astronomical. Joe Burrow and the Bengals are 5th in the league in passing and 4th in the league in points scored per game. The Titans are 26th in the league against the pass. With Simmons in the middle of the defense, there was at least some hope that the Titans could create enough pressure to keep Burrow from having a career-type day. How are the Titans going to do that now? They aren’t. The Simmons trade should open up snaps for Femi Oledajo and Keldric Faulk on the defensive lines. They are two young players that the Titans spent high draft picks on in hopes of them being able to disrupt the quarterback. We haven’t seen that from either of those guys to this point. It is time for them to step up. If the Titans are going to have a chance to win this game, they are going to have to be able to keep pace with the Bengals offense. The Bengals pass defense hasn’t been very good allowing 233 yards per game. Cam Ward has probably heard people talking this week about how the Simmons trade means they have given up on him. If he wants to quiet that talk, he needs to come out and have a big day against a pretty soft defense. The Titans opened as 10.5-point underdogs at FanDuel . That number moved to +11.5 when the trade was announced yesterday. I just don’t see a way where they are going to be able to cover, much less win this game. DT Daron Payne showed up on the injury report today with a foot injury and was listed as questionable. Now he has been ruled out for Sunday night’s home game against the Philadelphia Eagles. NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo is reporting that Payne suffered a significant foot injury that will land him on injured reserve and keep him out for the foreseeable future. DT Daron Payne (foot) has been downgraded to out for Sunday’s game https://t.co/haed2M4NbY — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) October 30, 2026 #Commanders DT Daron Payne suffered a significant foot injury that will knock him out for the foreseeable future and and likely land him on IR, sources tell me and @RapSheet . Crazy. — JP Finlay (@JPFinlayNBCS) October 30, 2026 Daron Payne was drafted in the 1st round of the 2017 draft, and has been a staple on Washington’s defensive line.
