title: Washington Commanders vs Philadelphia Eagles Week 8: Five Questions with Bleeding Green Nation
summary: It’s week 8 of the NFL season and the 1-4-1 Washington Commanders will be facing a 2-5 Eagles team at home at Northwest Stadium on Saturday at 8:20 p.m. ET. The Eagles started the season with two straight wins, but have since lost their last 5 games. I covered the overview of the Eagles in […]
full_text: It’s week 8 of the NFL season and the 1-4-1 Washington Commanders will be facing a 2-5 Eagles team at home at Northwest Stadium on Saturday at 8:20 p.m. ET. The Eagles started the season with two straight wins, but have since lost their last 5 games. I covered the overview of the Eagles in the week 1 matchup article , so I won’t rehash the same points here except for the basics. Instead, I’ll focus on what has changed. On offense, Eagles QB Jalen Hurts will miss the season due to blood clots and is replaced by backup Tanner McKee. McKee is a 3rd-year NFL player who is more of a traditional pocket passer than the athletic Hurts. Although McKee has played well in limited action prior to this year, the Eagles traded for Andy Dalton this past offseason and made him the immediate backup to Hurts. Dalton’s poor play in limited action week 3 led to Dalton being demoted and McKee seeing the field when Hurts was eventually ruled unfit to play, though it’s a reasonable question if the offseason moves may have hurt his confidence. Another big change in the Eagles since week 1 is the fast that almost their entire offensive line has been reconfigured multiple times. RT Lane Johnson retired (replaced by 2026 3rd-round pick Markel Bell), C Cam Jurgens was traded, and LG Landon Dickerson was out with injury and is now back. WRs Devonta Smith and Dontavion Wicks are also out for this game due to injury, leaving a lot of the receiving game in the hands of 2026 1st-round pick Makai Lemon. On defense, the Eagles are healthier, primarily dealing with injury to LB Jihaad Campbell, who has been ruled out of week 8. Despite their health, the Eagles defense has declined precipitously in 2026 to be the 5th-worst pass defense by yards allowed and the 6th-worst rush defense by yards allowed, as well as ranking poorly in advanced stats . One theory behind the defense’s decline is that they are getting beat up from being on the field all the time due to the collapse of the offense. Through Week 7, the Eagles defense has been on the field for 67.3 plays/game , 4th-most in the NFL. Certain players have had a harder time than others, with slot CB Cooper DeJean suffering from a high missed-tackle rate and notable drop in coverage quality . I asked Brandon Lee Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation five questions to better understand the state of the Eagles and what to look for in this game. 1) What has changed for the Eagles since the last time these teams faced off? Let’s exclude the Jalen Hurts situation from this, since it requires a lot of nuance and has been covered elsewhere. Might be more efficient to list what hasn’t changed. BGN alumnus Jimmy Kempski put together an “ Eagles season from hell tracker ” which details all the crazy stuff that’s been going on. In broader strokes, the offense has been really bad and ineffective. These struggles can be explained in part due to Lane Johnson unexpectedly retiring and the Eagles getting hit hard by injuries. But it’s hard to argue the coaching staff has made the most out of the talent they’ve been given to work with. The offense did show some signs of life against the Cowboys in Week 7 … but the Dallas defense is pretty awful, so, it’s hard to know how much of that success will carry over moving forward. The Eagles’ defense, which was supposed to be their biggest strength this season, has underperformed lofty expectations. They’re coming off their worst (or second-worst) performance of the 2026 campaign after getting bullied by the Cowboys on Monday night. The Eagles have poured way too many resources into their defensive front to be as ineffective as they were against Dallas. They didn’t make Dak Prescott look the slightest bit uncomfortable, logging zero quarterback hits. And the Eagles also got shoved around in the run game. It’s hardly hyperbolic to qualify the Eagles as one of the worst teams in the NFL right now. They rank bottom five in DVOA, point differential, and weighted EPA per play on both offense and defense. 2) Will the Eagles be sellers or buyers at the trade deadline or stand pat (and why)? If they make trades, what kind of trades would you foresee? They SHOULD be sellers. This isn’t a season worth salvaging. This isn’t to suggest Howie Roseman should be selling players for merely whatever they can get for them. The price has to be right in each deal. But I expect the Eagles to be receiving offers that will be worth their while. There are different groups of players that the Eagles could be looking to sell. Some are in the no-brainer category in terms of players who are entering contract seasons and don’t figure to be long-term pieces in Philly. Those guys include the likes of Moro Ojomo, Riq Woolen, Dallas Goedert. And then there are bigger names like Saquon Barkley (whose situation could be complicated by injury issues) and Zack Baun. Again, I’d be surprised if the Eagles unload those guys unless the price is simply too good to turn down, as was the case with the Cam Jurgens trade. The Eagles shouldn’t be opposed to buying if there’s value to be had in acquiring a player who projects to be a long-term contributor. But there’s no need for any short-term rentals. 3) Eagles fans have made a lot of Nick Sirianni’s winning percentage, but what does he do to contribute to that winning percentage and how much do you think he deserves credit for it vs roster talent, a great DC, etc? Will he be around next year? In fairness, it is a pretty crazy winning percentage. 9 of the 11 head coaches who currently rank ahead of him are in the Pro Football Hall of Fame. The question you pose is fair. As a Sirianni skeptic, I can struggle to see the value he brings to the table. And I think this season is really bearing out the idea that he’s been heavily carried by elite general managing and a great defensive coordinator. With those two aspects not being as strong this season as they have in the past, the team suddenly looks a lot worse as Sirianni struggles to provide answers to persisting problems. Perhaps I’m underestimating the significance of Sirianni having multiple years on his contract left but I struggle to see him back next year based on Jeffrey Lurie’s precedent of not tolerating offensive struggles. Three of the Eagles’ worst offensive seasons in this century were 2012, 2015, and 2020. What happened after each of those years? The head coach was fired. The Eagles had another one of those very bad offensive years in 2025 … but the team understandably didn’t want to fire their head coach one year after winning the Super Bowl. But is Lurie really going to tolerate another season where the offense is an abject failure? Doesn’t seem likely to me. 4) How much influence does Howie Roseman have beyond traditional GM responsibility of roster construction and cap/contract management? Does he help decide which coordinators to hire, which players to feature, dissect what went wrong or right on gameday, etc? The Eagles are a GM-centric organization. Roseman’s fingerprints are all over this franchise. He definitely has a voice in decisions that are more traditionally left to the head coach. There’s no arguing that this setup hasn’t worked well for the Eagles; they’ve won two Super Bowls and been to three with Roseman as a driving factor. But the configuration does have some drawbacks, as seen in the aftermath of their championship successes. [Editor’s note: this question was somewhat inspired by reading this article on what transpired at the end of the Doug Pederson era .] 5) What is your realistic best-case scenario for the Eagles rest of season and offseason? The best-case scenario is that the Eagles win out! Oh … you said “realistic.” It behooves the Eagles to lose as many games as possible. They shouldn’t (nor won’t) “tank” in terms of players/coaches not trying to win because that’s just not how their incentives work. But the team’s focus should be beyond the 2026 season. They need to sell some players ahead of the trade deadline. They…

title: Ahead of Eagles SNF game, Commanders fans split on trade deadline strategy
summary: In this week’s Reacts survey, we asked Hogs Haven readers two questions regarding where things stand with the burgundy & gold as we exit the bye week. The first question was our weekly pulse check on fan sentiment: Are you confident that the Washington Commanders are headed in the right direction? The second question tackled […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 01: Daron Payne #94 and Chase Young #99 of the Washington Commanders pressure Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles as he throws during the third quarter at Lincoln Financial Field on October 01, 2023 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Tim Nwachukwu/Getty Images) | Getty Images In this week’s Reacts survey , we asked Hogs Haven readers two questions regarding where things stand with the burgundy & gold as we exit the bye week. The first question was our weekly pulse check on fan sentiment: Are you confident that the Washington Commanders are headed in the right direction? The second question tackled the looming November 10th NFL trade deadline, gauging what general manager Adam Peters should do with a 1-4-1 roster that is facing a unique set of circumstances across the division. Here is how Hogs Haven readers voted and what it means heading into Sunday night. Question 1: fan confidence holds steady during the bye week Yes : 22% No : 78% Visit our partners at FanDuel To the surprise of virtually nobody, there was very little movement in confidence this week. With Washington idle in Week 7, fans had neither a frustrating fourth-quarter collapse, nor an invigorating upset to dramatically swing sentiment one way or the other. The modest 4-point dip from last week’s 26% simply reflects the lingering reality of sitting at 1-4-1 after 6 games played. Expect that relative calm to evaporate completely in next week’s survey. With a massive division showdown against the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday Night Football, fan sentiment is primed for a major swing depending on how those 60 minutes unfold under the lights at Northwest Stadium. Question 2: should Adam Peters be active at the trade deadline? Our second prompt asked: What should general manager Adam Peters do ahead of the November 10 trade deadline? The results revealed a fascinating split across the fan base: No, they should be sellers : 29% Yes, I support any good trade : 26% Only if Washington wins weeks 8 & 9 : 18% Yes, but trade nothing more than a Day 3 pick : 12% Do nothing; Adam Peters and Dan Quinn are lame ducks : 9% Yes, but no more than a Day 2 pick : 6% Under ordinary circumstances, a team sitting at 1-4-1 near mid-season would have an open-and-shut case. Standard operating procedure in the NFL dictates that teams 3 games under .500 sell off expiring veteran contracts, accumulate future draft capital, and shift focus toward next season. That reality clearly drives the plurality of our voters, with 29% selecting “No, they should be sellers” as the single most popular individual option. When paired with the 9% who favor standing completely pat, roughly 4 in 10 respondents (38%) want no part of acquiring talent at the deadline. Yet look beneath that plurality, and the broader numbers offer a somewhat different story. Collectively, 62% of fans—roughly 6 in 10 survey respondents—remain open to Peters acquiring players. That includes 26% who endorse any deal that improves the roster, 18% who want to see back-to-back wins over the Eagles and Rams before pulling the trigger, and 12% who are comfortable buying — as long as Peters protects premium capital by dealing only Day 3 picks. Why does a 1-4-1 football team have a majority of its fan base open to buying? The answer lies in the bizarre state of the 2026 NFC East. Through 7 weeks, the division features just one team with 4 wins. Furthermore, Washington’s post-bye schedule eases up considerably compared to the gauntlet faced in September and early October. If the Commanders can string together 3 wins between now and November 12 th (with 2 of those games played ahead of the trade deadline), contending for an NFC East crown remains mathematically possible and practically viable. It can’t be stressed enough, however, that this door remains open only if Washington wins this week vs the Eagles. A victory pulls Washington right back into the division mix while dropping Philadelphia to last place in the NFC East standings. By contrast, a loss would drop the burgundy & gold to 1-5-1, hand them a crippling 3rd divisional loss, and effectively put a pin in any legitimate hopes of competing for the division crown. What the comments say: why the fan base is split 60/40 The community discussion in the comments section of the survey article highlighted the tension reflected in the voting numbers. The ‘do nothing’ (or sell) party On the cautious and selling side of the ledger, commenters stressed the danger of sacrificing future draft assets for short-term fixes. Commenter Henry Foxwell kept it direct: “I don’t want to see us give up any more draft picks! We’re hosting the NFL Draft in April. Let’s keep all of our picks, please.” Others pointed out the risk of acquiring high-priced rentals for a squad still struggling to finish games. EdDC referenced Seattle’s recent trade for guard Quenton Nelson, noting that sending mid-round capital for an impending unrestricted free agent makes little sense when long-term extensions are far from guaranteed: “This is why I did not want the Commanders to rent him for the rest of the season. Surely, Nelson will explore all his options and choose his best fit… That’s not the Commanders, who are struggling to achieve mediocrity and have much building to do.” Commenters like BIGCMR and Rdskn04 took an even harder line toward a full teardown, advocating to sell assets and amass picks for 2027. Of course, with injuries to Terry McLaurin and Daron Payne , the Commanders are rather short of ‘salable assets’ at the moment anyway. The ‘do something’ party On the other side of the debate, respondents who supported acquiring help pointed out the necessity of protecting Jayden Daniels and avoiding an outright surrender of the season. Commenter Barnunn pushed back against perpetual rebuilding cycles, noting that “buyers want to win. sellers want to give up and quit.” For many in the pro-buy camp, the priority isn’t chasing a one-year playoff rental, but utilizing Peters’ cap flexibility to acquire younger pieces who can stick around beyond 2026. PDXskin summarized that dual approach well: “buyer for the long term (younger players in need of scenery change), seller for the short-term (vets on expiring contracts who most likely wont be resigned)” As Alex Rowsey noted, the schedule will make the decision for the front office soon enough: “If we’re still in a position to realistically win the division at the deadline, then yes, go for it and do what you can to win the division. If winning the division is no longer realistic, then sell.” A little of everything: Week 8 preview: Eagles at Commanders All eyes turn to Northwest Stadium this Sunday night as the Commanders host the division rival Philadelphia Eagles on national television. Philadelphia enters the matchup bruised and battered, having dropped 5 straight contests and playing without quarterback Jalen Hurts, leaving Tanner McKee to command the offense. Washington comes off its bye relatively healthy, with Jayden Daniels practicing fully and playing good football. full_text: Commanders receiver Treylon Burks was designated as questionable to play Sunday night’s game against the Philadelphia Eagles due to a foot injury. That’s especially notable for Washington’s first game without Terry McLaurin, who suffered a season-ending torn patellar tendon against the 49ers in a Week 6 loss heading into a bye. While Antonio Williams will see an increased snap count and target share, Burks is the presumptive replacement at the X receiver position. Not having him against the Eagles would be a setback and force the unspectacular Dyami Brown into increased action. Burks was among four Commanders listed as questionable on the official Commanders injury report, which was released on Friday. Tight end John Bates (shoulder), defensive lineman Johnny Newton (pectoral) — he’s technically still on IR — and defensive tackle Daron Payne (foot) are also questionable. Payne showed up on the injury report for the first time on Friday, which is never a good sign and implies that he got hurt during practice. While he isn’t the dominant force he once was, losing Payne for any stretch of time would be a significant blow. Defensive lineman Javon Kinlaw (knee) was ruled out of Sunday night’s game, as expected. The Eagles will be without linebacker Jihad Campbell and receivers Davonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks, though running back Saquon Barkley will be available. full_text: The Washington Commanders finished up their last full practice of the week before they host the Philadelphia Eagles at Northwest Stadium on Sunday Night Football. DT Javon Kinlaw (knee) is the only player that will be ruled out, with other injured players set to get evaluated today to see if they’re good to go for Sunday night. The Commanders hired former head coach Steve Wilks to help on defense, and his role is already increasing from what was originally reported. He was with the team for last week’s Monday night football game in Week 6, and he’ll be on the sidelines with the team. He has commitments to his alma mater App State, and won’t be at every game, but will be assisting DC Daronte Jones this week. Quinn was asked about hiring a part-time coach, and said he has done that himself, but only offensive coaches in Dallas like Brian Schottenheimer and Ben McAdoo. title: Commanders GM Adam Peters talks NFL trade deadline, Antonio Williams
summary: The Colts dealt superstar guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks earlier this week.  The Commanders did not make a play for him.   Washington general manager Adam Peters was clear about that in his weekly (paid) interview with 106.7-FM The Fan on Friday morning. He addressed the NFL trade deadline and several other topics […]
full_text: The Colts dealt superstar guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks earlier this week. The Commanders did not make a play for him. Washington general manager Adam Peters was clear about that in his weekly (paid) interview with 106.7-FM The Fan on Friday morning. He addressed the NFL trade deadline and several other topics during the interview, including receiver Antonio Williams, cornerback Amik Robertson and the state of the Commanders coming out of their bye week. Also, Peters revealed that receiver Terry McLaurin is having Friday surgery to repair a torn patellar tendon. Here are the highlights from that interview – the full session can be found below – as Washington steamrolls into a vital Sunday night matchup with the Philadelphia Eagles. On the NFL trade deadline We’re looking at everything. Any position on our team where we can make our team better for the present of the future, we’re always going to look into that. Whether it’s wide receiver of any other position that you can think of, we’re going to look for us to get better. There aren’t a lot of opportunities to do this. There are times where teams are looking to move on from guys you’re interested in and those are opportunities where you can make a move. On Antonio Williams First and foremost, I want to give a shout out to Terry. He’s having surgery today. For all those who do so, please say a prayer for him. He’s a big part of what we’re doing and what we’ve done. I just want to send him some love here today. Moving forward with Antonio, every single day he does something special in practice that shows you what kind of talent he has, what kind of instinct he has as a receiver. The sky’s the limit for him. With Terry going down, that creates more opportunities for others and people will have to step up. We’re still hoping and expecting that Antonio will do that. He’s definitely capable of that. On the Amik Robertson and his guarantee We went out and signed Amik for a reason, because he’s a straight dawg. He’s a very good player. He has the utmost confidence and has an edge and an attitude and impacts a defense. I love that he’s on our team. Listen, that’s the mindset you want. For sure that’s bulletin board material if you do subscribe to that, but I’ve always said that, if you need bulletin board material to get ready for a division game on Sunday night, then – all the material and motivation – that’s kind of a problem, you know? On Chig Okonkwo We have high hopes for him. He had a slow start because he got hurt, and now we’re seeing what that’s going to look like within our offense. We really haven’t seen the full extent of what he can do within our offense in terms of catching and running. We’re going to continue to give him those opportunities. With Terry down and other guys that have been down, that gives other guys opportunities in terms of Antonio and Chig – and we think we can get even more from Chig. On Steve Wilks When that opportunity came about, it was a no brainer. It’s something we had talked about and it came into fruition. He had some other obligations with (Appalachian State), where he had some commitments. He wasn’t working in the league this year, so we thought it was a great opportunity. We looked into a number of different possibilities for this role and he was the best fit. … Within the short time he has been here he has aquitted himself well, which I knew he would. He has fit in seamlessly. … Having an extra set of hands is always good and we’re thrilled that he’s here.

full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 27: Sonny Styles #52 of the Washington Commanders defends a pass against Jadarian Price #8 of the Seattle Seahawks during the second quarter at Northwest Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 30 October 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Commanders Roundtable No more excuses: Week 8 is a must-win for the Commanders The Commanders’ Most Dangerous Opponent Might Be Themselves Here’s the uncomfortable truth: this matchup has every ingredient for Washington to beat itself. The Eagles’ defense, despite an inconsistent season, has a way of elevating against the Commanders. Jordan Davis is still a dominant interior presence. Jalen Carter has flashed elite-level disruption at times. And there is a very real pattern — backed up by years of history — where Washington’s interior offensive line can’t sustain the protection Daniels needs; the penalties pile up, and a winnable game slips away. They need to limit the self-inflicted mistakes and drive-killers if they want a chance. The bye week was supposed to be about more than rest. Dan Quinn had extra time to address the mental errors — the false starts, the miscommunications, the clock mismanagement that cost them a win outright against the Giants. Over the last three weeks before the break, Washington committed 33 penalties, 16 on offense, including seven false starts. Getting to 2-4-1 with a divisional road win on Sunday night doesn’t fix the season — but it changes the entire conversation. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE ESPN Ranking the best 2026 NFL rookies: Arvell Reese, Denzel Boston, others in top 10 We polled five NFL analysts and reporters — Matt Bowen, Kalyn Kahler, Jeff Legwold, Jordan Reid and Ben Solak — to form a consensus ranking through Week 7. T-1. Sonny Styles, LB, Washington Commanders Stats: 46 tackles, 1 sack, 1 INT, 1 FF Drafted: No. 7 Styles’ speed is what made him a top-10 pick, and he has put it on full display this season. In Washington’s only win , he went stride for stride with Seattle running back Jadarian Price to break up a deep pass. Later in the third quarter, he caught up with tight end Eric Saubert and stripped the ball at the goal line — though Saubert recovered it for a touchdown. (He also had his only interception in that game.) Styles even made a strong debut, trucking Eagles running back Saquon Barkley on his way to sacking quarterback Jalen Hurts. Styles has 13 tackles in Washington’s past two games, which suggests he’s only improving as his rookie year continues. — Kahler To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Last Man Standig (paywall) Commanders 2027: Who stays, who goes and what the defense still needs Get past Sonny Styles and there are more questions than answers with Washington’s defense next season including decisions on pending free agents Daron Payne and Frankie Luvu, and salary-cap Outlook: The 2026 season might mark the end of the line for Payne in Washington. There’s always the chance a new deal with the 2018 first-round pick gets worked out, but players with options generally aren’t keen on taking a pay cut to stay with the same team. And I don’t see Washington — or any team — matching Payne’s $22.5 million average annual salary. Though his pass-rushing stats haven’t popped as hoped, Payne remains a mountain of a man against the run. That’s why he’ll draw interest if Washington becomes a seller ahead of the trade deadline. If Payne goes, Washington has a massive hole to fill. Kinlaw has been fine. But fine enough to justify a $16.9 million cap charge? The bigger question is what this group looks like without both Kinlaw and Payne. Newton’s status as a former second-round pick probably keeps him around for depth. We haven’t seen enough to project tangible upside. He’ll have roughly half a season to show what he’s got after Washington opened his 21-day practice window, approximately 11 weeks following pectoral surgery. Settle’s $9.7 million cap hit makes him a viable restructure candidate. For more from Ben Standig, click here The Athletic (paywall) The Commanders’ first-year coordinators were both risks. When does the payoff arrive? The struggles of these Commanders don’t completely fall at the feet of new offensive coordinator David Blough and new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. But with a game against the Philadelphia Eagles that could alter coaching careers coming up Sunday night, both assistants are being examined. All spring and summer, their plans and strategies sounded interesting. In practice? “We would love for it to be perfect right now,” Blough said Thursday. “We know that’s not the case.” “Inconsistent,” Jones said. This was Quinn’s choice and Quinn’s risk. He stripped former defensive coordinator Joe Whitt Jr. of his play-calling duties during the 2025 season and fired him thereafter, eventually hiring veteran defensive assistant Jones away from the Minnesota Vikings to do a job he hadn’t performed at the NFL level. The organization wanted a more collaborative offensive staff that might design a system that could take some of the burden off quarterback Jayden Daniels, so it moved on from offensive coordinator Kliff Kingsbury and elevated Blough, who began the 2025 season as the assistant quarterbacks coach and was not even four years removed from his career as a backup quarterback. If Quinn had hired and empowered first-year coordinators in Year One of his tenure and the team was 1-4-1 and the on-the-job training was difficult but necessary, fine. But he didn’t. He installed them in Year Three, and not only handed them the keys but allowed them to build the cars from the ground up. What you have, then, is a work in progress on both sides of the ball at a time when the Commanders can’t afford to take baby steps. Through six games, Blough’s offense ranks in the bottom half of the league in both yards per play and points per game. Jones’ defense is ranked 22nd in yards per play and 31st — next-to-last — in points allowed per game. That’s some combination of “meh” and “oh no!” with the season — and therefore the future of Quinn and the entire coaching staff — in the balance. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE On video with a midweek report. Going inside what we heard Wednesday: some numbers that reflect the pace of play and why perhaps Daniels and the O can be helped with more urgency. The pass rush. And more. @ESPNRichmond https://t.co/mbNAXIMLhe — John Keim (@john_keim) October 29, 2026 Commanders Roundtable Dan Quinn (again) explains the addition of Steve Wilks to the Commanders offensive coaching staff Though the initial expectation was Wilks will not expected to be with the team on gameday, Grant Paulsen of 106.7 reported that will change on Sunday night with the veteran coach expected on the sidelines. Wilks joined the Commanders as a part-time assistant through the week where he assists with the defensive game planning under defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. Wilks officially began working with the team ahead of the week six primetime loss against the San Francisco 49ers, though it was a move that was in the works. full_text:
The spooky season is here, and the NFL uniforms are looking scary good in Week 8. The Jacksonville Jaguars and Detroit Lions lead the way as they debut their respective Rivalries combinations. 

 

 Jacksonville's look is nicknamed "Bold City," and the team will wear the uniform against the Indianapolis Colts , who debuted their own "Rivalries" design in Week 3 . The uniform includes a teal-glossed helmet with a gold face mask and "904," Jacksonville's area code, on the front and "Duuuval," the team's rallying cry, on the back. The white jerseys include black numbers and "Jaguars" in cursive. They both feature gold trimming, while the numbers have a teal shadow and jaguar-print pattern. A similar pattern appears on the black pants, which also have a teal stripe that includes gold trim running down the side. One neat detail is the names of Jacksonville neighborhoods hidden within the spots on the pants. 

 Detroit's "Defend the Den" threads will be worn vs. the Minnesota Vikings . The Lions' all-silver combination has various details with a message, including italicized black numbers that lean forward, meant to create the illusion of motion. The shoulder sleeve design of Honolulu blue meeting black mimics the gaze of a lion when it eyes its prey. The same appears as a pant stripe on the uniform's bottom half. And of course, Detroit's iconic car and racing culture are represented. The Honolulu blue lid's Lions decal is in carbon fiber black as a way to connect to that culture.

full_text:
Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season is here. Will Lamar Jackson play against the Bills? Who is going to take home bragging rights in the battle for L.A.? Can Kirk Cousins lead the Raiders past the Jets to snap Las Vegas' four-game skid?

 We're here to get you ready for the action. First, our NFL Nation reporters take you inside the locker room with the best thing they heard this week, and ESPN Research provides a key stat to know. Then, analytics writer Seth Walder makes a bold prediction for each matchup, fantasy analyst Eric Moody shares fantasy football intel and betting analyst Pamela Maldonado hits betting insights for each contest. We also have Football Power Index (FPI) game projections, and Maldonado, Moody and Walder all give us final score picks for every game.

 Let's get into the full Week 8 slate, which culminates with a "Monday Night Football" matchup between the Bears and Seahawks on ESPN . (Game times are Sunday unless otherwise noted, and all odds are via DraftKings.)

 
 Jump to a matchup: 
 BAL-BUF | MIN-DET | IND-JAX 
 ATL-TB | TEN-CIN | ARI-DAL 
 CLE-PIT | LV-NYJ | LAC-LAR 
 KC-DEN | NE-MIA | PHI-WSH 
 CHI-SEA 

 Thursday: CAR-GB 
 Bye: NO , NYG , SF , HOU 

 
 

 What ESPN Analytics says ... 
 

 

 
 

 Ravens (4-3) at Bills (5-1) 
 1 p.m. ET | CBS | BUF -3 (54.5 O/U) 

 What we're hearing on the Ravens:  Coach Jesse Minter had a reason for putting his players in pads for Wednesday's practice. "[It] felt like with the run game that we're getting ready to defend, that we really needed some work in that area," Minter said. Baltimore knows it has to be physical in order to stop Buffalo RB James Cook III , who ranks second in the NFL with 104.5 yards rushing per game. The Ravens haven't allowed 100 yards rushing to a running back in 21 straight games. -- Jamison Hensley 

 What we're hearing on the Bills: QB Josh Allen admitted that playing against Lamar Jackson affects his approach to a game, saying that looking across the sideline and seeing a fellow MVP QB is reason enough that his offense can't ever let up. With the Bills ranking bottom three in the NFL in total defense, scoring defense and passing defense, that's doubly true. But the best news for Allen might be star WR  DJ Moore 's renewed health. Moore, who has been Allen's most dependable field stretcher when healthy, says he's still mad at himself for missing the Bills' past two games but knows the time away helped stabilize his injured shoulder . -- Nick Suss 

 

 Stat to know: The Bills lead the NFL with 14 rushing TDs this season, which is tied with the 2004 Chiefs for the third most by any team in its first six games in the Super Bowl era (since 1966), behind the 1975 Dolphins (16) and 2023 Dolphins (15). -- ESPN Research 

 Bold prediction: The Ravens will intercept Allen on a play-action pass. Baltimore's defense ranks only 18th in EPA allowed per opponent dropback, but it is  first on play-action plays. And the Bills run play-action at the fourth-highest rate in the league. -- Walder 

 Injuries: Ravens | Bills 

 Fantasy nugget:  Moore has struggled to stay healthy this season, but he has been one of Allen's favorite targets when on the field, averaging 1.8 fantasy points per target with a 15.9-yard average depth of target. This game has one of the highest projected totals of the week, and Baltimore has allowed the eighth-most fantasy points per game to WRs. See Week 8 rankings . -- Moody 

 Betting insight: Since 2024, Ravens games have gone over the total 71% of the time (29-12), the NFL's highest over rate. Buffalo scores more points per drive than anyone but also allows the most. With Jackson ( ankle ) set to return, Baltimore can attack that defense through the air. Allen gets his chances against a Ravens defense that just struggled against the Bengals'  Joe Burrow . Both offenses have ways to keep scoring. Read more . -- Maldonado 

 Maldonado's pick: Ravens 31, Bills 28 
 Moody's pick: Bills 31, Ravens 27 
 Walder's pick: Bills 30, Ravens 27 
 FPI prediction: BUF, 61.4% (by an average of 2.9 points)

 

 Matchup must-reads: Ravens list QB Jackson as full participant in practice ... Why the Bills have been historically good, and bad, through six weeks ... Inside the complicated injury history of Ravens' Jackson ... NFL suspends Bills' Gardner-Johnson for one game for spitting 

 
 

 Vikings (6-0) at Lions (4-2) 
 1 p.m. ET | Fox | DET -3 (46.5 O/U) 

 What we're hearing on the Vikings: As well as the Vikings' defense has played, there is widespread conviction within the organization that the offense needs to elevate if the Vikings are going to continue winning during a difficult stretch of their schedule. The Lions lead the league in offensive scoring (28.3 points per game). Can the Vikings match them if necessary? "I know that we're going to need to be the reason why we win some football games this year, offensively making plays in critical moments," coach Kevin O'Connell said. -- Kevin Seifert 

 What we're hearing on the Lions: On paper, the Lions' defense versus the Vikings' offense appears to be weakness versus weakness. Detroit's defense allows a league-high 391 yards per game, and Minnesota has the 29th-ranked total offense (281.7 yards per game), but the Lions allowed a season-low 17 points in Week 7 and aren't underestimating the Vikings in any phase of the game. "Yeah, you could take numbers and throw them out the window because what they're doing is what it takes to win," defensive coordinator  Kelvin Sheppard  said. The Lions might get some wins against the mighty Minnesota defense, because Detroit ranks second in EPA per play against the blitz. But QB Kyler Murray and the Vikings' offense should have success against a Lions defense that ranks 31st in EPA per play. -- Walder 

 

 Injuries: Vikings | Lions

Hockenson could be one of Murray's top targets against his former team. Hockenson has scored at least 13 fantasy points in all three games this season in which he has received five or more targets. Detroit has also allowed the most fantasy points per game to TEs, making Hockenson an excellent option this week. See Week 8 rankings . -- Moody 

 Betting insight: Vikings games are 2-13 over/under in their past 15 games, including five straight games going under. I expect Minnesota to make Goff uncomfortable after sacking him five times in each of their meetings last season. Detroit's defense gives Murray a chance, but he hasn't done much against easier opponents. I'm not counting on him turning this into a back-and-forth game. Read more . -- Maldonado

title: Where the 2026 Vikings rank among worst 6-0 NFL teams ever
summary: Aaron Schatz ranked the worst 6-0 teams ever by DVOA and point differential. Where do the 2026 Vikings land, and what's next for them?
full_text:
Let's start with this: Only good teams go undefeated. It's one thing to win a game or two, but if you're starting 6-0, you're a good team. The Minnesota Vikings are undoubtedly a good team.

 But not all 6-0 teams are created equal. The 1999 Rams beat their first six opponents by an average of 25.7 points. That is dominance. Compare that with this year's Vikings, who have won four of their six games by less than a touchdown.

 So, are the Vikings the "worst" 6-0 team in NFL history? To answer that question, I used my proprietary DVOA (Defense-adjusted Value Over Average) ratings and simple point differential to look at every team that started 6-0 since the move to the 16-game season in 1978.

 The good news for the Vikings is not only are they not the worst 6-0 team in the past 50 years, but that there's a team that was a little worse that won the Super Bowl.

 Here's a look at eight of the worst 6-0 teams of all time, and what history says will happen next.

 

 
 

 8. 2012 Atlanta Falcons 

 DVOA: 18.6% (ninth) 
 Point differential: +58

 The Falcons started the 2012 season 6-0 by feasting on an unsustainable turnover margin. They had 17 takeaways in the first six games and turned the ball over only seven times. The Falcons picked up a 27-3 win over the Chargers, but also four wins by less than a touchdown, including a last-second 55-yard field goal they needed to beat the Raiders, who finished 4-12.

 

 The Falcons were at least balanced in their good-but-not-greatness, however. DVOA ranked them ninth on offense, 11th on defense and 10th on special teams after six games.

 What happened next: The turnover margin was, in fact, unsustainable. In their remaining 10 games, the Falcons had a turnover margin of just plus-3. However, they still went 7-3 over the remainder of the season. An easy schedule that ranked 27th in average DVOA of opponent helped. In the playoffs, the Falcons won a hard-fought battle over the Seahawks 30-28 but then fell to San Francisco 28-24 in the NFC Championship Game when Atlanta's attempted late comeback drive ran out of gas on the 10-yard line.

 
 

 7. 1985 Los Angeles Rams 

 DVOA: 17.8% (eighth) 
 Point differential: +44

 This team was surprisingly similar to this year's Vikings, driven by excellent defense (second in DVOA through six games) and special teams (fourth). Instead of a free agent quarterback from another NFL team, the Rams' offense was led by CFL star Dieter Brock in his only NFL season. Unlike the current Vikings, the Rams were a run-first team with superstar running back Eric Dickerson.

 What happened next: The Rams shut out Kansas City in Week 7 and then stumbled, with a 4-5 record the rest of the way. That still gave them the NFC West title by one game over San Francisco. In the divisional round, the Rams shut out Dallas 20-0. Then, the eventual champion Bears destroyed the Rams 24-0 in the NFC Championship Game, and Brock went 10-for-31 with 66 passing yards.

 

 

 6. 2026 Minnesota Vikings 

 DVOA: 17.5% (sixth) 
 Point differential: +51

 The Vikings have won their first six games in an incredibly imbalanced fashion. They rank 30th in offensive DVOA, ahead of only the 1-6 Titans and 0-6 Chargers. The Vikings also rank second in defensive DVOA, trailing only Seattle (due to opponent adjustments), and first in special teams.

 As I noted earlier, four of Minnesota's wins have been by one score, with the exceptions being their season-opening 39-22 win over Green Bay and a 23-13 victory over New Orleans in Week 5. However, the Vikings lead the league in point differential per game at 8.5, ahead of the 49ers at 8.3.

 

 What happens next: The problem for the Vikings going forward is that offensive performance is more predictive of the future than defensive or special teams' performance. That's the main reason the Vikings rank only 16th in ESPN's forward-looking FPI despite being undefeated. The FPI simulations give the Vikings an average of 11.7 wins this season, with just a 4.7% chance to win the Super Bowl.

 It's worth noting that by average DVOA of opponent, the Vikings have played the second-easiest schedule in the league so far, ahead of only Kansas City. They have the fifth-hardest-rated schedule going forward, including the second-toughest schedule of opposing offenses behind only Tennessee.

 

 

 5. 2000 Minnesota Vikings 

 DVOA: 13.8% (11th) 
 Point differential: +43

 Unlike this year's Vikings, the 2000 edition was driven by offense: Daunte Culpepper, in his first season as an NFL starter, throwing to Randy Moss and Cris Carter. The Vikings ranked fourth in offensive DVOA but 23rd on defense after six games. Five of their six wins came by one possession; the lone exception was a 28-16 win over Chicago, which was 1-5.

 What happened next: The Vikings went 5-5 over their final 10 games, although the final loss to the Packers came with their starters sitting on Christmas Eve. By the end of the season, the Vikings had dropped to 18th in DVOA, exceedingly low for a team with an 11-5 record. The Vikings won their divisional round matchup with the Saints, who were only 15th in DVOA, and then were embarrassed 41-0 by the Giants in the NFC Championship Game.

 

 

 4. 2006 Indianapolis Colts 

 DVOA: 11.8% (ninth) 
 Point differential: +49

 The 2006 Colts were the polar opposite of the 2026 Vikings. After six games, the Colts ranked second in offensive DVOA with Peyton Manning at quarterback but just 22nd on defense and 30th on special teams. Only one of their first six opponents finished the season with a winning record (the 10-6 Jets).

 

 What happened next: The Colts kept winning to start the season 9-0 before they lost to the Cowboys in Week 11. The Colts finished the season 3-3 and finished 12-4. By the end of the regular season, the Colts led the league in offensive DVOA but were 25th on defense and special teams.

 Then, safety Bob Sanders returned from an injury, and the Colts' defense totally flipped the switch. They held Kansas City and Baltimore to fewer than 10 points in the playoffs. They came back from a 15-point halftime deficit to take out the rival Patriots in the AFC Championship Game. Then, the Colts beat the Bears 29-17 to win the Super Bowl. It's hard to imagine that this team provides any guidance on what will happen with the Vikings, because the Colts' powerful offense makes them such a clear contrast.

 
 

 3. 2015 Carolina Panthers 

 DVOA: 11.0% (seventh) 
 Point differential: +52

 The Panthers ranked seventh in DVOA on offense and defense after their 6-0 start. They were an interesting team because they were quite imbalanced on both sides of the ball. They were much better running than passing, but the defense was much better against the pass than the run. Despite the low DVOA, three of their first six wins came by multiple scores.

 What happened next: The Panthers marched through the easiest schedule in the NFL that season, not losing until Week 16 against the Falcons. The Panthers' defense improved, eventually finishing second in the NFL by DVOA. Quarterback Cam Newton was named league MVP. In the playoffs, the Panthers dispatched the Seahawks and Cardinals before a 24-10 loss in Super Bowl 50 to the Broncos. We'll get to Denver in a moment.

 

 

 2. 1983 Dallas Cowboys 

 DVOA: 9.7% (seventh) 
 Point differential: +50

 The Cowboys didn't look bad through their first five games, although their wins were built on a lot of defensive and special teams touchdowns, which tend to be unrepeatable. The Cowboys were only 14th on offensive DVOA but sixth on defense. In Week 6, the Cowboys needed overtime to beat Tampa Bay, which finished the season 2-14, and that's the main reason they rank as one of the two worst 6-0 teams.

 

 What happened next: The Cowboys improved a bit and finished the season fifth in DVOA. They went 6-4 over their final 10 games. Though the first two losses were very close, they were destroyed by Washington (31-10) and San Francisco…

title: Michael Penix Jr. shows he could be Atlanta's QB1
summary: Penix has been mostly above average after 17 games as an NFL starter, and that's really all Atlanta needs him to be.
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. -- All Michael Penix Jr . wanted to do was get back on the field. That was the goal after he suffered a torn left ACL last November.

 In the meantime, the Atlanta Falcons could consider him only a question mark. It was the quarterback's third ACL surgery. He had torn his right ACL twice in college. In 12 career NFL starts, Penix also had not shown quite enough to be considered a sure thing.

 So, the Falcons hedged their bets. They signed veteran Tua Tagovailoa in the offseason after he was released by the Miami Dolphins and stated outright that he would compete with Penix for the starting job.

 Fast-forward seven months and Penix, since his return, is working on turning that question mark into an exclamation point.

 In Week 7, Penix helped lead the Falcons to a 29-20 win over the previously undefeated San Francisco 49ers , who had former Falcons coach Raheem Morris -- the man who helped draft him -- scheming against Penix as defensive coordinator. The performance earned Penix his first NFC Offensive Player of the Week honor.

 "We were down 14-3 and he was great," Falcons offensive coordinator Tommy Rees said. "He was unflappable."

 Atlanta has won three of its five games since Penix came back in Week 3. On Sunday, the Falcons (3-4) have a chance to reach the .500 mark against the NFC South rival Tampa Bay Buccaneers and move into a share of first place.

 "When [Penix] is out there, this is a completely different football team, and I really truly believe that he's a franchise quarterback," Falcons safety Jessie Bates III  said.

 Penix has now started 17 career games, the equivalent of a full season. The raw numbers are not breathtaking, but they are good. Penix has completed 61.5% of his passes for 3,914 yards with 21 touchdown passes and seven interceptions.

 If those numbers were applied to the NFL's 2025 season, Penix would have been eighth in passing yards and tied for 18th in touchdowns. The advanced stats tell a similar story. Since his rookie year, Penix is 17th in both EPA per dropback (0.03) and success rate (45.4%).

 Those numbers don't necessarily jump out as elite. But they do establish a baseline. Penix has been at least as good as the average NFL starter in those 17 career starts.

 This season those numbers have trended upward for the most part. Penix is ninth in ESPN QBR (67.1), 13th in EPA per dropback (0.09) and 19th in success rate (43.9%).

 The Falcons don't need Penix to be the best quarterback in the NFL statistically. They just need him to facilitate things for an offense that has running back Bijan Robinson , wide receiver Drake London and tight end Kyle Pitts Sr . He has achieved that to this point.

 "The goal is to win," Penix said. "That's been the goal from day one: win. We got to win football games, and we got the team to do it. We got the coaches to do it."

 The Falcons will have to make a decision on Penix as early as this coming offseason. He'll be heading into his fourth season, meaning Atlanta must figure out whether it will pick up his fifth-year option.

 The team would love nothing more than for Penix to be, as Bates said, its franchise quarterback. The Falcons have not had one since Matt Ryan was traded in 2022. They also have not made the playoffs or had a winning season since 2017. Winning would go a long way toward solidifying Penix as the Falcons' guy.

 Although Rees notes that Penix still has room to grow, the team's focus is less on his stats and more on its week-to-week game-planning.

 "Mike's preparing the right way," Rees said. "He's really detailed in how he approaches the games. He was able to produce for us on the field. There's still things we want to improve. There's still things that we want to enhance that he's doing, magnify the things that he does really well. I think we're just all hungry for more right now and not really paying too much attention to, hey, this benchmark or this landmark."

 That time will come, though. Probably soon. The good news for Penix is that as long as he stays healthy, he can control his own destiny.

 "I think he's grown a lot as a player and he's been doing a lot of great stuff for the offense, man, and I think he wants to continue to get better, obviously," Robinson said. "But yeah, I think his process has been really good and I'm excited to get to keep playing with him every game coming up. And I know he's excited, too."

title: NFL Week 8 predictions: Upsets, fantasy sleepers, stat lines, TD scorers, more
summary: Tough day coming for Derrick Henry? Browns pulling an upset over the Steelers? Fantasy potential for Geno Smith? Let's predict 15 things for Week 8.﻿
full_text:
Week 8 of the  2026 NFL season is underway after the Packers defeated the Panthers on  Thursday night . But what will happen in the remaining 13 games? We have 15 predictions from our NFL experts.

 First, betting analyst Pamela Maldonado picks two underdogs who could win outright. Then, analytics writer Seth Walder projects stat lines for three players. Fantasy football writer Eric Moody suggests three sleepers, and analyst Matt Bowen predicts three players who will find the end zone. Finally, analyst Ben Solak lays out four wild-card predictions.

 Can the Browns pull off an upset over the Steelers? Could Ravens running back Derrick Henry have a rough stat line against the Bills? Is Jaguars tight end Brenton Strange a sneaky play in fantasy? And will Lions quarterback Jared Goff throw his first interception of the season? Let's make 15 big predictions for the Sunday and Monday action.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Upset picks | Projected stat lines 
 Fantasy sleepers, surprises 
 TD scorers | Other predictions 

 
 

 Maldonado predicts two upsets 
 

 Cleveland Browns +3.5 (+160 moneyline) at Pittsburgh Steelers 

 Pittsburgh's preferred way of scoring is by passing near the goal line, but Cleveland's defense has made those throws difficult this season. That could mean another afternoon of coach Mike McCarthy having to settle for field goals.

 On the other side of the ball, Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson needs to get the ball out quickly and avoid sacks that kill drives. I'm taking the points because Pittsburgh hasn't shown enough offensive consistency to trust it to create separation, and Cleveland is capable of winning outright.

 
 

 

 Baltimore Ravens +3.5 (+142 moneyline) at Buffalo Bills 

 Buffalo allows opponents to convert 45% of third downs, giving quarterback Lamar Jackson chances to extend drives instead of needing big plays every possession. His passing matters here because Buffalo is tougher against the run, and Baltimore's patchwork line hasn't consistently opened holes for running back  Derrick Henry  this season.

 Quarterback  Josh Allen will obviously challenge Baltimore, especially off play-action. But I don't trust Buffalo's defense to protect a lead. Assuming Jackson is healthy enough to play effectively after returning from a high ankle sprain , Baltimore can win this outright.

 

 

 Walder predicts three stat lines 
 

 Alex Highsmith and Nick Herbig , Edges, Pittsburgh Steelers : Combined 2.0 sacks, 5 pressures, 5 tackles

 Neither Highsmith nor Herbig has had the expected start to the season, with a combined 5.0 sacks and, even more surprisingly, below-average pass rush win rates at edge. But this Browns matchup provides an opportunity for each player to get back on track.

 Both mostly play opposite the opponent's left tackle, who in this case is rookie Spencer Fano (15th percentile in pass block win rate). And they'll each be chasing down Watson, who has taken sacks at a huge 9.7% clip in 2026, the second-highest rate among qualified quarterbacks.

 
 

 Laquon Treadwell , WR, Indianapolis Colts : 5 receptions, 61 yards, 1 touchdown

 That's right, it's 2026 and we're talking Laquon Treadwell stat lines! He has a 49 open score in ESPN's receiver scores , which is honestly better than I would have guessed. But that's not why I'm expecting him to have a good performance.

 The main reason is that Jacksonville's  Jarrian Jones  is one of the cornerbacks Treadwell will go against Sunday . Jones has surrendered 1.8 yards per coverage snap this season, per NFL Next Gen Stats, which is second worst among all outside corners with at least 150 coverage snaps. He has been targeted 24% of the time, higher than all other NFL cornerbacks.

 
 

 Derrick Henry , RB, Baltimore Ravens : 16 carries, 48 rushing yards

 Here's a number that caught me off guard from 2026: The Bills' defense ranks first in yards allowed before contact on opponent runs. And another set of numbers that stood out: The Ravens run outside zone at the third-highest rate in the NFL (49%), while the Bills have allowed just 2.8 yards per outside zone run.

 The story around Henry has long been that he's elite once he gets going but not as dangerous if he gets hit early -- even relative to other running backs. In other words, Buffalo might be better equipped to stop the Ravens' run game than anticipated.

 

 

 

 Moody predicts three fantasy sleepers 
 

 Brenton Strange , TE, Jacksonville Jaguars (42.7% rostered) 

 Strange might have slipped through the cracks while Jacksonville was on bye last week. He has had at least seven targets and at least 13 fantasy points in two of his past three games. Now, he faces a Colts defense that has allowed five touchdowns to tight ends this season. For fantasy managers looking to replace  George Kittle or Isaiah Likely during their byes, Strange is worth a look.

 
 

 Geno Smith , QB, New York Jets (22.2%) 

 Smith scored 23.4 fantasy points in a loss to the Dolphins last week , his second-highest total of the season. He now faces his former team , the Raiders, who have allowed the fifth-most fantasy points per game to quarterbacks. With wide receivers Garrett Wilson and Omar Cooper Jr . as Smith's primary playmakers, he is worth considering as a streamer in Week 8.

 
 

 Ryan Flournoy , WR, Dallas Cowboys (18.1%) 

 Flournoy has seen at least four targets and scored at least 11 fantasy points in three consecutive games. The Cowboys have averaged the ninth-most yards per game over that stretch.

 Dallas also has a favorable matchup against a Cardinals defense that has allowed the 12th-most fantasy points per game to wide receivers and the second-most to quarterbacks. Flournoy is on the streaming radar as a flex option in deeper leagues.

 

 

 

 Bowen predicts three touchdown scorers 
 

 Quinshon Judkins , RB, Cleveland Browns 

 Judkins scored two touchdowns in Cleveland's Week 7 win over the Titans , and he has seen at least 17 touches in each of his past four games. Plus, going back to the Browns' Week 4 matchup versus the Steelers, he had 96 total yards and a score on 23 touches. Look for Judkins to play a volume role again Sunday in Pittsburgh , with plenty of opportunities to get in the end zone.

 
 

 Omar Cooper Jr ., WR, New York Jets 

 The rookie out of Indiana can flat out play. In Weeks 6 and 7, his first games back since a Week 1 ankle injury , Cooper had over 100 receiving yards and a touchdown in each game. He can separate vertically with explosive strides, and he has the motion/movement traits to see the ball on the schemed touches.

 I see Cooper continuing his touchdown streak Sunday versus a Raiders defense that has given up 16 receiving touchdowns this season, tied for the second most in the league.

 
 

 Blake Corum , RB, Los Angeles Rams 

 Corum has scored a touchdown in each of the past three weeks, and his role in the Rams' offense is expanding with at least 11 touches in two straight games. With that increase in volume and a matchup against a Chargers defense that has allowed nine rushing touchdowns on the season (tied for second most), Corum should get in the end zone.

 

 

 Solak makes four more predictions 
 

 Colts RB Jonathan Taylor and Jaguars WR Brian Thomas Jr . will say their farewells 

 This AFC South matchup features the top two players on our trade candidate rankings . And I'm predicting that both playmakers will take their final snaps with the teams that drafted them Sunday. With another loss, the Colts could probably move Taylor for two Day 2 picks. Meanwhile, another empty stat line for Thomas leads him to ... the Chiefs ?

 
 
 

 Ravens-Bills will set a 2026 scoring high 

 The highest-scoring game of the 2026 season thus far is the 96-point match between the Bears and Panthers in Week 1 ( 59-37 ) -- that's good enough to rank 12th all-time among NFL regular-season games. I'm feeling a 52-45 overtime game between Buffalo and Baltimore, as both teams should look to throw…

title: Will the Bills' defense stop them from winning a Super Bowl?
summary: Buffalo's defense ranks among the worst in several key statistical areas, including the third-most points allowed.
full_text:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. -- The Buffalo Bills have Super Bowl expectations and an offense good enough to make their goals become reality. But there's legitimate reason to wonder whether the Bills' defense could hold the entire operation back.

 The Bills (5-1) come out of their bye week ranked 30th in points allowed per game (28.5), 31st in yards allowed (386.8), 31st in passing yards allowed (285.8), 27th in third down conversion rates (45%) and last in first downs allowed per game (25.7).

 So as they prepare for their Week 8 game against the Baltimore Ravens ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ), the question of whether the Bills can achieve their goals with the defense playing the way it has through the first six games looms large.

 "Our best football has to be ahead of us, whatever that means," Bills coach Joe Brady said. "You never want to peak early in the season. If you're playing your best football in September, there's a problem. And so how do we continue to improve? How do we continue to learn?

 

 "If we're playing our best football right now, it's not going to look good as the season goes. So I hope better is ahead, and that's what we're chasing."

 For "better" to be ahead, that'll have to start with better in the secondary. Only the Detroit Lions are allowing more passing touchdowns per game than the Bills, and only the Washington Commanders and New Orleans Saints have allowed a higher success rate on pass attempts. The seven defensive backs who've played the most snaps for the Bills combine to allow a passer rating of 107.8, which sits five points better than Bills QB  Josh Allen 's rating -- and he's the front runner for MVP -- this season.

 First-year Bills defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard concedes his defense's woes are mostly to do with the back end. The Bills are top 10 in quarterback pressure rate and quarterback knockdown rate despite games against QBs with well-known quick releases like Matthew Stafford , Kirk Cousins , Jared Goff and C.J. Stroud .

 But while the adjustment to Leonhard's preferred 3-4 scheme has paid off for the rush mechanism, the same can't be said for the coverage apparatus, which is taking a longer time to adjust to Leonhard's favored style of more match coverage and fewer disguises in the back end.

 

 "There's too many times where we look confused when I don't think there's enough options for us to be that confused," Leonhard said.

 To Leonhard, this is less a personnel issue and more a communication issue. It's a matter of trust. Each play, depending on coverage calls, has its own "lead communicator." Once that player makes a decision about what he sees, the other defenders in the back end have to respond and react with their own observations. And the chatter can't end once the ball is snapped.

 "Every person has a different angle of the offense," fifth-year cornerback Christian Benford said. "Everyone should be vocal about what they're seeing. Everyone should be talking pre-snap alerts, post-snap. It'll help us all play as one string."

 The Bills don't have to look far for valid excuses for lacking secondary chemistry. Along with safeties Cole Bishop and Damar Hamlin and fellow cornerbacks Maxwell Hairston and Jordan Hancock , Benford's one of several holdovers from former coach Sean McDermott's regime having to adjust to a new way of doing things under Leonhard.

 Combine that adjustment with the offseason arrivals of rookie Davison Igbinosun and veterans  C.J. Gardner-Johnson  and Dee Alford , offseason injuries that limited Hairston's and Bishop's reps, in-season injuries that have forced Benford, Alford and Hancock to miss time and Gardner-Johnson's ejection and looming suspension for spitting, and it's a wonder any group of five DBs has ever taken more than a couple snaps together.

 But again, this is a team with Super Bowl aspirations and the calendar's about to give way to November. Coming off a bye week, the expectation has to be for early-season communication issues to correct themselves.

 Maybe that's where a familiar voice with an outsider's perspective comes in.

 At the start of the bye week, the Bills signed two-time Pro Bowler  Tre'Davious White  to the practice squad. White started 16 games for the Bills last season but spent the first few months of this season watching the Bills from his couch. He says he got so invested in the Bills' "Monday Night Football" win over the Los Angeles Rams  in Week 5 that he put one of his old helmets on so he could watch the game through his facemask.

 

 White says his role as communicated to him by coaches and front office is to come in and be an extension of the coaching staff. A sounding board. A truth-teller. Someone who tells teammates what he sees through the eyes of a nine-year veteran.

 So what's he seeing now that he's back in the fold?

 "A lot of guys haven't played together," White said. "That comes with a lot of reps and a lot of doing it over and over, a lot of trial and error. As a defensive back, it's all about communication and being on the same page. It's a new defense for everybody. Those are the growing pains of being in a new system.

 "The guys are open to the coaching. They're open to getting better. We know we have to get better to go where we want to be. That's the job."

 This is, as even Brady will admit, a lot of negativity about a team tied with the best record in the AFC. Brady's whole coaching philosophy essentially boils down to the idea that good enough isn't good enough, though.

 Any time he's asked about the defense's struggles he finds a way to spin the narrative toward why he thinks the offense hasn't been good enough either. An offense that, remember, leads the NFL in scoring and yards per play.

 

 So the question at hand is less a matter of whether Brady and Leonhard think the Bills' defense needs to be better -- they obviously do -- and more a matter of whether the buttons they're pressing to ensure things get better end up working.

 As for what those buttons are, veteran pass rusher Bradley Chubb says the message has been "full steam ahead." The emphasis is on communication and trust, sure. But it's less about trust in the sense that players need to believe their teammates know what to do and more about trust in the sense that no one player has to go out of his way to make up for all the deficiencies.

 The unit and the scheme as Leonhard's designed are, in the coaches' opinions, strong enough to course correct.

 "The message was just to put our identity on tape each and every day," Chubb said. "That's on the practice field, that's in the meeting room. Our identity as a team, as a football team, as a defense is to play hard, play fast, play physical, not letting up, no relenting.

 "I feel like if we approach it with that mindset on the field, in the meeting room, on the game field, that's just been a message to go all out."

title: With 10 games left and Ejiro Evero out, what's next for Panthers' defense?
summary: Here are three reasons for optimism as Carolina makes a defensive coordinator change to Todd Wash.
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers (3-4) are moving in a new direction on defense following Friday's firing of defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero .

 On Thursday night, the Panthers lost their second consecutive game, falling 27-19 to the Green Bay Packers  at Lambeau Field.

 With Evero now out of the mix, Carolina will look to improve the league's 23rd-ranked defense, which ranks third worst in the NFL against the run through seven games. During the former coordinator's tenure the unit ranked 30th in scoring defense, 28th in pass rush win rate and last in rushing defense, so there's room for improvement heading into Carolina's final 10 games of the 2026 season.

 

 The Panthers next play Nov. 8 against the visiting Denver Broncos .

 Evero's departure is an opportunity to switch things up under coach Dave Canales entering the midway point of his third season at the helm. And given the outlook of the defense and the main characters in it, there are reasons to believe the group can improve in short order.

 Here are three reasons for optimism as the Panthers change coordinators and switch up their defense entering that Week 9 game:

 

 Todd Wash will be the new voice calling plays on defense 

 Carolina will hand the defense to interim coordinator Todd Wash for the remainder of the season. Wash was one of two assistant coaches on that side of the ball who had a coordinator background, the other being secondary coach Renaldo Hill.

 Wash served as defensive coordinator for the Jacksonville Jaguars from 2016 to 2020. During the 2017 season, Wash oversaw the league's No. 2-ranked defense and helped guide the Jaguars to the AFC Championship Game under coach Doug Marrone. Wash also has a long history with Canales and general manager Dan Morgan. The trio worked together with the Seattle Seahawks from 2011 to 2012, as Wash and Canales were assistants under then-coach Pete Carroll and Morgan worked as a scout in the front office.

 Wash has a background with several different schemes. His hybrid front in Jacksonville mixed and matched odd- and even-front tendencies with four- and three-man trench groups.

 

 Given the Panthers' midseason coordinator switch, Wash might still need to lean on Evero's scheme, but he can toy with the fronts in the weeks ahead. Carolina struggled to rush the passer and stop the run during Evero's tenure, and Wash, a longtime defensive line coach, could try to make the most of his well-paid top-tier talent in the front seven by altering game plans around the base principles of Evero's system so players aren't learning on the fly.

 Defensive linemen Derrick Brown , Bobby Brown III and Tershawn Wharton have scheme versatility. So, too, do outside linebackers  Jaelan Phillips , Patrick Jones II and Princely Umanmielen . Inside linebackers Devin Lloyd and Bobby Okereke can adapt as well if needed.

 

 Injured players will be making their returns 

 The secondary was down to its fifth and sixth cornerbacks Thursday night at Green Bay. Marco Wilson , a practice squad elevation, started the game opposite rookie Will Lee III , who was replaced by Chau Smith-Wade after Lee suffered a hamstring injury midway through the game and was ruled out.

 Starting cornerbacks Jaycee Horn (quad) and Mike Jackson (groin) have been out for their league-mandated four games on injured reserve, and they are eligible to return to action once they are cleared to perform. According to Canales, the pair is making good progress with rehab behind the scenes. Their returns would be huge for the defensive backfield and for the unit overall.

 Phillips, who has missed the past two games with a hamstring injury, should return eventually. It would have been tough for Phillips to return on a short week on Thursday, so the Panthers took it easy on the top pass rusher ahead of their final 10 games. Bobby Brown, who had a hand injury that kept him out of the game at Green Bay, should also be able to return in the weeks ahead.

 

 

 There is some upside with the youthful roster 

 On Thursday, safety Zakee Wheatley (pick No. 151 in the 2026 draft) collected the first interception of his pro career. Rookie linebacker Jackson Kuwatch (pick No. 227) forced his first fumble on special teams.

 The youth movement in Carolina -- and on defense especially -- should be in full force for the weeks ahead. Wheatley, Kuwatch and other members of the 2026 class have flashed, and now Wash -- who is likely auditioning to be retained as coordinator -- can open the floodgates.

 Wash has already overseen a defensive line in which second-round pick Lee Hunter has been a mainstay all season. He has also been unafraid to give a quality role to undrafted lineman Aaron Hall early on. Other up-and-comers such as Kuwatch, Wheatley and safety Lathan Ransom (2025 fourth-round pick) could benefit from the switch in perspective from Evero to Wash.

 The Panthers' front office has invested draft picks in those players -- along with Smith-Wade and Umanmielen -- and with Wash getting the interim tag, the new playcaller could try to spotlight the youth over some of Evero's favorites down the stretch.

title: 2027 NFL draft order projections for Round 1, chances for top pick, more
summary: ESPN's Football Power Index projects the 2027 NFL draft order for Round 1, complete with each team's chances to pick in the top five, in the top 10 and at No. 1.
full_text:
The 2027 NFL draft is still months away, but with the 2026 season underway, we're starting to track pick order in Round 1. Which teams are in position to add elite prospects in the top 10 next April? What about the top five ... or even at No. 1?

 What follows is not the current draft order based on records. It is a projection of what ESPN's Football Power Index thinks the order ultimately will be by the end of the season. Each week during the season, the FPI projects the draft order by simulating the remainder of the season 10,000 times. Game probabilities are based primarily on the model's team ratings and game locations. The draft order is determined by the records the model projects for each team after 17 games, as well as each team's average draft position across the simulations.

 So where do things stand? Here are the full sortable projections, complete with each team's chances to pick in the top five, in the top 10 and at No. 1.

 
 See more on the NFL draft 

 
 

 First-round picks that have been traded: 

 
 The Chicago Bears ' selection was dealt to the Tennessee Titans in the Jeffery Simmons trade . 
 The Green Bay Packers ' selection was dealt to the Dallas Cowboys in the Micah Parsons trade . 
 The Indianapolis Colts ' selection was dealt to the New York Jets in the Sauce Gardner trade . 
 The Los Angeles Rams ' selection was dealt to the Cleveland Browns in the Myles Garrett trade . 
 The better of Dallas' two selections (either its own pick or the Packers' original pick) was dealt to the Jets in the Quinnen Williams trade .

title: Joe Burrow's trust makes Tee Higgins level up for Bengals
summary: No receiver in the NFL has been better on tight window throws this season than the Bengals' Tee Higgins.
full_text:
CINCINNATI -- When Tee Higgins sat alongside Ja'Marr Chase to ink their nine-figure contract extensions with the Cincinnati Bengals , the expenditures seemed like a luxury.

 The two wide receivers' contracts totaled $276 million, a lot of money to commit to one position group. But over the past two seasons, they have given the Bengals their money's worth.

 Chase has been a two-time All-Pro selection and is on the verge of being the most decorated receiver in franchise history. Higgins has been no slouch, either. Especially this season.

 Through seven weeks, Higgins has been one of the NFL's most productive receivers. And as Higgins gets deeper into his career, this season has reinforced his standing on one of the league's most dynamic offenses.

 "We're going to keep feeding him," said quarterback Joe Burrow , who added that getting the ball to Chase is also a top priority. "But the way that Tee's playing right now, it's hard not to throw his way."

 Entering Sunday's game against the Tennessee Titans (1 p.m. ET, CBS), Higgins is fourth in the NFL in receiving yards per game (95.2). The seventh-year player is on pace for easily the best season of his career.

 The value of what the 6-4, 220-pound Higgins brings to the offense has been apparent since the Bengals took him in the second round of the 2020 draft. And that specific style of receiver -- a tall, long player who can win on the outside -- is clearly something the Bengals favor. This year, Cincinnati used a fourth-round pick on 6-3, 218-pound wide receiver Colbie Young , someone Burrow said has the "same archetype as Tee."

 But Higgins has proved this season why he has often been referred to as a "1B" option alongside Chase and is one of the league's best receivers in his own right.

 According to Next Gen Stats, Higgins has been one of the top receivers on tight window throws. When a ball has arrived with less than a yard of separation, Higgins has a league-high 7.1 expected points added on catches in those situations. He has also caught six of nine targets into tight windows for 99 yards, one touchdown and no interceptions.

 "When you're Joe Burrow and the ball's got to leave your hand, knowing that he's going to go get it and at the very least he's going to go protect it is a powerful thing," Bengals offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher said.

 Sometimes Burrow has made up his mind long before most quarterbacks think about raising their arms to throw. For example, Burrow hit Higgins for a 19-yard completion against Baltimore in a look that seems absurd on tape. When Burrow started his throwing motion, Higgins was still several yards behind Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey . But Burrow trusted that he and Higgins were on the same page and fired the ball into the vacant space in the middle of the field.

 "If it was somebody else, maybe I don't make that throw," Burrow said. "But I trust Tee and I know Tee's going to see exactly what I'm seeing and go and get that thing."

 Throughout this career, Higgins has remained as understated as possible, which is another reason why he's a good fit alongside Chase.

 When Higgins spoke after the win in Baltimore on Sunday, he was quick to deflect any praise.

 "Whether the ball was coming my way or not, I'm just happy we got the win," he said in the locker room.

 But if anyone knows why Higgins has been so good this season, it's his potential understudy. When Young, Cincinnati's rookie receiver, was in high school in Binghamton, New York, he went to a camp at Clemson ahead of Higgins' last year in college. From there, he started watching tape and studied what made Higgins a great receiver.

 Now, Young is getting to see it daily. He pointed to the work ethic Higgins and Chase displayed in the months leading up to the season, from showing up to voluntary workouts to working together in Miami in the summer.

 Said Young: "Everything they do in offseason leading up to here is showing up."
